member of the commission. − mr president, it would be fair to say that the negotiations of the eu-mercosur association agreement have not made the progress the european commission would have liked. for sure we have done good work since resuming negotiations in 2010 at the request of mercosur itself. however, so far these negotiations have mainly focused on the normative part of the agreement, that is to say the ground rules and principles that should provide the basis for commitments between both sides to open up their respective markets. now these are very important issues and we have achieved some valuable progress on several chapters, for instance on rules of origin and services investment. however, the negotiations have not yet gone into the heart of the matter, namely on the additional access that we have to give to each other for industrial and agricultural products, services, investments and public procurement through the reduction of tariffs or the dismantling of other barriers. it is clear that the current approach has reached its limits as recognised by both sides at the end of the last negotiation round. the eu has argued that the best way to make progress now would be though an exchange of market access offers on goods, services and investments and public procurement. but so far mercosur has been unable to agree internally and to respond to us on how to move towards an exchange of market access offers. i would first want to discuss this with us at the highest level. that is why i will participate next week in a meeting with mercosur counterparts at the celac-eu summit in santiago de chile on 26 january 2013. we must bear in mind that the internal situation of mercosur is rather complex and this is not without consequences to the negotiations. first there is the question of who is in and who is out of mercosur. the current suspension of paraguay, the slow accession of venezuela and future enlargement to bolivia, might complicate or delay further work though not decisively in our view. if the necessary strong political will is present in mercosur, solutions can be found. secondly, there is an increasing tendency in parts of mercosur to adopt protectionist measures which may cast certain doubts on the likelihood and of political will which could be mustered to open markets. i will use the opportunity of the forthcoming ministerial meeting in santiago de chile to take stock of the situation and engage with mercosur partners in a way so that we all agree on what is needed in order to move negotiations forward and instruct our negotiators accordingly. in spite of the difficulties, the eu remains committed to negotiate a balanced, ambitious and comprehensive agreement with mercosur. such an agreement could generate very considerable gains for both regions. in times of crisis we need to ensure new sources of growth for eu citizens and businesses. rest assured that parliament will be informed of further developments. i have in preparation of the summit meeting in santiago discussed the matter with colleagues in the region and our feeling is that, yes, they have difficulties in coming to offers; they are probably not going to do it within a fortnight, but they are also anxious not to put an end to the negotiations because they see the political consequences of this. but i think they have to make up their mind. either they engage in free trade negotiations – and it will not be easy for us either, you know, to put forward offers – or they take the protectionist route. but they have to choose. you cannot have them both and the european union in the coming weeks, months, will have to choose what to do. are we going to continue pressing, pushing, waiting? or are we going to take action before the wto? it is obvious for a number of measures and regulations that have been made by a number of member states of mercosur – especially argentina, but not limited to argentina by the way – that sooner or later we have to choose our service as well. so we are close i believe to a decisive moment but i think on the other hand that we should try to get to a reasonable understanding and to make progress in this summit meeting next week. of course, if you ask me to do so i will report on that meeting as soon as possible.

mr president, commissioner, the european union and mercosur must promote and develop their bilateral relations. and of course both are interested in improving trade, no doubt. but what i think we should bear in mind very carefully is the impact of a greater opening of the community market to imports of agricultural products from these countries, especially in the beef, chicken and citrus sectors. the 2011 impact study, commissioned by the commission's directorate-general for agriculture, did not hide the impact that acceptance of the requests made by the mercosur countries in the agricultural chapter could have. according to that study, agricultural income in the union would suffer a fall that would vary from one member state to another, but in total, it was estimated that thirty-three thousand jobs would be lost across europe. it should also be borne in mind that the forecasts of the agricultural organizations are much more alarmist and pessimistic than those made by the european commission. i do not think that we are living in a time when we can increase imports from third countries in sectors such as beef, citrus and chicken without demanding clear reciprocal measures. the consequences of an agreement with mercosur would be in addition to those arising from the reform of the common agricultural policy which we are now negotiating.

the rapporteur, mrs schleicher, has made a number of points which i would like to stress. when the people's group asked me to draw up this report, i knew that i had a major challenge: to amend a regulation, posei, which is a vital instrument for the outermost regions of the union and for the citizens who live in those regions, at a time of particular economic difficulties. it was necessary to draw up a report which, while maintaining all the positive aspects of the previous regulation, would tackle the task of adapting it to the present circumstances; it was necessary to seek a balance between all the sectors to which it was addressed, while promoting local production, maintaining the unique landscape of our islands, promoting transparency, seeking the effectiveness of the programmes, contributing to the maintenance of employment by increasing the possibilities for growth, and all this in a complicated situation. we are all suffering from the terrible economic crisis in the european union. but it is precisely the outermost regions that are among the most affected. the canary islands, for example, have only one in two young people in work, and the overall unemployment rate is already over one third of the working population. the crisis is affecting the most remote and isolated areas of the continent, and the regulation, which has been negotiated with the council of ministers of the european union and the commission, provides a small respite by maintaining and strengthening as far as possible european support measures for these regions. i am pleased that in the tripartite negotiations we have been able to agree on the achievement of our main priorities, which allows us to send a message of hope. it also implies a tangible recognition of the economic value of a sector which is emblematic for many of these areas, such as the banana sector, which is the motor of rural development in many territories where the possibilities for diversification are very limited. the aid granted to this sector comes at a time when producers need more than ever guarantees to maintain an adequate level of competitiveness vis-à-vis imports from third countries. the amended regulation also takes account of the need for diversification of production, including this objective as one of the essential objectives which member states must henceforth respect when drawing up their programmes. the european parliament has also managed to include an unprecedented clause requiring the european commission to carry out impact studies on these regions when negotiating trade agreements with third countries or following agrarian reforms. i would also like to stress that the agreement reached enshrines the spirit of solidarity that exists between the outermost regions by promoting trade between them. a significant part of the posei programmes is intended to ensure the supply of these areas, which are characterized by a strong dependence on external supply. the agreement contains some changes to the special supply arrangements, while introducing the principle that these arrangements must not cause any damage to local production. it also reinforces the principle that products from third countries must comply with veterinary and plant health safety standards equivalent to those required of european producers. as regards the financing sheet, it is true that we wanted it to be increased, although we were very aware of the difficulties involved. we were able to lower our legitimate and justified claims to reach an agreement acceptable to all: the maintenance of the financial statement without linking it to other programmes. finally, i would point out that the agreement reached provides for the commission to study the functioning of posei in 2013 and to present a report on it, which could be followed, if necessary, by legislative proposals. it is a report which should examine the effectiveness of this aid scheme and the decisions taken under the common agricultural policy. flexibility, agility, transparency and less red tape are the key elements of this reform.

mr president, commissioner, minister, we have reached the key point in the reform process of the common fisheries policy. and it is time to ask ourselves whether this is the reform we were hoping for and, above all, whether it is the reform of all and for all. when we look at the reform work, we find ourselves faced with a proposal which was originally intended to be somewhat ambitious and balanced. it called for fish stocks to be brought up to sustainable exploitation levels, proposed extending multinational fishing plans to all fish stocks in the european union, and banned the odious practice of discards. all these obligations were facilitated by the flexibility afforded by regionalisation. on the other hand, and in line with the europe 2020 strategy, business growth was encouraged by establishing a system of transferable fishing concessions, for a long period of time, through which the industry could be able to plan its economic activity in the medium and long term, facilitating investments, increasing its competitiveness and making it independent of subsidies, also increasing its responsibility and reducing discards. however, today it seems clear that much of this ambition has been lost along the way. the reform we have negotiated so far is intended to be particularly focused on the environmental aspect. and i think, despite some issues, it's a challenge that we all accept. i will not go into the details of the rules, we all want to ban it, but we also want to make it feasible. i sincerely believe that the success of this reform will be determined by the regionalisation model we finally design. and finally, i conclude by answering the questions i asked at the beginning: this is not the reform that was sought, and today it is not the reform of all, nor for all. i hope that during the tripartite dialogues we will be able to make progress towards this. as chairman of the committee on fisheries, i will not give up on the cfp for all.

a regional basis in the future, and the way in which our stocks are managed – whether by regionalisation, whether by msy and whether we look at biomass or mortality in measuring that, whether it is in writing. − in favour. the programme of options specific to the remote and insular nature of the outermost regions (posei) was set up in 1991 to provide support for the french overseas departments and was extended the following year to cover the outermost portuguese and spanish regions. nine regions are currently covered by the programme, namely: guadeloupe, french guyana, martinique, réunion, saint-barthélemy and saint-martin in france; the azores and madeira in portugal; and the canary islands in spain. a tenth region, the french overseas department of mayotte, is currently scheduled for inclusion under the scheme. the ep is in favour of the competent authorities continuing to have a wide margin of flexibility in managing programmes since it is at regional level that measures can be adapted most effectively to meet real needs. this flexibility should be guaranteed, as should increased consultation with the sectors concerned.

in writing. − smes are the backbone of the european economy. there are 23 million smes within the european union and they represent the 99% of businesses. but these are difficult times for them. the economic situation has provoked a demand decrease leading to a reduction of industrial activity and creating problems in accessing finance. therefore, and taking into account their heterogeneity across europe, approaches to assisting them should be equally diverse. these approaches may be regulated by the small business act, which member states have committed themselves to implementing together with the commission. for this reason i support the resolution.
the rapporteur. - mr president, commissioners, ladies and gentlemen, first of all i would like to thank the alternative rapporteurs. the report before us is the product of a large majority, obtained thanks to the generosity of all, which has allowed for a broad consensus. the labour and social situation has worsened during 2012 and the forecasts for 2013 are pessimistic. over the past 12 months, the number of unemployed has increased by two million and has reached the level of 25 million unemployed in the european union. indicators point to a trend towards higher levels and deeper forms of poverty and social exclusion, with an increase in employed poverty and social polarization in many member states. this situation calls for urgent measures to prevent further unemployment and social problems. we therefore believe that the following is necessary. first, a greater commitment to achieving the objectives of the europe 2020 strategy. commitments made by member states and their implementation during 2012 have been insufficient. member states should make the necessary commitments to achieve this objective in their national reform programmes. another point is that we must achieve a budgetary balance that ensures the sustainability of public finances and our welfare system. however, it should also be stressed that this balance must be achieved through fiscal consolidation which does not jeopardise the potential for future growth and job creation and which takes account of the specific situation of each country. growth and job creation must also be the highest priority above other considerations. member states should adopt all necessary structural reforms, including: reform of labour taxation, which incentivises employment; promote and support self-employment and start-ups; improve the business environment; facilitate access to finance for smes; regularise informal and undeclared work in employment; reform labour markets to make them more flexible, dynamic and inclusive; and modernise wage-setting systems to match productivity developments; and exploit the high employment potential of sectors such as the green economy, health and social care and ict to create jobs. youth unemployment is also one of the major problems facing the european union and should be one of its highest priorities. we have reflected this in the report and have put forward proposals which should be adopted without further delay. in this respect, the rapid implementation of youth guarantee schemes, but with the corresponding funding, is key. another important point is the increase in poverty and social exclusion. the solution of these problems must be a central element of national and european union social policy programmes. member states should implement integrated active inclusion strategies and make new commitments to address this situation, in particular in relation to poverty among the employed population, poverty among people with limited or no links to the labour market and poverty among older people. i shall not say more because of the limited time available, and i simply hope that the council and the commission will take note of the report which we have adopted by a large majority.
president-in-office of the council. − mr president, i agree with the previous contributions that this is a critical time for europe and, in that context, i very much welcome this opportunity to discuss with parliament the european semester. this is a really vital tool for helping us to address the current economic challenges that we face, and it is a high priority for the irish presidency. recalling our presidency’s focus on stability, growth and jobs, we see an effective semester process, along with the banking union proposals, as an integral part of securing stability in our union. this particular semester is, of course, only the third such exercise. it began with the publication of the commission’s annual growth survey last november, and it will now be for the irish presidency, working together with the president of the european council, to ensure that it is completed successfully and contributes to delivering on the wider objectives under the europe 2020 strategy. our key objective as the presidency will be to ensure that all relevant council formations work in a coordinated and consistent manner towards a thorough preparation of both the march and the june european councils. the european semester is, of course, not an end in itself. it is a coordination tool to help us reach a number of policy goals, in particular the five headline targets set in the europe 2020 strategy for smart, sustainable and inclusive growth. the fact that the european semester is primarily a means to an end is important. we cannot simply agree on policy guidance and then assume that our task is done. the semester has to be implemented in the member states and by the member states. this is the only way that it will produce concrete results, even if we have to accept that these will sometimes take time. the focus on implementation is all the more relevant as the whole semester exercise becomes regular and more familiar. there is wide agreement on the current priorities, which have not changed from last year. following the publication by the commission of its annual growth survey, the european council has confirmed the five priorities. these are differentiated growth-friendly fiscal consolidation, restoring lending to the economy, growth and competitiveness, unemployment and the social consequences of the crisis, and modernising public administration. i know that this parliament has been following this exercise particularly closely, and that it has consistently insisted on the need, in such a wide-ranging exercise, for policy coherence. the irish presidency is adopting an inclusive approach which draws on the views of many different council configurations. environment, telecommunications and transport ministers have already addressed the semester in their december meetings. their debates point to the need for a better integration of environmental and climate policies into economic decision-making, a strengthening of both the implementation and enforcement of the digital agenda and a willingness to exploit fully the various synergies between telecommunications, transport and energy. the ecofin council had an initial discussion on the annual growth survey on 22 january and will now prepare its response. several ministers reiterated that there is no contradiction between growth and consolidation. work will continue, in particular, on restoring normal lending to the economy. the needs of smes, non-bank financing, and the impact on stability are among the issues which need to be addressed. work is continuing. the epsco, education, energy and competitiveness councils will debate the european semester in february. based on their input, as well as that already received from other council configurations, the presidency will put together a synthesis report which will constitute a basis for policy guidance which is due to be adopted by the spring european council. i cannot, of course, predict now what will be the key messages of this report, but i can say that we will focus on the key topics, and will not avoid – where necessary – more controversial issues, such as structural unemployment, poverty or europe’s leadership in the area of technological development. i want also at this point to underline the importance of the contribution of the single market to this year’s exercise. we are very pleased that the commission has presented – for the first time – a report on the state of the single market in the context of the 2013 annual growth survey. this is a particular priority for the irish presidency. we very much hope, working together with parliament, to make swift progress on the remaining files of the single market act i, as well as to take forward work on the single market act ii. the issue of single market governance is an issue of considerable importance to the council and indeed to this house. the presidency welcomes very much the contribution of the committee on the internal market and consumer protection, and particularly mr schwab’s report before us today, to the debate on how we might improve governance to facilitate the speedy and effective implementation of single market legislation, particularly in the services area. i congratulate this parliament on the close interest that it has taken in the european semester. i welcome the draft report from ms ferreira, on which it is due to vote tomorrow. many of parliament’s priorities correspond to those of the council and of this presidency. an obvious example is the youth guarantee burden that the european productive economy has to carry in order to sustain our social model, our cherished way of living. we need to reverse this downward trend. we can reverse it provided that we continue along the path of reform; not reform for its own sake, but reform for the sake of sustainable growth and job creation. what should be done to drive job creation and productivity? that is the environmental objectives without hampering job creation and competitiveness. all of these policies on growth will be reflected in the country-specific recommendations of this year’s european semester, and i trust that the member states will continue this work in their national reform programmes. furthermore, we need to pursue consistent fiscal consolidation. public debt in the european union has risen from around 60% of gdp before the crisis to around 90% next year. it is at that level of 90% that public debt becomes a drag on growth. thus there is really no alternative to pursuing smart and consistent fiscal consolidation. public finances in the european union are improving, and confidence is therefore growing. we can see the impact of the reinforced economic governance, thanks in no small part to the six-pack. that is why it is essential to stay on the path of reform. making real progress on our policy agenda by making effective use of the european semester will be a crucial test of europe’s credibility. in this context let me make a final point which is very much of common interest. you are well aware that the adoption of the two-pack is a necessary foundation for rebuilding for sustainable growth and job creation. to this end, i very much look forward to having a constructive and productive debate with you here today.

because when you once again present us with an increasingly optimistic future before this parliament, when you tell us that we are gradually emerging from the crisis and achieving our objectives, without giving a single explanation of what has happened so far, without making a single self-critical analysis of what has happened so far in the european union as a whole, i simply think that your words have no credibility and, moreover, that all you do is to push millions of citizens to think that the commission does not work for them. because, of course, commissioner, this is not the first strategy that has been put before us in this parliament: it is the third time that the commission has used the same strategy, that it has promised us economic forecasts that it has been correcting quarter after quarter, year after year, and which are therefore being systematically breached. does the commissioner not think that instead of revising the economic forecasts, the underlying strategy of the commission to ensure that these economic forecasts are met should be revised? does mr rehn not think it would be more appropriate, rather than correcting those forecasts, to change some things politically? i will give you some alternatives: the first, as i say, is to make deficit reduction timetables compatible with economic growth and job creation. there are studies which tell us that, simply by speeding up the timetable for reducing the deficit, we could save 85 billion euros a year. not the 100 billion promised in july over seven years, of which we have not yet seen anything, but 85 billion real euros per year to, for example, strengthen the youth employment guarantee fund in a vigorous, european and sufficiently funded way, and not that marketing ploy which the commission proposed to us a few months ago and which has been reduced to a mere recommendation, without any financial or budgetary guarantee. another alternative is to get down from the political arrogance in which they seem to be framed and to recognize that there are divergent fiscal multipliers: how is it going to be the same today to reduce one point of public expenditure in greece or spain as in germany, france or italy? of course, within the european union there are different countries with better economic accounts, where greater efforts can be made from the point of view of austerity, but it is also true that today, in some countries, these excessive austerity efforts are killing us economically and suffocating us socially. they are pushing the citizens to the depths of despair. and of course they also keep their word: stop demanding that the member states, through their national reform programmes, do what the commission and the european council are committed to do: fiscal union, banking union and budgetary coordination. and of course, do not talk to us about competitiveness at any price, because competitiveness at the cost of lowering wage costs and the cost of pensions; competitiveness at the cost of the lack of protection of citizens, who are left without collective agreements; competitiveness at the cost of dismantling our european social model, mr commissioner, competitiveness at any price, for this this parliamentary group does not count. answer to a "blue card" question. mr bokros, if you are referring to the price, to the cost of the risk premium that our country, spain, has today, i would say that it could be lower if, as i said before, the commitments made by the european council in july had been implemented within the time limits, and in particular with regard to the banking union. but as regards the policy of self-sufficiency - which, i do not deny, must be implemented in our country and in the rest of the euro area - i believe that it must be implemented within different time limits from those set by the european commission today, because in spain, after making an effort of several points of gdp in cuts in public spending, the reduction of the deficit is not going to be the foreseeable one, which was being negotiated with the commission. in other words, the more public spending cuts we make, the more difficult it is for us to meet the deficit targets set by the european commission, and all we get is despair.
madam president, we are faced with a report, the schwab report, which is important and well-constructed, because both some states and certain associations of businessmen constantly denounce the existence of administrative obstacles, of different regulations and of obstacles which prevent the existence of the single european market. many examples could be given here now. i will mention only two: there are large supermarkets which have been denounced because they require that the meat they sell for sausages be of national origin; or biomass pellets, which have to comply with different regulations in each member state. this parliament must push for the destruction of all these barriers and walls which fragment the markets. let us not forget that the single market is the seed that has given rise to the european union, in accordance with the teachings of the founding fathers. moreover, despite the many difficulties that the european union always faces, we must continue to build it and to move forward, to quote what humphrey bogart says to ingrid bergman in the film casablanca: 'we will always have the internal market'.
madam president, commissioner, minister creighton, the european semester is an opportunity to identify the strengths and weaknesses of our system and to make clear what our road map is. and it's especially important at a time when building trust is paramount. parliament, as the institution representing the european citizens, has an obligation to make its position clear. in this case, we must begin to set the tone for much-needed economic growth, which is essential to tackling a worrying level of unemployment, especially youth unemployment. i agree with commissioner olli rehn that we need a strong policy and industrial base in europe. and i hope that the trade policy that commissioner de gucht is designing will be in line with this need. i would also like to call for accountability. we are playing a very big game here: our future and that of future generations. but i would also like to appeal to us not to fall into the false debate between austerity and growth. they're two sides of the same coin. we must be firm and deliver on the fiscal consolidation targets, but we must also be open to the possibility of making those targets more flexible and adapting them to the current economic reality and the present economic needs, as already set out in the six-pack. the european parliament must ensure and monitor that this is done, creating the environment of trust mentioned above, which is so necessary to overcome the crisis.
mr president, in the context of the european semester, we have to continue with deep reforms and fiscal consolidation. the euro zone debt is not the us debt, and we cannot print money as the americans do. in spain, the central government has imposed public deficit targets on the regions that make no economic sense. a 0.7% gdp target for regions is totally unfair. regions provide public health, education and welfare state services. at the same time, the spanish central government continues to build high-speed trains and increase military spending. this year, spain is allowed to have a 4.5% deficit that should be fairly shared between central and regional governments, as the european parliament voted last month in the public finances report. however, the spanish central government wants to keep 85% of the margin allowed by the european commission, even though the central government represents only 50% of total public expenditure in spain. i have a question for commissioner rehn. do you think that spain’s public deficit target is fairly shared between the different levels of government?
the commission has already made a number of proposals in this area. this reflects the importance which parliament attaches to the european semester, and i hope that the spring european council will take parliament's recommendations into account. i am convinced that mrs creighton will be our first advocate in that european council. i also thank the commissioner for his contributions, who has stayed until the end of the debate. the european semester is a very important step in the improvement of the european union's economic governance, but transparency and democratic legitimacy must be key points in this process. the national parliaments and the european parliament still play a very limited role in its elaboration. mr mann said that, and he's right. if we want european citizens to understand and support the measures agreed in this semester, it is necessary that parliaments, together with the social partners and civil society, have a say in the report's priorities. the next few months are going to be difficult, as the economy is still showing signs of great weakness and the social impact of the crisis is still very severe. at a time when financial stability has improved substantially, although there are still significant risks that we must not relax, the return to growth and job creation must be a priority. it is important to strike the right balance between budgetary consolidation and economic measures on the one hand and social policy and measures for growth and employment on the other. in view of the still persistent deficits and high debt levels, continued fiscal consolidation programmes are necessary to ensure the sustainability of public finances, but must be carried out in a differentiated, proportionate and growth-friendly manner. the committee on employment and social affairs has succeeded in reaching a result which has the support of the majority of its members and which we hope the european council will take note of.
mr president, i would like to say here that i fully support the policy of this document, and i think that the commission must be strongly supported in the new conference. however, i would like to support amendments nos 13, 47 and 49, in which we believe that there should be an exception for polar bears, namely the one requested by the government of canada and the one requested by the inuit. why would you do that? because canada has had an agreement with the inuit for years, regulating their hunting and their way of life - since the inuit live off bears - and they have managed to multiply the number of bears in addition to practicing their traditional customs. then, we must reward those governments and those peoples who have been able to maintain their traditions and live together while multiplying and preserving the species. i think the world of prohibition has to be able to recognize the exception. an exception in which the coexistence between animals and people constitutes for a people its way of life, its way of feeding. this is an intangible cultural heritage which is based on the preservation of the natural environment, on the protection of animals, and which must be able to coexist with those harsh measures which we should even increase in the case of those who are hunting bears in russia and establishing an illegal market, or animals in africa, and who are destroying the system we have inherited from our ancestors. i therefore ask, and i repeat, that amendments nos 13, 47 and 49 be supported, since the canadian government has protected this exception and has demonstrated its viability.

in writing. − in favour. with the accession of bulgaria and romania, the european union enlarged its customs union. consequently, the eu was obliged under wto rules (article xxiv(6) of gatt 1994) to enter into negotiations with wto members having negotiating rights in the schedules of any of the acceding members for the purpose of agreeing on a mutually satisfactory compensatory adjustment to offset the increase in bound duties and the resulting meaningful losses. such adjustment is due if the adoption of the eu’s external tariff regime results in an increase in tariffs beyond the level for which the acceding country has bound itself at the wto, whilst taking ‘due account of reductions of duties on the same tariff line made by other constituents of the customs union upon its formation’, as required by paragraph 6 of article xxiv.
in writing. - i am voting in favour of the report because the member states need clear guidelines for employment policies now more than ever. unemployment is the main problem in europe, especially in countries like mine, which had an average unemployment rate of over 25% in 2012 and in the case of youth unemployment this percentage is over 55%. the spanish socialists took a first step last week by proposing to the main political forces and trade unions an employment pact to begin taking action as soon as possible to remedy this unsustainable situation. however, the eu cannot leave member states to act alone in the face of this difficulty which is putting thousands of families at risk of poverty and social exclusion. we need to send clear guidelines to the 27 and it also has to be the eu that ensures the creation of skilled and trained employment and a workforce that is responsive to changes in the economic and labour markets.
in writing. − we started the week with a new record number of unemployed in spain: 4.98 million people are unemployed, an increase of 132 055 people compared to december 2012. despite the high unemployment rate, active employment policies to help the unemployed worker find a job again that is appropriate to his or her abilities are almost non-existent. the amount of the active policies has decreased by 21% compared to 2011. in addition to requiring increased budgetary allocation, these policies need to be modernised, taking inspiration from successful unemployment activation models such as those implemented in sweden, austria or denmark. i therefore welcome the commission's proposal that the guidelines for the employment policies of the member states set out in the annex to the council decision of 21 october 2010 be maintained during the current year and taken into account by the member states in their respective employment policies. those guidelines are essential for the achievement of the objectives of the europe 2020 strategy.
in writing. the aim of this directive is to impose deadlines on member states for deciding on the prices and reimbursements of medicinal products, with the aim of removing barriers to access to the pharmaceutical market. the aim of the commission's legislative proposal is not to guarantee that people living in the european union have access to universal health care and medicines free of charge, but rather to impose a series of requirements on member states in terms of prices and reimbursements which, under the laudable pretext of ensuring transparency, will in practice mean a subordination to the interests of the pharmaceutical industry and the possibility for the latter to unilaterally impose its prices on the states. i therefore voted against this report, in order to oppose the further dismantling, increasing cost and precariousness of public health services in the european union.
in writing. abstention from voting. the commission proposal was not acceptable, as it was largely dominated by the interests of the pharmaceutical industries. in particular, it was intended to shorten the time taken for the examination of the pricing of new medicinal products, which would considerably weaken the quality of the evaluations of these products. the proposed directive would also have weakened the tasks of the health technology assessment (hta) institutions and the high health authority, which assesses in particular the medical service provided by medicinal products. the commission is also proposing to extend the scope of the directive to include the protection of the environment and the environmentally friendly use of energy. so we decided not to.
madam president, i voted in favour of this report because i share its objectives and i think it is a step forward compared to what we have, but i hope that in the negotiations which are now opening some improvements will be considered which, incomprehensibly, have not been included in this procedure. we want a more sustainable sector, but we do not yet have a european map that precisely identifies where there is over-fishing and over-capacity. this would help us to control and correct the fisheries precisely. it would also help us to achieve maximum sustainable yield within a set timeframe that we share. we have not adopted a definition of small-scale fishing today. the amendments voted on excluded fleets and professionals using sustainable fishing gear and techniques such as 'hunting' or 'live bait', which favour the quality of fresh and processed product. i hope that, like regionalisation, it will allow policies to be adapted to this diversity of the sector. finally, i would say that we must achieve a more progressive and open system of governance. the sector, practitioners, associations, processors, consumers and scientific institutions need to play a more active and transparent role in the cfp, which also needs long-term management plans based on scientific data. i hope we can achieve that in the future.
in writing. - i voted in favour of the rodust report on the european parliament's position on the reform of the common fisheries policy and against the commission's initial proposal. while all sectors agree on the recognition of the major shortcomings of the common fisheries policy and the need for reform of the policy, the commission's good intentions do not end the centralisation of the cfp and will lead to further liberalisation of the sector. on the contrary, the cfp should take account of the complex and diverse reality of fisheries in the eu and define, in addition to environmental objectives, a clear support for the socioeconomic dimension of the cfp. i have supported the european parliament's position, however, because it improves on the commission's position in its desire to ensure the livelihood of the marine environment through sustainable fishing. it opposes transferable fishing concessions and proposes a gradual ban on discards, the promotion of maximum sustainable yield and the need for long-term planning to restore fish stocks by 2020.
in writing. - i voted yes. the european fleet is oversized and has consequently overfished to dramatic limits. we had to correct the course and we did. parliament has finally voted today in favour of a sustainable eu fisheries policy. in particular, parliament has backed plans to require sustainable fishing levels from 2015 onwards, to allow fish stocks to be restored to abundant levels by 2020. the key is that more fish in the sea means more profitable fishing for fishermen, so this will benefit both the environment and the sector. the commission has also voted to put an end to the nonsense of mass waste, stressing that the priority is to promote more selective arts. the greens also welcome the fact that parliament has supported our proposal to make fishing rights conditional on the guarantee of better social and environmental practices, with a view to rewarding the more sustainable artisanal fishing sector. the overall result is therefore certainly positive.
in writing. - i voted against the reform of the common fisheries policy (cfp) because it has not been designed to take account of the different territorial realities, nor has it been adapted to the great differences between the segments of the european fleet. i believe that the implementation of the cfp in 2014 will have harmful consequences for the mediterranean fisheries and aquaculture sector, and especially for the catalan fisheries sector. this cfp establishes a policy which focuses on the characteristics of the high and very high-altitude fleet, and does not include the coastal or littoral fleet characteristic of the mediterranean sea. the proposed discard method does not take into account the unique discard problem in each fishery. without prejudice to progress on environmental aspects, it is necessary to take account of economic, environmental and social aspects in an equitable manner. the sector is currently facing a high price disparity and high production costs. for this reason, it is not appropriate to reserve the structural funds exclusively for environmental protection policies and actions, in order to ensure the development and maintenance of the fisheries and aquaculture sector.

in writing. - i voted in favour of this report, which supports a legislative proposal aimed at reducing the noise level of motor vehicles. the text includes measures such as the creation of a noise labelling system for new vehicles, while setting lower noise limits for new passenger and freight vehicles. it also sets standards for the manufacture of hybrid and electric vehicles that must be audible to pedestrians. measures such as those provided for in this regulation are very necessary, as continuous exposure to high levels of noise caused by traffic causes health problems for the urban population, and it is estimated that more than half of the eu's urban population is exposed to noise levels above 55 decibels. i have therefore supported this proposal which contains measures aimed at protecting public health as well as the environment.

in writing. − in favour. the technical conservation measures for fishery resources are among the key elements of a regionalised approach to fisheries management and come on top of the annual/biannual decisions on catch possibilities. technical measures lay down the rules on fishing zones and fishing gear used, as opposed to quantities (fishing effort) and/or catches (tacs and quotas) authorised. technical conservation measures are rules, which our fishermen throughout the european union must follow on a daily basis when undertaking a fishing expedition in order to ensure that however and wherever fishing activity is carried out, it is done so in a sustainable manner. the measures relate to minimum landing sizes, minimum net mesh sizes, zones and closed seasons, limiting by-catch, the criteria to use more selective fishing gears and measures designed to protect the marine environment and have thus a considerable impact in achieving the objectives of the common fisheries policy (cfp).

the next item on the agenda is the debate on the basis of the council and commission statements on a peaceful solution to the kurdish question in turkey.
president-in-office of the council. − mr president, honourable members, this afternoon’s debate on the kurdish issue takes place only a few weeks after the terrible and brutal killings of three pkk activists in paris last month. we share parliament’s profound shock at those killings but they serve to underline to all of us the importance of settling the kurdish issue; that is in the interests of all concerned. a settlement would play a vital role in helping ensure the security and the stability of the region. the kurdish issue also has important implications for eu enlargement, which is a key policy of the european union and a particular priority for the irish presidency. it is important for turkey’s accession process, and is raised regularly in the context of the accession negotiations. as a candidate country, turkey has to meet the copenhagen political criteria, including the stability of institutions guaranteeing democracy, the rule of law, human rights and respect for and protection of minorities. the kurdish issue has implications in all of these areas, but also extends to related areas, such as cultural rights and socio-economic considerations. the eu’s accession partnership with turkey includes a number of priorities which particularly relate to the situation in the east and south-east of the country. these highlight the need for turkey to develop a comprehensive approach to reducing regional disparities. this means improving the situation in the region so as to enhance the economic, social and cultural opportunities for all turkish citizens including those of kurdish origin. clearly, the kurdish issue constitutes a major and longstanding challenge for turkey. continuing terrorist attacks make it harder to reach a solution. i wish to reiterate here that the eu and its member states strongly condemn terrorism in all forms and are working closely with turkey to combat the terrorist threat. the pkk is listed by the eu as a terrorist organisation. within the eu, the pkk is involved mainly in fund-raising, including through criminal activity. this has led to arrests in a number of european countries. the eu and its member states are also active in cooperating with turkey in combating terrorism and associated criminal activities via counter-terrorism training and information exchange. whilst much of these activities are devoted specifically to addressing the pkk, we are also working closely with turkey in tackling all forms of terrorism, including in the global counter-terrorism forum in which the eu and turkey co-chair the working group on the horn of africa region. whilst the eu has consistently condemned pkk terrorism, it is clear that the wider kurdish issue can only be addressed through a peaceful, comprehensive and sustainable solution. it is a conflict which has claimed far too many victims over the course of three decades and which has created a climate of instability and profound mistrust. against this background, the eu is fully supportive of the ongoing talks between the turkish government and the pkk aimed at ending the conflict. this is a significant new initiative which offers a positive perspective for the future. we welcome these moves, and we call on both sides to use this opportunity to make real progress. we also welcome the fact that there is cross-party support, and backing from civil society, for this initiative. there is a clear indication that there is a real desire for peace. we will continue to encourage an approach which is inclusive and broad-based. this is essential if it is to have a chance of success. a successful outcome would also play a crucial role in turkey’s own reform process. it would help encourage further political and constitutional reform which is important for turkey’s eu accession. mr president, honourable members, this is a courageous initiative and we need to recognise it as such. we are at the start of what is likely to be a lengthy process. not everybody is committed to it succeeding. indeed there will always be some who attempt to derail such a process for their own misguided ends. the killings in paris remind us tragically that there is strong opposition to any negotiations from some quarters. but such events cannot be allowed to derail negotiations. our own experience closer to home shows that any peace process requires both courage and commitment. we should therefore give our full and unequivocal support to this initiative. i am sure that members here will join me in offering their own support.
member of the commission. − mr president, throughout the years we have consistently underlined that finding a solution to the kurdish issue and to all the problems in the south-east of turkey requires the widest possible contribution of all democratic forces and an open and frank public discussion that should be conducted in full respect of the basic fundamental freedoms. that is why the ongoing kurdish issue. the fact that the process has met the support of all stakeholders, notably the opposition, and has been welcomed by important parts of turkish society gives us more reasons to be optimistic and to believe that the process is truly result-oriented. a successful outcome would not only put an end to a conflict that has claimed tens of thousands of lives over the past three judicial reform package, actually addressing the key problems related to freedom of expression and other fundamental rights; and it would facilitate the redrafting of the constitution with respect to the rights of citizenship. in this regard, a solution of this issue would have a strong impact on the accession process of turkey as such, as it would further consolidate the role of the european development and the political and cultural rights of citizens of kurdish origin.
i would like to express the support of our group for the process of dialogue which has been opened in turkey for a peaceful solution to the kurdish question. it is probably the most difficult and complex challenge that is presented in the process of modernisation and democratisation of turkey. it has very powerful and determined adversaries, both inside and outside turkey. and we have seen, with the murder of the three kurdish militants in paris a few days ago, how far these adversaries can go. however, all turkish problems have a kurdish dimension at their core, and it is very difficult to imagine a situation of democratic stability in turkey without the kurdish question being resolved or being put on a path to a solution. that is why we welcome the start of these talks. we believe that the first objective should be to put an end to violence, terrorism and hostilities. we heard what pkk leader abdullah öcalan said to the kurdish parliamentarians and representatives who visited him in prison on 3 january: "the era of violence is behind us". i wish it were! but concrete confidence-building measures must be taken, and the first of these is, without a doubt, an end to violence. then there is a path, which will be complex and difficult, of political reform, to deal with the kurdish question in turkey. i once read an article by a historian who said that if national problems were ever to be solved in the world, the kurdish problem would be the last to be solved. i hope not! but it is a very complex problem. but there are things to do. there is the opportunity for a new constitution that recognises and protects the linguistic rights of the kurds in the media, in school and in the courts; there is the possibility of a fairer interpretation of the anti-terrorism laws in turkey, so that they do not mean a repressive protection against the affirmation of the cultural identity of the kurds; and there is an electoral reform pending that could allow the expression of their position in democratic institutions.

president-in-office of the council, on behalf of the vice-president of the commission/high representative of the union for foreign affairs and security policy. − mr president, it is my pleasure to address you on behalf of the high representative and to outline the eu’s work programme for the upcoming 22nd session of the un human rights council. fully committed to a strong and effective multilateral human rights system, the eu is becoming ever more active in bringing its human rights priorities to this important multilateral forum, and thereby asserting that the united nations matters. the awarding of the 2012 nobel peace prize to the eu recognised our sustained effort to promote and protect human rights worldwide. we take this as an encouragement to work even harder for this cause. the adoption of the eu human rights strategy and action plan and the appointment of stavros lambrinidis as eu special representative for human rights will help us to deliver on this task. throughout the last year, the un human rights council in geneva has again demonstrated its willingness to respond to the calls of millions of citizens for their rights. we have warmly supported the fact that more and more partners and other regional groups bring specific country situations to the human rights council. turning to the 22nd session, let me first underline that the acute crisis in syria must stay high on the agenda of the human rights council. the recent report of the un international commission of inquiry presents an alarming account of the increasingly sectarian nature of the conflict in that country. strongly committed to the fight against impunity, the eu will insist on the need for accountability for the serious human rights violations, including crimes under international law, perpetrated in syria. moreover, the mandate of the commission should be renewed further, and we will push for a one-year extension to give it a solid basis for its work. the eu will also continue to draw the attention of the international community to the persistent critical human rights situation in the democratic people’s republic of korea (dprk), which requires greater scrutiny. together with japan, the eu will present a resolution proposing the creation of an independent investigative mechanism, or commission of inquiry, in support of the special rapporteur, whose mandate should be renewed. the eu will also reinforce its calls on the government of the dprk urgently to improve the human rights situation in the country. remaining seriously concerned by the worrying human rights situation in iran, the eu will actively work for the extension of the mandate of the un special rapporteur, and press to increase the backing for this mandate through outreach and demarches, building on the recent work in the context of the un general assembly resolution on iran. the eu believes that the issues of accountability and reconciliation in sri lanka should stay on the agenda of the hrc, and is moreover concerned about recent attacks on the independence of the judiciary in that country. looking ahead, as last year, a key eu priority for the june session of the council will be the situation of human rights in belarus, which continues to give rise to grave concern. the reports of human rights abuses in mali are of increasing concern and should be discussed, based on the report of the high commissioner for human rights, which focuses on the north of the country. the eu also appeals to the authorities to immediately investigate the reported human rights abuses and to hold those responsible for human rights violations to account. the eu calls for a rapid mobilisation and deployment of human rights observers. moreover, in this or subsequent sessions, the eu will support the call for the council to address the state of human rights in bahrain, the democratic republic of the congo, eritrea, south sudan and sudan. we will also closely follow developments in the human rights situation in north africa, russia and in some of the central asian countries. it is heartening that one country regularly on the agenda of the council in recent years, myanmar/burma, is a source of good news. this is due in no small part to the tireless international attention and our collective support to the many democracy and human rights activists in the country, including nobel peace and sakharov price laureate daw aung san suu kyi. the eu welcomes the cooperation with myanmar/burma which led to the consensual adoption of a general assembly resolution in december 2012, reflecting the important recent progress in the country while also recognising remaining human rights concerns, for instance the remaining political prisoners as well as the situation of the rohinga in rakhine state and in the ethnic areas. the resolution, which will be presented at the 22nd session of the human rights council, will encourage further reforms. i am now turning to the thematic priorities of the eu. given our conviction that freedom of religion or belief is an inalienable human right and an essential pillar of safe and prosperous societies, the eu will again present a resolution on freedom of religion or belief. this year we will also aim at the consensual extension of a strong, independent mandate for the special rapporteur. high representative/vice-president ashton is concerned by the increasing number of acts of discrimination based on religion or belief across the world, and has condemned on several occasions the violence against persons belonging to religious minorities everywhere in the world. gender equality and women’s empowerment is also a core priority for the high representative, and we are very supportive of the holding of a high-level event celebrating the power of empowered women on 26 february. as in previous years, together with latin american and caribbean countries, the eu will devote particular attention to the rights of the child, this year focusing on the right to the enjoyment by children of the highest attainable standard of health. throughout the year, the eu will also work with a cross-regional group of like-minded partners to continue to keep the issue of discrimination and violence against individuals based on their sexual orientation and gender identity on the agenda of the united nations, in follow-up to the landmark resolution of the human rights council session of june 2011 and the successful cross-regional activities in new york. the eu will advocate freedom of association and assembly and pay special attention to the promotion and protection of freedom of expression, notably through the internet. we all recognise that the work of human rights defenders and civil society organisations is essential for democratic societies, and restrictions placed on ngo activities are a growing concern in many countries. the eu regularly defends the role of civil society representatives and human rights activists in the un context. we are strongly concerned by reports of threats and reprisals affecting those who cooperate with un human rights mechanisms, including the human rights council and its special procedures, and we strongly condemn and speak out against such incidents. as the full realisation of human rights is important for achieving sustainable development, the eu is pleased that the ‘mainstreaming panel’ of the human rights council will this year discuss the integration of human rights into the post-2015 global development agenda which the eu will advocate in line with the corresponding commitment in the human rights action plan. the march session of the human rights council is also a worldwide gathering of human rights activists. the human rights council is a crucial body for the promotion of universal human rights standards and the un’s main forum affording worldwide scrutiny of the human rights performance of all countries. with this in mind, the eu reaffirms its attachment to the universal periodic review (upr) and calls upon all un member states to effectively cooperate with this universal mechanism. the eu is also making every effort to preserve the universality of the upr and continues to appeal to israel to resume cooperation with the human rights council more broadly and with the office of the high commissioner. in closing, allow me to emphasise that the unwavering support of this house is very important for the success of our efforts. we look forward to the participation of a european parliament delegation in the high-level opening week of the council. we count on your engagement and continued vigilance to push us further to make good on our commitments. we know that you will use contacts with your counterparts in support of our initiatives and advocate new issues that should be taken up by the international community.

in writing. − in favour. recent projections anticipate that immigration could slow down the process of population ageing. these projections are based on the assumption that several eu member states will loosen their immigration restrictions in order to prevent major imbalances in the old-age dependency ratio. without migration, the eu population will decline from 495 million to 416 million people by 2060 while the old-age dependency ratio will increase from 25 to 62%. with migration, the population could grow to 506 million people while the old-age dependency ratio will ‘just’ increase to 53%. more or less simultaneous with the above-mentioned significant population changes, the european union is currently experiencing a spatial transition: it is indeed becoming highly urbanised, rapidly so. in the 1970s, 60% of the population lived in urban areas, while today already 80% of the population is urbanised. an additional increase of 5% is expected by 2030.
in writing. the 16th conference of the parties to the convention on international trade in endangered species of wild fauna and flora (cites) will take place in bangkok from 3 to 14 march. cites regulates international trade in species, i.e. the export, re-export and import of live and dead animals, plants and derivatives. it has a twofold benefit: it protects endangered species while increasing european protection against invasive species. illegal trade in animals and plants is a serious threat to many species. despite increased monitoring and surveillance, it continues to persist. in this connection, the european parliament resolution, which i supported, considers that the eu should intensify its efforts to prevent the poaching of elephants and rhinos, and should also aim to include several species of sharks in the list of animals whose trade should be controlled and raise awareness of poaching of polar bears. in addition, the text addresses a number of concerns about the transparency of the decision-making process or the financing of the objectives of cites, hence my vote in favour.
in writing. − in favour. the european union should play a leading role in the protection of endangered species, by taking an active part in negotiations on the cites convention and promoting the removal of loopholes that aggravate the situation. i thus deplore the fact that there have been allegations about member states and european union citizens being used as intermediaries in the transfer of rhino horn into vietnam or other countries where it has high commercial value and thereby stimulating demand and further poaching.
in writing. - i was unable to vote in favour of the guidelines for the 2014 budget - other than the commission - because i am seriously concerned about the current limitations on members' ability to speak in our respective languages, both in official meetings and when tabled amendments. in addition, the delay in obtaining access to parliamentary working documents translated into certain languages means that the official languages are being placed in a hierarchical order which violates the principle of multilingualism and degrades democratic rights when we carry out our parliamentary activities. moreover, the cuts in the budget for translation and interpretation mean job losses in the sector and a degradation of the services and working conditions of professionals, so i would like to reiterate our defence of the principle of stable recruitment and to express my disagreement with the reduction of the amounts allocated to translation and interpretation.
in writing. - as regards amendment no 17, i agree with the single seat, as i have said on several occasions through my own initiatives, but i am voting against it because there are already various initiatives under way in this respect; and we must await their conclusions.
i agree, mr president, that the european authorities must be more active in promoting corporate social responsibility, with a stronger and clearer legal framework. we also need a transnational level to achieve meaning and effectiveness. i also believe that this way of doing business must be a sign of european identity and a commercial asset in an environment where the installation of values such as those we need in economic activity requires the involvement of entrepreneurs, workers, consumers and public authorities. and i speak on a global level because sometimes the first bad behaviour is by european companies in other parts of the world. but, likewise, i think that the extension of this way of being and doing has two keys that i would like to see reflected. the first is that it is essential to think small in order to involve and complement global action. once again, the initiative close to businesses and individuals calls for a role, guarantees that commitment and augurs us success. the second is that social economics carries in its dna a way of doing things that by definition fits into this concept. i therefore believe that the social economy needs and deserves further regulatory recognition at european level and can play a leading role in social responsibility throughout the productive fabric.
in writing. − in favour. our group succeeded in convincing the epp rapporteur to explicitly call on the commission to propose a legislative proposal on the transparency of the social and environmental information provided by companies. our sources reassured us that the commission has actually already drafted a proposal for a directive, which should be presented right after the plenary vote. the legal affairs committee will claim primary responsibility for the directive.
in writing. − corporate social responsibility (csr) is a concept whereby companies integrate social and environmental concerns in their business operations and in their interaction with their stakeholders in a voluntary basis, and can bring benefits both for enterprises and society. we must take greater account of social and environmental considerations, and the lowest price may no longer be used as an award criterion. although some progress has been made, some companies have not yet integrated csr behaviour within their core strategies. therefore, i support this report which aims to encourage companies to become more involved in csr.
in writing. - while the report expresses concern about the precariousness of the world of work, the violation of trade union rights, the increase in human rights violations and the destruction of the environment, concerns which i share, i could not vote in favour of the report, since it does not propose any binding measures for companies to fulfil their social responsibility. the socialist rapporteur, mr howitt, supports the commission's proposal in its communication 'a new eu strategy 2011-2014 on corporate social responsibility' and considers that it is more appropriate to promote voluntary cooperation between companies, trade unions, non-governmental organisations and international institutions than to apply rules which require companies to apply codes of conduct on social, labour and environmental matters which exist as principles but are not usually translated into practice. i have therefore not been able to support this short report, as i believe that the current approach to corporate social responsibility is insufficient and that binding measures should be promoted as well as public investment programmes and a higher taxation of capital.
in writing. − abstention. the report is the newest element of a constantly weakening yearly exercise of the employment committee writing a report on corporate social responsibility. the result of an s&d rapporteur negotiating only with his epp (and alde) counterparts is a weak, almost empty report based on a cheap deal of big political groups agreeing on not mentioning the words mandatory, control mechanism, binding, regulation or anything similar in the text (in exchange for not mentioning voluntary either). on the other hand, it contains an indirect reference to extraterritorial jurisdiction in the most extreme cases of human or labour rights violation. our amendments on binding csr provisions or reference to a potential regulation have been rejected.
in writing. − in favour. vat fraud costs the eu and national budgets several billion euro every year. in some serious cases, vast sums are lost within a very short timeframe, due to the speed at which fraud schemes evolve nowadays. for example, between june 2008 and december 2009, an estimated eur 5 billion was lost as a result of vat fraud in greenhouse gas emission allowances.

member of the commission. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the commission has already made a number of proposals. after the terrible chain of events, with the earthquakes, the tsunami and the floods, which not only caused thousands of deaths and billions of dollars in damage to cities, communities and infrastructure, but also had a catastrophic effect on the nuclear power stations, we very quickly launched the european stress test: a stress test which should not be a light stress test, i.e. not be used from the outset to confirm that everything is fine in europe, but which, on the contrary, should not trigger an automatic shutdown, but which should be, if possible, a sober assessment of the technical safety of our 135 nuclear power stations in the european union. this stress test is carried out in three stages: first by the owners and users of nuclear power stations, then by the national regulators who are responsible for this by law, and then with peer reviews at european level, with for the first time a fellow austrian in germany, a german in france, a frenchman in the czech republic being part of a team to check the safety technology in the nuclear power stations of the european union. ukraine, armenia, switzerland and russia were closely involved, which means that we have also achieved some things for the security review outside the european union. one person's stress test wasn't severe enough, the other's was far too severe. i'm sure i didn't make any new friends in paris, london and prague, quite the opposite! the results are in and we will take further action on that basis. firstly, we have agreed with the national regulators that national action plans are to be drawn up. what do the member states, what do the regulators, what do the governments want to do next on the basis of the findings of the stress tests in the member states? the action plans are available, are being evaluated by us and will lead to the necessary retrofitting measures. we expect an average of up to 200 million euros more sensible and necessary investment per nuclear power plant. this will cost all nuclear power stations in europe between eur 15 and 25 billion but it will be a sensible, well-managed cost . we have been asked by the european council to continue the nuclear safety directive, not in 2014, but now, and we are happy to do so. i shall go to the commission in april and then, at the end of april, i shall present to the public how we intend to reform the nuclear safety directive, what new material conditions we intend to insert into it, what findings from the stress test we believe are appropriate for european safety legislation. i hope that this is still in time to examine this commission proposal in parliament before the european elections and the campaign before them, that is, if possible in the second half of the year, to obtain your support and then to obtain a majority in favour in the council. let's not kid ourselves. the council's willingness to accept a continuation of the nuclear safety directive is very muted. many member states do not really want europe to set safety standards, they see this yes or no to nuclear power as a full competence of their government, parliament, regulator and not the european level. i believe, however, that in other areas of life - transport, food regulations - we are right to have european standards which serve the citizen, and that nuclear energy also needs a european safety framework and strict material requirements at european level. you asked, madam president, how we feel about compulsory insurance. we will be proposing binding rules during the year on how to ensure protection for victims, how to make insurance compulsory for potential victims. we are thus taking as a starting point the very different systems which exist at national level and are seeking to develop a european framework on the basis of what has been achieved in the member states. we have some more exciting questions to answer. i'll give you an example: the colleague in charge is joaquín almunia. we shall be able to discuss the exciting question of whether our european competition law and our european state aid law allow for certain price guarantees for new nuclear power stations. i am not dealing with this subject purely on my own initiative, but there are very specific proposals for a new market design. market design is going to be the buzzword of 2013, i promise you that! the british government, for whom i have great respect, wishes to make the following request. the commission is proposing to introduce a price guarantee for both gas and nuclear power stations that it is selling, so that anyone who invests in a new nuclear power station in the uk will be guaranteed a feed-in tariff for up to 30 years. if the market price were below this tariff, the difference to the guaranteed price would be financed from the english state budget. the proposal from mr cameron. i'm not the nuclear safety directive will be successfully completed in the second half of this year with you and the council.
