mr president, i see the negotiations on a trade and investment partnership as a historic opportunity to strengthen the relationship between the european union and the united states. in previous resolutions, this parliament had already called for these negotiations to be launched. we now have a unique opportunity to inject new dynamism into this relationship. this is a new dynamism which is very convenient at a time of deep economic crisis on both sides of the atlantic. a new dynamism is also opportune politically, because many believe that the transatlantic relationship could lose momentum because of the united states' turn towards asia. a new dynamism when many consider that what we call the west is losing its leadership role in a multipolar world in which the brics are the ones growing, especially china. a new dynamism, commissioner, which will boost world trade, since the negotiation of this agreement will probably help to accelerate various trade negotiations which are now stalled. the agreement also opens up a wider atlantic perspective, given the free trade agreements that the european union and the united states have or will soon have with other american countries, including mexico, canada, the central american countries, colombia, peru and chile. a new eu-us agreement could lead, with the necessary adjustments, to a very large free trade area including all the above countries. in short, a large triangular area encompassing the european union, the united states and canada and several latin american countries. in addition to the positive effect on the bilateral relationship, the agreement will have a wider atlantic dimension, to which must be added its beneficial global repercussions due to its inevitable global projection, as elmar brok has mentioned earlier.
mr president, if this important transatlantic agreement is successful, the two great economic blocs of the world will constitute the largest free trade and investment area that has ever existed. the european council in brussels on 14 and 15 december adopted a resolution on the situation in the middle east. efforts will be made to eliminate tariffs and open up the respective markets to investment, services and public procurement. in addition, efforts will be made to harmonise standards and requirements for the marketing of goods and services. the latter is a key strategic component. it should be noted that the world economy is increasingly moving from the atlantic to the pacific, which is of particular concern to europe, which may be relegated to a secondary position on the world economic stage. this transatlantic agreement will guarantee the european union a position on the world economic stage. there is a general political will to move forward swiftly and decisively, as the necessary conditions for a firm commitment by both sides have never been met before. but we can't fool ourselves, because the road will certainly not be easy. during the negotiations, the european union must take account of and be mindful of the particular sensitivity of certain areas, such as agriculture, and ensure that the fundamental values of neither party are affected. in view of this, it is time for the european union to act with high vision and ambition. this is a unique opportunity that neither the european union nor the united states can afford to miss.
mr president, we are facing a possible agreement, a desired agreement, an agreement between two great powers. the council has said: an open agreement, a fair agreement, and the commissioner has asked for a broad mandate. but we must not fail to recognise and tackle the difficulties that exist. the resolution contains many points, but the points specifically point out that we are faced with two different models: in principle, from the agricultural point of view, we note that the united states has large, industrialized and aided farms. in europe we have small farmers, a poor cap and, of course, family industries. as regards gmos, this is an issue that the united states does not want to let go of, but how can we establish a health guarantee? for industry, services and smes, it is an opportunity, but smes and industry need transparency, access and simplicity. the scope of the mandate cannot therefore absolve us of our responsibility.
madam president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, we are here to solve the problems of our citizens, to make life much easier. we are talking about article 5 here, and we need to analyse it, to know what we can do to correct what is not working or what is working worse. to make the instruments at our disposal, as we know, the effectiveness of macro-regional strategies, which give answers to citizens, to problems, to challenges, especially for the future, more profitable. we must look to the future because, as my colleague mr kandenbach has said, we must find a solution to this problem. we know that europe will not be built in a day. it will be done gradually, but above all with the will and the ambition to be european and to make europe more european every day. we must continue to move forward and be ambitious in setting up new macro-regions. the point of attention must also be placed, as this parliament has said, on the atlantic and mediterranean macro-region. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. i would like to ask the commissioner whether he expects to see a macro-regional strategy for the atlantic and mediterranean regions in the near future.
blue card question. what is it? madam president, commissioner, i would like to ask you, as i have asked others, something that is not sufficiently mentioned in this debate. a terrible tragedy has occurred in bangladesh. there have been over 1,000 deaths, we are all shocked. but, a lot happens in the european union, weeks and months go by and people forget. what i would like is that measures be taken that are irreversible and that prevent such events from happening again today, not only in bangladesh but also in china, singapore, korea and other countries in southeast asia where there are no conditions for either physical security or social security for these workers. in short, our most immediate instrument is the multinational textile companies with european headquarters, which we can impose very strong sanctions on to prevent them from producing again in these textile companies. do you support that measure?
madam president, dunning said in a footnote to capital: capital is horrified by the absence of profit. if the profit is adequate, capital becomes bold; at 20%, it becomes impulsive; at 50%, it becomes reckless; by 100%, it will violate all human laws, and by 300%, no crime will frighten it, even if it runs the risk of being hanged. yes, the fundamental problem is that european capital is partly responsible for this crime, as is a corrupt, inhumane system based on exploitation, deregulation, offshoring and tax havens. this is the fundamental problem, which no one from the european union, from this neoliberal european union, wants to touch, because it lives on business, on the accumulation of capital at the expense of european employment, at the expense of european public services and at the expense of human lives, because there is no mercy, it is about accumulating capital at any price.
mr president, the sinking of the bangladesh factory, with more than 1 100 dead, which - as the commissioner has said - is not the only one, is a tragedy and provokes outrage about the working conditions and the very facilities where they work in bangladesh. the european union is the largest importer of textile products, which also harms our own imports because of the speculation that occurs with low-wage production there. what we are asking for in the resolution are measures that the commission can take, such as guaranteeing the right to trade unionism, also responsible conduct on the part of multinationals. the commissioner said that 24 companies had joined - few companies compared to those who buy such large quantities of textiles in bangladesh. and the gsp, which has been said to be a small but important number, could be conditional on those who do not comply with ilo standards and human rights. we must not only say that we must work, but we must do it. there have been many accidents and concrete measures must be taken.
mr president, this terrible tragedy is an example of negligence, a sad accident, an example of complicity, of the impunity of the exploitation of poverty. many people lost their lives and many injured people lost their jobs too. bangladesh is the second largest textile exporter in the world and european garment companies that contract or subcontract from bangladesh must comply with international social responsibility practices. i know what i'm talking about because i live in a country that has one of the leading textile exporting companies. because these women, who work in the textile industry, have low wages, undignified working conditions and work short-term, under pressure. we have a shared responsibility, between those who consume, those who produce, those who direct. commissioner, it is with regret that the previous commissioner has abandoned this debate. when it comes to commercial matters, it stays, but when it comes to human rights, it goes away. we are asking, commissioner, that the european union's trade agreements include a binding clause on corporate social responsibility.
mr president, i would like to pay tribute to the victims of bangladesh in these words: i am concerned about the frontal gaze, the gaze we have in europe, limited to ourselves but not seeing others. how far can we go? we are not going to go as far as we decide to do so in order to put an end to the abuses, the conditions of misery and slavery, as the united nations considers them, where workers are paid less than 30 euros a month and work in conditions which are not only unsafe but above all unworthy. the european union cannot ignore the red lines which are drawn against the fundamental rights of third country nationals. we don't want for others what we don't want for ourselves! we have to change the nature of corporate social responsibility. good practice is not enough; we must respect the ilo, oecd and un conventions, binding standards, and put an end to political cynicism and guarantee security, dignity and social rights. nothing more or less than enforcing the founding treaty.
mr president, what has happened in bangladesh is not an accident, it is the consequence of years of promoting and enabling the globalisation of capital and production in the face of the globalisation of trade unionism, social justice, human rights and the social welfare of workers. and then we make resolutions like someone lifting a weight off their shoulders. it is not just resolutions that are required: it is a shift from a voluntary business ethic to a demanding business ethic. and the european institutions have enough mechanisms and strength to be able to raise the demand for corporate responsibility, to raise measures that make it clear who complies and who does not. and make it public. who practices this new slavery, and who doesn't. and let it be known. and who is having exemplary behavior as an entrepreneur, even what pedagogy is reserved for consumers. we cannot go from resolution to resolution, we must go from action to action if we want the european union to be a europe of dignity, of citizens of dignity, who also consume with dignity. in this case, what is needed are commitments and measurable actions to prevent such tragic deaths.
mr president, mr daul is right to trust the democracy of the socialists, because we are certainly a group, perhaps not the most important but not the least important of all the groups, which has always defended democracy in europe. and we are defending it in other countries where there are governments which the group of the european people's party usually respects and protects, including in this parliament. mr. daul was asking if we were being held hostage by anyone. we are not hostages to anyone, we are servants of our values and our democratic principles.
in writing. - i voted in favour of this report because it is purely technical in nature, since it only proposes the change of date to ensure legal certainty in the customs area. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. this report is merely trying to change the dates laid down to ensure that there is a community customs regulation in force at all times. this report is not part of the union's customs policy which will have to be dealt with in the european parliament through another report and therefore does not create problems and ensures that there is a rule at all times. that is why i voted in favour of this report.
in writing. − in favour. the directive contains only one article extending the date of application of the existing community customs code to 1 november 2013. the existing ‘community customs code’ (i.e. the legislation which provides for the procedures to control the import of products to the eu territory) is currently under revision and will be replaced by the ‘union customs code’, mainly in order to be better adapted to the new digital environment. negotiations between the parliament and the council on this new union custom code have just been finalised. however, it was not be possible to formally adopt in plenary this new legislation before the date of expiry of the existing community customs code in june 2013. therefore it has been necessary to adopt a technical directive extending the date of application of the existing code, in order to avoid any legal gap.
in writing. - i voted against this report because it seeks to restore trade preferences with a country where, despite having ended forced labour, according to the ilo itself, the army continues to exercise undemocratic control over society. violence and repression against minorities, the recruitment of child soldiers, etc., create an extremely fragile situation where the re-establishment of exports can only have negative effects on the workforce and positive effects on multinationals. the reopening of trade in such fragile contexts usually coincides with the worsening of security conditions in the country and new violence. by restoring tariff preferences, the eu is only seeking to consolidate its economic influence and its neo-colonial power. i therefore voted against this report.
in writing. − against. the greens have a particular interest in burma. concerning the particular gsp issue, inta greens proposed a conditioned positive approach, with a provisional ‘yes’ for 18 months, close monitoring and political accompanying to make sure that promised improvements will be irreversible, also in the light of a recent human rights watch report (1), a report by the european council on foreign relations (2), an appeal by cetri (3); and finally a us decision of 3 may 2013, to maintain targeted sanctions. with this perspective, we supported david martin’s position on resolution 110(2), adding language on ongoing problems and the need to further monitor envisaged eradication of forced labour and other human rights violations. though in inta the initial text was weakened by epp-ale-ecr amendments, the greens finally supported it, in order to avoid the worst (a rejection of the whole text). however, in plenary, the final text was too weak to be voted in favour, so we opposed.
in writing. - i voted against this report because it attempts to impose once again a criminal neoliberal ideology, whereby states must be mere servants of international capital, making their costs as cheap as possible in order to attract foreign investment as the only way of generating economic growth. this ideology, which the international oligarchs present as the neutrality of market mechanisms and competitiveness, hides the complete fraud that sovereign law must accept the designs of capital. the report seeks to strengthen mechanisms whereby international investors can claim monetary compensation for losses on their investments and to reduce the independence of member states in exercising political control over international investments. that is why i voted against.
in writing. i voted in favour of the establishment of this management framework for financial accountability. when a trade dispute arises for the european union or for the member states, they can now know what their responsibilities are if a trade dispute is brought before a member state or the eu. this framework allows the european union and the member states to deal with their trading partners in a calm manner. this is therefore a breakthrough in the field of trade negotiations, which is why i voted in favour.
in writing. − in favour of the amended proposal, also in favour of postponing the final legislative vote. we as greens, believe that foreign investors should not have direct access to international tribunals, which discriminates against domestic investors who do not have this option. like domestic investors, also foreign investors should be required to seek remedy through domestic courts. only if domestic courts decline a claim, a foreign investor might be granted additional rights, which however should by default be framed in a state-to-state dispute, as is the norm under wto trade remedy rules. we recognize, on the other hand, that eu member states would block any commission initiative to come to an eu-wide investment protection agreement with a third country, if such agreement would provide for considerably less investor protection than their bits with third country did so far. in short, should isds be scrapped from the commission's repertoire, the new european competence on investment would simply be boycotted case by case. thus, we support the new eu competence against the resistance of the member states.

on the internal market and consumer protection adopted its report, practically unanimously, on 17 may 2013. i would like to thank the alternative rapporteurs and all the technical teams who have contributed to the arrival here today of a document which will undoubtedly give greater prominence to european consumers and their associations in the period 2014-2020. the four main objectives are: first, to strengthen consumer safety; second, to raise consumer awareness; third, to increase compliance and ensure redress; and fourth, to adapt consumer rights and policies to changes in society and the economy. the promotion and protection of consumer rights are core values of the european union and must be easily and effectively exercised in basic sectors such as food, health, energy, financial and digital services, transport and telecommunications. the protection of personal data is also an essential condition for the protection of european consumers. good consumer information and education reduces the risks of dangerous or counterfeit products, speculative financial products and misleading advertising. consumer education should therefore be lifelong and start in school. the recent and still ongoing financial crisis has highlighted the urgent need to protect and inform consumers in the area of financial and banking services. consumers deserve more impartial advice and access to the information and tools necessary for fair and effective redress. the role of consumer associations must also be strengthened in all areas, and the necessary legal and economic measures must be taken. their collaboration with public institutions should be encouraged and a register of european associations should be set up. the agenda we are presenting is also in the final phase of the digital single market, which requires online consumer protection, legal certainty and guarantees of consumer rights. at the global level, european consumers are facing new challenges such as the globalisation of markets, financial deregulation, the digitalisation of the economy and an ageing population. the commission should therefore consider taking measures leading to the creation of a collective redress mechanism at union level and there is a growing need for reliable, comparable and accessible information for consumers. today, when inequalities are growing throughout the european union, the solidarity perspectives of the european social model are more necessary than ever. thus, mortgage contracts for the usual dwelling should be suspended when defaults occur due to causes beyond the control of the consumer, such as unemployment. these cases should be resolved through monthly payment moratoriums, installment payments and rental options. in the european union of the 21st century, nanotechnology and genetically modified organisms must be properly regulated and products containing them must be properly labelled. there is a need to provide better protection of the rights of vulnerable consumer groups such as children, the elderly or people with disabilities. the need to take legal action against unfair trading practices and contractual terms and to protect consumers who the rapporteur. - mr president, ladies and gentlemen, madam president-in-office of the council, dear commissioner cecilia malmström, i am glad that tomorrow we will finally be adopting my report on reception conditions, as well as the others on this first asylum package. i am glad that it has been many years of work by my team, the secretariat of the committee on civil liberties, justice and home affairs and the human rights organisations, especially the unhcr, as well as by many people involved in the commission and in the council - such as commissioner malmström, with her tenacity, and commissioner barrot in the past. but i am particularly pleased because i believe that with this directive the european parliament is removing the backbone of the return directive, also known as the shame directive. that dark page of this parliament will be overcome - i hope - with the help of my report. europe should not be seen as the policeman who expels immigrants. europe is above all a land of asylum, which defends those who defend freedom, those who are persecuted for defending it, and which ensures that asylum seekers are treated with dignity while their cases are being dealt with. this parliament has worked hard for two legislatures to improve european asylum legislation. in the last parliamentary term we visited the main reception centres throughout europe. we have seen dramatic situations: some inevitable, because of the tragedies that occur every day beyond our borders; others avoidable - i hope - thanks to this new package to improve the reception conditions for people seeking asylum. we are going to destroy with this legislation the cruel and inhuman automatic which leads the asylum seeker from persecution in his homeland to flee to europe - so often synonymous with freedom - only to end up crossing the european border in prison. asylum seekers can now only be detained on six assessed grounds. this directive is also designed to avoid situations of deprivation of protection which condemn claimants to destitution. moreover, if europe wants to keep up with the most diverse and dynamic country in the world - the united states - it must allow asylum seekers to work and earn a living for themselves as soon as possible. i believe that we must help those in need, but we must also allow them to become self-sufficient as soon as possible. i know that among the asylum seekers there are many highly qualified people who could earn a living without any additional cost to the coffers of our states. that is what is happening in the united states and that is what will happen here because the economic storm will pass and we will again be talking about our labour needs, manual and intellectual, even if it is temporary. in short, i would like this report to be my small contribution to the european parliament in respecting human dignity, whatever its origin in europe. yes to the directive on humanity, on dignity, no to the directive on shame!
president-in-office of the council. − mr president, i am very pleased to be here today, representing the irish presidency of the council, to mark this important stage in the completion of the second phase of the common european asylum system. this project, as many of you will know, has been an important goal of the irish presidency of the council, and i am very pleased that we have been able to play our role in reaching some of the final compromises necessary for agreement on the procedures directive and the eurodac regulation. i wish to acknowledge particularly the role played by previous council presidencies, most recently and notably the presidencies of cyprus, denmark and poland, in the legislative process, which is now in its final stage. indeed, since the first half of 2009 the legislative package on asylum has absorbed the energies of no fewer than nine council presidencies, all of whom have worked with the co-legislator and the european commission to forge the agreements, the final elements of which are now being put in place. we are in the final stage of concluding a project initiated in june 2008 with the publication by the european commission of its policy plan on asylum in which it announced its intention to build on the existing legal framework in the field of asylum. the initiative of the commission was quickly taken up by the european council, adopting in october 2008 the european pact on immigration and asylum in which the european council stated that the time had come to take new initiatives to complete the establishment of the common european asylum system and thus to offer a higher degree of protection. the entry into force of the lisbon treaty in december 2009 modified the legal framework for asylum policy and provided for a uniform status of asylum, a uniform status of subsidiary protection and common procedures for granting and withdrawing the two forms of international protection. it is to be welcomed that the legislative instruments for the second phase of the common european asylum system have been based on the new treaty provisions, thus ensuring compliance with the principle of non-refoulement and the 1951 geneva convention on the status of refugees and its 1967 protocol. in adopting the stockholm programme in december 2009, the european council renewed its commitment to the establishment of a common asylum procedure and a uniform status for those granted international protection. the european council also stated that, while the common european asylum system should be based on high protection standards, due regard should also be given to a fair and effective procedure capable of preventing abuse. it is fair to say that the overall compromises developed during the legislative process have been informed by the strategic guidelines laid down by the european council in the stockholm programme. in this regard i would like to acknowledge the creative contributions of all those in the council, the european parliament and the commission, which have allowed the negotiations to be brought to this successful conclusion. these new instruments provide for a number of important improvements: the new legislative framework further harmonises national asylum systems, the common standards are more protective and fully in line with the evolving case law of the court of justice and the european court of human rights, and the new rules will enable member states to operate efficient asylum systems capable of tackling abuse. this second phase of the common european asylum system has seen the establishment of the european asylum support office. the office, in malta, which is now fully operational, is an important element in the development and implementation of the common european asylum system and is contributing to the strengthening of all forms of practical cooperation between the member states. the dublin system remains a cornerstone in building the common european asylum system, as it clearly allocates responsibility for the examination of asylum applications. it is fair to say that the importance of the dublin system was reflected in the intensive and creative negotiations which have taken place since the legislative proposal of the commission was presented in december 2008. one of the innovative elements arising from the negotiations was the inclusion in the dublin regulation of a mechanism for early warning, preparedness and crisis management. the mechanism allows for an active and early response to situations where the asylum system of a member state is subject to particular pressure or has problems in its functioning. it provides for structured and escalating actions in order to address any deficiencies and problems before the situation becomes a fully-fledged crisis. this provision is an important element in laying strong foundations for the mutual trust built upon member states’ individual responsibility for adhering to their eu and international obligations in law and in practice. responsibility and mutual trust are the pillars on which the common framework on genuine and practical solidarity in the field of asylum should be built. in this regard, it is important to note that solidarity and responsibility go hand-in-hand. each member state should ensure that it has in place a well-functioning and robust asylum system to enable it to cope with migratory fluctuations and to allow it to receive solidarity measures. an essential element to a credible and sustainable common european asylum system is that member states build and maintain sufficient capacity in the national asylum systems. following the guidance of the european council, the member states are urged to support each other in building this capacity. the european asylum support office has an important role in coordinating this endeavour. i would like, in concluding, to express my particular thanks to your rapporteurs, who have worked so hard to make these agreements possible and who have already spoken so eloquently: sylvie guillaume for the asylum procedures directive; monica macovei for the eurodac regulation; cecilia wikström for the ‘dublin’ regulation and antonio masip hidalgo for the reception conditions directive. we should, of course, not forget the contribution made by jean lambert who, as the rapporteur for the qualification directive, contributed to our reaching an agreement in 2011, and give more general thanks to commissioner cecilia malmström for her assistance in helping and guiding the brokering of some of the vital compromises which have made these agreements possible. in conclusion, as president of the council, i very much look forward to following the debate, which represents such an important milestone in the establishment of the common european asylum system.
member of the commission. − mr president, the second phase of the common european asylum system has been several years in the making. i am very happy to be here with you today to speak the day before it is hopefully adopted by a large majority in this plenary. fifteen years ago, the eu had no common rules on asylum. basic minimum standards have since been adopted, and today we are to make a decisive step towards a true common system. this is, in many ways, a historic achievement. these negotiations, as you all know, have been tough. they have been long and very difficult, but thanks to the great work done by you, the rapporteurs, i am delighted to say that we achieved the results which will make a difference. it shows how much difference the european parliament can make. i would like to thank all of you present: antonio masip higaldo, cecilia wikström, sylvie guillaume, monica macovei, jean lambert, and all the shadow rapporteurs and all the others involved, especially in the committee on civil liberties, justice and home affairs, for your hard work, your support and your dedication on this. i would also, of course, like to thank the irish presidency. there were many presidencies before you, but it was the irish presidency which managed to conclude on the final, very difficult, but very important, issues. let me mention some of the improvements that the new asylum package will make. thanks to the new asylum procedures directive, asylum procedures will be quicker, more efficient and fairer to asylum seekers. all asylum seekers will receive early assistance in the procedure to minimise errors and reduce hardship due to long procedures. there will be a general deadline of six months for normal asylum procedures. asylum seekers will no longer have to wait years for a decision. this will, of course, reduce human suffering, and also save money because people will not depend on financial and social assistance. the new rules in the asylum procedures and reception conditions directives mean that asylum seekers with special needs will be quickly identified. they will receive the necessary support to explain their claim, and adequate reception conditions. there will be greater protection for unaccompanied minors and victims of torture. in the new reception conditions directive there are rules ensuring that detention of asylum seekers will be applied only as an exception, on six limited grounds. this is a huge improvement compared to the current rules. all the necessary guarantees need to be available, including free legal assistance. the conditions in detention centres need to be adequate, especially for vulnerable people. in addition, the new reception conditions directive will provide for quicker access for asylum seekers to the labour market. that way, if exceptionally they have to wait for more than nine months for a decision, they will be able to support themselves instead of relying on state help. this will also, in the case of a positive decision, speed up the integration process. the new dublin regulation will give asylum seekers more rights and protection in the procedure for determining the responsible member states. this procedure will also be more efficient and clearer, avoiding conflicts of competence between member states. in parallel to the commission’s infringement powers, there will be a mechanism to detect early problems in national asylum or reception systems, and to address the root causes before these problems develop. it will be equipped with solidarity measures for those whose problems stem from a particular pressure. this is an achievement of the new dublin regulation. i also want to mention the court judgement from last week, to which mrs wikström made reference. the commission and i attach great importance to that. the ruling confirmed that our views on the interpretation of the current dublin regulation were correct. the court confirmed that the unnecessary transfer of children between member states should be avoided. with a view to ensuring the child’s best interests, the application must be examined in the state where the child is present. the commission is ready to live up to its commitment under the joint declaration in which we undertook to allow a quick adoption for the recast regulation and we will consider revising article 8(4). if we make a proposal, the european parliament and the council will thereafter be called upon to exercise their legislative competences on the matter. in any case, the ruling of the court of justice is to be taken into account by all member states in the implementation of the asylum rules, as it has already become part of the eu acquis. the qualification directive has already been adopted, but we should mention it again. it clarifies the grounds for granting international protection and therefore will make asylum decisions more robust. it will also improve access to rights and integration measures for beneficiaries of international protection. finally, in the package we have the revised eurodac regulation. this will allow law enforcement access to the eu database of the fingerprints of asylum seekers, under strictly limited circumstances, in order to prevent, detect or investigate the most serious crimes, such as murder and terrorism. the commission was made aware in the last couple of days of a new proposed change to the variable geometry recitals in the eurodac regulation. the council’s legal service argued they should be deleted. the commission proposal put forward the recitals. we considered them helpful to clarify the legal clarity of application of the new acquis. in view of all the efforts that have been made to finalise this file and in order not to prevent the adoption, we can accept the deletion of those recitals. however, we strongly urge that such deletion be accompanied by a statement clarifying the participation of the associated countries in the recast regulation. this is the minimum necessary for clarity and transparency with the associated countries. during the adoption of eurodac, the commission offered to undertake two tasks that i am happy to confirm today. firstly, following consultation with member states and parliament, the commission intends to publish in due course an indicative, non-binding model – a eurodac law enforcement request form – to be sent by the designated authorities to the verifying authorities, which reflects the criteria set out in article 20(1). secondly, article 40(5) of the recast eurodac regulation calls on mr president, as chairman of the committee on civil liberties, justice and home affairs, i join in the congratulations of the rapporteurs who have distinguished themselves in the conduct of these files which form part of the asylum package, and those who celebrate the result, which is not perfect but represents a step forward: first, because of its content; and secondly, because it closes a first circle of a chapter in the history of the european union, from the treaty of amsterdam in 1999 to the conversion of the area of freedom, security and justice into a european policy subject to the ordinary legislative procedure, which this european parliament as legislator understands, with the construction of a common european asylum system, characterized by the principles of protection of human dignity and reinforcing legal assistance, the rights of minors and the most vulnerable persons in reception, in the conditions of detention, in the regulation and procedures and, above all, in its legal guarantees. and it is very good for european citizens to know that this european parliament, which has spent so much time over the last four years talking about the governance of the euro and talking about the financial aspects of the crisis and banking supervision, is not only concerned, in addition to that, with the labelling of yoghurts, but also with the fundamental rights of people and, in particular, the most vulnerable people who knock on the door of the european union and want to know that the european union is not a wall of incomprehension and selfishness, but also this representation of european citizens who want to be faithful to the european social model and be a reference of reliability and submission to the rule of law.
mr president, i would like to congratulate mr masip and mrs wikström, mr macovei and mr guillaume. today we are taking a big step towards the area of freedom, security and justice, a big step towards a common european asylum system and towards the defence of the civil rights of those seeking protection. we cannot allow discriminatory or unequal treatment in asylum procedures, nor can we allow criminal networks to exploit possible weaknesses in our legislation. the measures we are discussing today are very important and balanced, but they are incomplete. actions relating to children, early warning, access to fingerprint databases, the approximation of rules or procedures for granting and withdrawing international protection or the establishment of mechanisms for the rapid determination of the member state responsible for processing an application are measures that strengthen and establish a common asylum policy, ensuring higher standards of protection. but what is lacking, mr president, is the subject of solidarity, of shared solidarity, and we still have a long way to go in this respect.
mr president, it is true that each member sees things in a different way and, indeed, as mr díaz de mera has said, we have taken a step - i would not call it a big one - but we have taken a step and, as he has denounced, in the end solidarity is lacking. that is because of the dublin regulation, which has been the framework that the commission itself has accepted and within which we have had to move. so we can say today that, despite all the progress we have made, we still do not have a common asylum system. we know that there are groups that are furiously opposed, but it is our responsibility to defend the values of those who are demanding for them the same values that we defend for ourselves. the early warning mechanism is not sufficient because the asylum problems, which are concentrated in certain countries in the south, are not temporary, they are structural. it is not that asylum seekers can come at a certain time because there are wars, etc., etc., it is that they are already in those countries and are in situations contrary to our principles. that is why the dublin regulation is not the solution, and so long as it exists, we will not have a common asylum policy. we have made progress, yes, but we are still far from what is sufficient and necessary.

the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the competition rules are applied in the member states, and i would like to thank the rapporteur for the work he has done. competition policy is a pillar of the community project: the prohibition of collusive behaviour and abuse of a dominant position, the rules on state aid and the control of concentrations are based on the treaty of rome and create value every day for businesses, consumers and taxpayers, and ultimately for all european citizens. in this report i would like to highlight four messages. the first is that while competition is always important, in times of crisis it is vital. in the absence of a community framework to address it, it has provided instruments to maintain the stability of the financial system, provide assistance to countries in difficulty and promote more transparent, open and innovative financial markets within the union. the commission - and this is stated in our resolution - must continue to give priority to the financial system, by continuing the investigations under way, by ensuring that the extraordinary public aid scheme does not go beyond what is necessary and by ensuring that the beneficiary institutions restructure at the lowest social cost, discipline the remuneration of their executives and do not gain any advantage over those institutions which have not needed aid. the second is that competition is a lever for sustainable growth and employment in a globalised environment. we need to get back on a growth path. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's financial resources are properly used. a level playing field is necessary for companies to base their success on their own merits, on their talent to meet social demands. the objectives of the europe 2020 strategy will not be achieved without enhancing the effectiveness of competition policy. the third message is that competition policy has an essential role to play in services of general economic interest. to monitor the proper use of public funds, to prosecute discriminatory behaviour and to enable technical progress to be converted into social progress, active competition policy development is necessary. their action in this field - and we have examples in our resolution on health, pharmacy and insurance - must be stepped up if the european social model is to have a future. and the fourth message is that competition contributes to consumer welfare. the commission has also proposed that the commission should be able to take action to ensure that the competition rules are properly applied. action in the food sector in favour of small and mediumsized enterprises and consumers must be continued and extended to other sectors so that economic improvements can benefit society as a whole. competition policy cannot be an obstacle to the restoration of the rights of those who have been shown to have been victims of irregular and illegal practices in the marketing of financial products, as has scandalously happened in my country. i hope that the house will confirm its support for paragraph 17 of the proposal in its vote tomorrow to enable justice to be done. i would like to conclude by expressing my gratitude as rapporteur to all those who have contributed to this report.

the rapporteur. - mr president, thank you very much, commissioner, for coming, even though it is late. in fact, the subject of debate today is one we have been talking about for a long time: illegal, unreported and unregulated fishing, that fishing which 'seems to be' to some people is particularly attractive because it has a lower price - i am talking about wholesalers or retailers - precisely because it has been done without complying with the environmental, social and other standards required of those who want to do things right and those who do things right. what is interesting and relevant to me in this debate is to highlight the importance not only of the measures that have been established but of the fact that these measures that exist are being enforced; this is the aspect that is giving rise to a great deal of debate. when we recall the process of drawing up the regulation now in force - the regulation on fisheries commonly known as iuu fishing - we recall the fierce opposition that some countries, especially those which are fish markets, showed at the time, not necessarily the fishing nations, but those countries, in the european union, which are a zone, a market area for that fish which is often imported. and here, in my view, arises one of the great questions we have to ask ourselves when we assess where we are today and how far we are progressing or not in terms of what is expected from a regulation of this kind. it is very good to have a text 'we have it', but this text must be applied, it must be implemented. when six months ago the commission finally presented us with a list of eight countries - belize, cambodia, fiji, guinea, panama, sri lanka, togo and vanuatu - we understood that these eight countries were a first sample of those countries which could end up on a list of countries which were not cooperating against iuu fishing. at that time - six months ago, i insist - it was a yellow card, it was not a red card. we are in june, six months have passed and we are waiting for that preliminary list to become a final list - and this is where i ask my first question to the commissioner: where are we on this issue? we do not know exactly which countries will remain, but there is one element which is of particular concern to me and that is the possibility, for example, that a country such as sri lanka may be left out, among other things because of its privileged relations or because of the influence that a country such as the united kingdom may have had on this issue. i would therefore like the commissioner to say something to us on this. this, as far as the frame. secondly, it is also important to explain that this measure affects eight countries which are not really the most important countries in this type of illegal, unreported and unregulated fishing. countries such as korea, russia, indonesia, the philippines, thailand, papua new guinea or even china should, in our view, be part of this list. we have enough information to know that these countries, in many cases, are not only not cooperating, but are engaging in practices that are clearly questionable - like korea, for example, or china, in some very specific respects. it is true that in the case of korea we have recently made some progress: we have learned, through a press release, of measures adopted by the korean government to start a process which we consider interesting, but we shall see where it leads. but the commissioner also knows very well that measures such as those adopted by the korean government, in the sense of simply establishing vms mechanisms or proposing stricter sanctions, are also no guarantee of anything. so we understand that this process has to be done right. the commission always insists that this is a complicated process and therefore we also ask that there be sufficient resources to enable the commission to have the equipment and the capacity to do the legislative work that is required to be able to make that list. so, mr president, this being the framework of the debate - and i conclude my first speech here - i would like to point out that the debate goes far beyond the report we are discussing and that the framework is as important, if not more so, than the report itself.
member of the commission. − mr president, firstly i would like to thank the rapporteur, mr romeva i rueda, and also the committee on fisheries (pech) for its contribution to this important file. yes, this is a very important issue. combating illegal fisheries worldwide is one of our main priorities and it will be, maybe, our first priority now since the work on the reform of our common fisheries policy is on track. referring to enforcement and control and combating iuu, we have a lot to do and we have to work on it together. i think that we owe a great many thanks to all the members of this parliament for the clear support given to the proposal on alignment of the iuu regulation with the lisbon treaty. parliament has to play an important role on this and we have to find a solution to these problems together. what have we done up till now? first i would like to emphasise that a lot of energy has been devoted to combating overfishing in the context of the common fisheries policy reform in the last year, and rightly so. in fact, sustainability is the red line that can connect this file to the reform and our position in general. our first priority as a commission has continued to be to enforce the existing rules in european waters. this is important too – what our member states are doing in european waters. so, for instance, in march of this year, we reduced the spanish quota for mackerel by 65 000 tonnes because of overfishing. in recent years, deficiencies in the control systems have also led to administrative enquiries and action plans being agreed with malta in 2011, spain in 2012 and latvia in 2013. we have some actions in the pipeline now for this. but, as mr romeva i rueda has pointed out, whilst we are getting our own house in order, we still import a lot of fish, so this angle exists of all these markets which are very interested in importing fish. that is why it is essential to ensure that international conservation rules are applied not only in eu waters, but also to the wild fish we import from other countries. our main priority was and is to work at the level of countries, at an institutional level. over the past three years, the commission has undertaken a process of identifying non-cooperating third countries. we have examined and we are still examining a lot of countries but, as mr romeva i rueda has already mentioned, this resulted in eight countries being given a ‘yellow card’ six months ago. what is the objective of this exercise? let us remember that the objective of this exercise is to bring about fundamental reform of the fisheries control systems. we want to collaborate with third countries in order to have satellite controls, inspections, laws allowing effective sanctions. during these last few months after we gave these yellow cards, we were able to convince some countries to move to an effective fisheries control system. in particular, fiji, togo, sri lanka and panama have made credible progress. these countries will receive additional time to implement the necessary reforms and adapt their fleets, but with these countries the cooperation is already there. concerning the rest of the countries: as we speak a mission is ongoing in one country, vanuatu, so i will tell you about this later. the other countries, the remaining countries, have not been that cooperative until now. if their current attitude remains the same, i will have no choice but to prepare the next steps. what will the next steps be? the next steps could entail trade measures to be adopted by the council on a proposal from the commission. this what we are preparing now. simultaneously, we have investigations and cooperation missions ongoing as regards further countries. a lot of other countries, some of them mentioned by mr romeva i rueda, are attracting our attention now. if no concrete progress is achieved with those countries, i intend to hand out, before the end of the year, during the autumn, a few more yellow cards. let me finish by thanking again mr romeva i rueda and the member states. i look forward to your support in order to prioritise the control issues during the coming months.

mr president of the european parliament, mr president of the european commission, ladies and gentlemen, i thank you for the invitation, which i am very honoured to receive, to address this house. i have a deep respect for the european parliament and its role in the european union. as i said in this house in september 2007, i am well aware of parliament's action and contribution to the process of european integration. i will not forget the frank and loyal support he gave me as prime minister during the months when i was leading the first portuguese presidency of the council in 1992. i am pleased to note the great development of parliament since maastricht. the treaty of lisbon has rightly consolidated its role as a co-legislator alongside the council. this is an option which promotes the democratic legitimacy of the union's decisions and contributes to the deepening of european civic culture. there could be no more appropriate place to share some thoughts on the challenges which i consider to be the most current and pressing for our states and citizens at this stage of the european project. in recent decades, the european union has become a remarkable political construct and a model for many. borders have been abolished, the free movement of people, knowledge and culture has been established, the single market has been established, the world's largest economic bloc and the single currency have been created, a community of belonging has been strengthened. however, we are sadly forced to realise that the inspiration and achievements we have made since the founding fathers cannot be taken for granted. economic growth in europe is weak and several countries are in recession, and unemployment is a dramatic reality. these are the two biggest challenges we face today and for which we have not yet found an effective response. it is not surprising, therefore, that they are joined by the growing divorce between decision-makers and citizens. it is exactly 28 years since portugal signed its formal commitment to join the european communities in the cloisters of the jerónimos monastery on 12 june 1985. accession to the european communities has brought the portuguese democratic process to a climax and has made a decisive contribution to the development of my country. since then, portugal has actively participated in the consolidation of the european project. portugal has brought to europe the legacy of its history, the hallmark of the atlantic dialogue, the universalism of its language and culture. our special ties of friendship with africa and latin america, the diaspora present in every corner of the world and the growing international affirmation of the community of portuguese-speaking countries are factors that contribute to the global projection of the european union, our values and our project. as you know, the portuguese are currently feeling the economic and financial crisis with all its serious social consequences particularly strongly. the last few years have been some of the most complex we have experienced in our recent history. since mid-2011, portugal has been undertaking a major effort of economic and financial adjustment and structural reforms within the framework of the programme agreed with international institutions. the process of consolidation has been progressing despite a much more unfavourable external economic environment than initially foreseen by the institutions involved and the asymmetric shock to which we were subjected. in my country, the severity of the recession has been manifest for 10 consecutive quarters, the unemployment rate has reached 17.7%, with youth unemployment at 42%. we are seeing a worrying increase in the risk of poverty. the portuguese are being asked to make very heavy sacrifices, and they have shown an admirable sense of responsibility, strengthening the bonds of solidarity and mutual aid which have made it possible to alleviate some of the most dramatic situations. mr president of the european parliament, ladies and gentlemen, this crisis has made clear the degree of interdependence between the member states of the european union in general and the euro area in particular. it is the logical result of the level of integration we have achieved. it is not possible today to dissociate the situation in a member state from the general european context. in short, we are a union and not just a collection of states and markets, and this makes a huge difference when it comes to understanding the current situation and defining the most appropriate responses. the efforts made by the european union over the past two years to support the financing needs of member states in the greatest difficulty, to strengthen the rules on budgetary discipline and supervision and to deepen the coordination of economic policies should be acknowledged. the european central bank, for its part, announced the possibility of intervening unlimitedly in the secondary market for sovereign debt. it was an important milestone in combating the speculative attacks that had been undermining the euro zone. despite these positive developments, we must admit that this crisis has exposed serious weaknesses in the union. apart from the slow and lukewarm response to the euro crisis, the european union's greatest failure has been and remains the promotion of economic growth and job creation. in 2012, the euro area saw output fall by 0,6%, and the forecast is for a further negative trend in 2013. the unemployment rate in the union has risen steadily over the last five years, with 26 million people out of work, including 5.7 million young people. the euro area is in its sixth consecutive quarter of output decline and its eighth consecutive quarter of investment decline. the divergence from the trend in the united states and japan is clear. for too long, attention has been focused on austerity to correct public account imbalances, relegating economic growth to a secondary role. the delay in implementing structural reforms has put competitiveness at risk. in several member states, companies face very negative financing conditions. the breach of trust has hurt, and continues to hurt, investment. the contraction in domestic demand across the euro area, by exacerbating the impact of the measures portugal had to take to meet budget deficit targets, contributed to deepening the recession and raising unemployment to socially unacceptable levels. when countries implementing programmes to consolidate public deficits are joined by contractionary policies in other member states, the consequence is a recession throughout the union, as we are now seeing. the situation is in stark contrast to the more expansionary policy options in other blocs of the world economy. it must be acknowledged, however, that it was not for lack of vision or for a few warnings from the european commission and this parliament that the objective of economic growth and job creation did not take priority earlier on the same level as that of corrections of budgetary imbalances. in december 2011, the president of the commission, addressing this parliament, said, and i quote: we cannot build our economic union on discipline and sanctions. we also need a europe of growth and jobs. and i need not remind you of the countless occasions on which, since the beginning of the crisis, voices have been heard in this house from members of the most varied political families, including portuguese members, including yours, mr president schulz, warning of the urgent need not to forget this priority. the hesitations and political constraints of the member states have delayed the recognition that financial problems in some countries affect everyone and that the eurozone crisis cannot be solved by imposing austerity policies on the states with excessive deficits. in the case of countries under adjustment programmes, for example, the advantage of fully operating automatic stabilisers could have been recognised earlier. that is, not insisting on increased fiscal consolidation efforts just because the economic recession reduces tax revenues. the situation of high economic and financial interdependence to which i referred earlier requires member states to coordinate their policies more closely. countries are no longer able to solve their problems on their own. but on the other hand, at european level, we are not yet fully equipped to be able to do this effectively. we are in a transitional situation. the instruments of the past are not enough for europe to answer the questions of the present nor to prepare for the future. we must therefore move towards a genuine economic and monetary union in all its aspects: banking, budgetary and economic. this must be an essential element of the european union's strategy. there have been some very important contributions to the debate on the next phase of european integration, notably the commission's blueprint for a deep and genuine economic and monetary union. here too the european parliament is called upon to play a central role. i am sure that you will be able to live up to your responsibilities and to the expectations of the citizens. mr president of the european parliament, ladies and gentlemen, just as the success of europe is fundamental to portugal, so too the success of portugal is fundamental to the success of europe. portugal has the support of the institutions and their partners. of course, in promoting economic growth and job creation. several areas are crucial to this objective. on the one hand, it is essential to improve the financing conditions of the economy, especially small and medium-sized enterprises, for which both the european investment bank and the structural funds are particularly important. at the same time, a response from the european central bank is essential to restore the normal functioning of the monetary transmission mechanisms throughout the euro area. the rapid operationalization of the banking union is also absolutely essential to combat the fragmentation of credit markets and to overcome the contagion of sovereign debt risk to the banking system, favouring the financing of economies on balanced and competitive terms. it is imperative to compensate for the excessive cost of credit to enterprises which weighs on the economies of some states, such as portugal. the cost of credit borne by portuguese companies is much higher than that of their european counterparts, which undermines their competitiveness, affects investment decisions and promotes justified feelings of injustice. it would also be very important for countries subject to adjustment programmes to be able to count on european incentives and support for the structural reforms they will need to undertake to improve their competitiveness in the global market and also to ensure the sustainability of public debt. for example, they may temporarily in writing. − establishing a community regime to prevent, deter and eliminate illegal, unreported and unregulated fishing is the only way to secure the future of the fisheries sector. the fishing activity must be rationally regulated and supported by rigorous and up-to-date scientific reports, aiming at the preservation of marine resources, ensuring maximum sustainable fishing yields and at the same time facilitating the socioeconomic development of the fishing sector, particularly in those territories where there is a strong dependence on productive activity as in the case of galicia. in this sense, it is unacceptable that some countries, such as those mentioned in this report, tolerate, by action or omission, illegal or unregulated fishing practices which have an obvious cost in environmental terms, and also a penalty for those fleets which, like the galician fleet, carry out sustainable fishing.
in writing. − in favour (it was my report). the eu’s illegal fishing blacklist is a crucial tool for clamping down on illegal fishing and meps have today given the go-ahead to a rapid procedure for adding countries to this list. with iuu fishing a major threat to vulnerable fish stocks, transparency of those states and boats involved is a crucial measure for tackling the problem. these proposals will clear the way for the eu to add other countries (like south korea) to the list of non-cooperating states, with listed countries facing possible sanctions. the commission must expand the current list to include other countries for which there is clear evidence of illegal fishing, notably south korea. with repeated cases of illegal fishing and related human rights abuses, notably in west african waters, the european commission must add south korea to the blacklist. it must also finally publicly list those vessels engaging in iuu fishing: this would be crucial to support efforts to address the problem.
mr president, with the directive we have adopted on the dublin regulation we have consolidated a situation which is absolutely unfair, especially for the border countries, such as greece and malta in particular. in european countries, on average, a suspected criminal cannot be held for more than 48 hours, or 72 hours, with the permission of the judge. after that, he's either on trial or he's free. our asylum seekers are three months, and up to six months, waiting for the resolution of their refugee status or their international protection. and when six months pass, which is the legal maximum, and there's no resolution, they leave the detention centers to be rearrested. this situation is not going to change because of the dublin regulation. the united nations has just called on germany and other member states to take in 10,000 syrian refugees. do we have to wait for the united nations to say so? why have we not already decided to give all these refugees in these detention centres the welcome they deserve?
some 8% of european citizens are now at risk of poverty and social exclusion, with women and children being the most vulnerable groups. there are even many children who only get food at school because their families can no longer provide food for them at home. this parliament has today given a positive response, including my vote, to help the most marginalised people who are suffering from poverty by approving the report on the fund for aid to the most deprived. the resources allocated to this fund must be increased to support the most deprived families and individuals in our society and to show solidarity with those suffering from the crisis.
in writing. - i voted in favour of this report because it improves the operation, the budget and the specific objectives of this fund. the report includes amendments to the text making special mention of the impact the crisis is having on women and minors. these social groups are being hit hard by the crisis while the commission works with outdated data. the percentage of the population living in poverty and the landscape of severe material deprivation has changed considerably since the beginning of the crisis. the number of women and children who have crossed the poverty line has increased and this requires action by all the institutions that can deal with this situation, which is reaching emergency levels in many european countries. that is why i voted in favour of this report.
in writing. - i voted yes. the european parliament's plenary today rejected the european commission's proposal to reduce by one billion euros the fund for aid to the most deprived for the period 2014-2020. we have advocated that the present 3.5 billion should be retained to help meet the basic needs of the poorest people. the new fund for european aid to the most deprived proposed for the period 2014-2020 will replace the current food distribution programme, which used agricultural surpluses under the cap. the new fund will have a wider scope, providing not only food but also basic material, such as clothing, and assistance to the most disadvantaged citizens of the eu.
in writing. - the economic crisis has exacerbated both poverty and social exclusion. in 2010, almost a quarter of europeans (116 million) were at risk of poverty or social exclusion. a figure that is increasing. under the europe 2020 strategy, the eu has set itself the target of reducing by at least 20 million the number of people living in or at risk of poverty or social exclusion by 2020. however, the capacity of member states to provide assistance has declined. social cohesion is increasingly threatened by the crisis. the eu must therefore respond to poverty. the european social fund is insufficient because it does not cover those citizens who are excluded from the labour market and who therefore suffer from extreme poverty. i therefore welcome the decision to create this new fund, which will complement existing cohesion instruments, in order to combat the worst forms of poverty by promoting social cohesion in the union.
in writing. - i voted against this report because it represents a new attack on the immigrant who is trying to reach the european union. the report aims to continue the line of criminalising immigrants, using the border control system of all eu member states to build a joint database to prevent immigrants from entering the eu from different member states. this database, developed in collaboration with europol, is a real institutional finger pointing to legitimize the activity of fascist and xenophobic groups operating within the eu. criminalizing the immigrant is against human rights and is a full-blown political aggression that will be carried out by these far-right groups. that is why i voted against this report.
in writing. − against. allowing law enforcement authorities access to the eurodac fingerprint database flies in the face of asylum seekers’ basic rights. in essence, this provision means all those who come to europe seeking protection from persecution will be treated as potential criminals from the outset. eurodac was intended to enable immigration authorities to identify asylum seekers, with a view to avoiding double applications. allowing police authorities to access the data for a totally different purpose is totally at odds with this and opens the door to discrimination. in caving in to this demand from eu governments, meps have undermined the credibility of the european parliament as an institution for defending fundamental and human rights.
in writing. - i voted against this report because it is an attack on the fundamental freedoms of europeans, the free movement of capital and goods is increasingly guaranteed, but not for the citizens of the european union. the fact that member states can temporarily close their borders in the interests of their own national interests is a further confirmation that the european union is only concerned with economic and commercial matters, but never with political matters. the background of border closures has been motivated by political events, large demonstrations, etc. allowing citizens of a member state to be isolated from the rest of europe to ensure "national security". i have voted against this report because it constitutes a restriction on the free movement of persons.

in writing. - i voted in favour of this report because it is a good initiative aimed at reducing the bureaucratic burden faced by small businesses in the european union. the report takes the view that the reforms undertaken will reduce the administrative burden by 25% and save more than eur 1.5 billion. administrative simplification in the field of small enterprises is essential to allow economic activity to develop. the report includes legislative amendments that exempt smes from statutory audits and numerous red tape obligations while maintaining the requirements for larger companies or those with subsidiaries. these changes can lead to a real reduction in the burden without encouraging the evasion which occurs mainly in these large companies. that is why i voted in favour of this report.
in writing. − in favour. annual financial statements prepared on a prudent basis should give a true and fair view of the undertaking’s financial situation. annual financial statements pursue different objectives and do not merely provide information for investors in capital markets but give account of former transactions and serve corporate governance. european accounting rules need to strike an appropriate balance between the interests of the addressees of financial statements and the interest of a company in not being unduly burdened with reporting requirements.
in writing. - i voted in favour of this report because it is a good source of information on the management and role of companies which issue units on regulated markets. the report introduces amendments which improve the transparency obligations on the activities of publicly traded companies. by making special mention of certain activities such as extractive companies, banking, telecommunications, etc. the most important sectors of the economy are thus obliged to render an account in a more transparent way. including exceptions for small issuers of shares, this report can be a tool to improve control over companies with shares, at least at the information level. that is why i voted in favour of this report.
in writing. - in a globalised world, where multinationals invest millions, often without considering the common good, it is absolutely necessary to strengthen all mechanisms that increase transparency, hence the positive vote on this legislative resolution. with this european directive, large mining, oil, gas and mineral companies will have to specify the payments made to governments for each project they develop, a particularly important measure to combat possible situations of corruption and abuse, so common in latin american countries, where multinationals have repeatedly demonstrated their ability to plunder the natural resources of these countries, with the complicity of local elites, without the whole of society benefiting from the wealth of their own territory. after the entry into force of this regulation, we will have the opportunity to know about payments above €100 000 as well as information on charges and payments for improving infrastructure, bonuses or fees. we now expect the member states to adopt these rules as soon as possible, especially when in many european countries, such as galicia, the government intends to open up mineral resources to multinationals that are committed to highly polluting technology, even in the face of strong social opposition.
in writing. − in favour. with growing volatility in global financial markets, investors are increasingly demanding more information about companies’ practices. it is clear that investors want improved transparency in order to gain a comprehensive economic picture of investment and risk. in addition, transparency in terms of disclosure is an important indicator of strong corporate governance. companies are increasingly adopting corporate governance standards, including transparency, by signing up to global reporting schemes such as the extractive industries transparency initiative (eiti), in addition to voluntary guidelines for multinational companies, such as the oecd guidelines for multinational enterprises and the global reporting initiative, which are setting the transparency agenda. given all of these initiatives, there is currently a risk of a fragmented response to transparency. it is therefore important to establish a framework for strong global standards in this area. the proposal to amend the 2004 transparency directive puts such rules in place for eu companies, reflecting standards put forward in the dodd-frank act in the us. this provides a strong starting point for achieving the ultimate goal of global rules in these areas.
in writing. - i voted in favour of this report because it involves savings in the agricultural budget, geared to direct payments, which are being introduced in a progressive manner, freeing up resources for other purposes. direct payments are a key resource for the activities of many farmers in the european union, but they are also a key resource for the large landowners who are able to maintain their fortunes and vast estates thanks to european public funds which treat them as farmers. that is why this report introduces a gradual cut in these funds, introducing the exemption for small farmers to protect the meagre aid they receive and attacking the fortunes of the biggest recipients who are an obstacle to rural development. that is why i voted in favour of this report.
in writing. − in favour. the commission proposed that smaller farmers receiving below eur 5000 would be unaffected, so that the cuts in direct payments are made on the biggest farmers. this is in line with our group position on small farmers. as this was also the comagri decision, most amendments related to this. otherwise am. 7 (ecr) called for no cuts in ms with average direct payments below the eu average. we rejected this logic because it is about targeting the biggest farmers (internal convergence in cap reform jargon), not ms inequalities (external convergence, which will also be dealt with in the cap reform). am. 12 extended the logic of the current funding period, where the modulation mechanism (reducing direct payments) from 2007-2013 did not apply to the outermost regions/smaller aegean islands; it would be reasonable to extend this by a single year.
in writing. - i could not vote in favour of this report because, although it seeks to improve the technical aspects of the functioning of administrative procedures at the borders of the european union, it implements and legitimises the shame directive. the report deals only with specific technical issues for a common border policy, such as common training for the staff of the different border guards, allowing exceptions during the operation of rescue services, recognising the validity of travel documents, etc. but all these technical aspects which seek to improve the present report are an improvement in the implementation of a terrible directive which criminalizes illegal immigrants within the eu and allows the detention of human beings who have committed no crime. it is because it implies the implementation of the shame directive that i have not been able to vote in favour of this report.
