member of the commission. - mr president, ladies and gentlemen, first of all i would like to thank mrs arlene mccarthy for this own-initiative report, which is an impetus, a source of enlightenment and encouragement for us in the work i am doing on this very important subject, since it concerns the very structure of the banking sector. for once, this is not a g20 request. we have worked with each other to implement all the g20 recommendations and we are almost done. this is a reform we need, by ourselves, and for ourselves. this remains a topical subject even if the g20 has not asked for it. several countries, not the least of which are london, berlin and paris, have implemented national reforms on this issue in a dispersed order, and other places and other member states are preparing to deal with this issue, even if they have agreed to defer their own legislation pending a european initiative. i would like to remind you that outside the european union, the united states has been concerned with this issue of financial stability since the 1930s, with the glass-steagall act. more recently, paul volcker's proposals and the affiliation clause for certain activities have continued this work in the united states. so i want to thank arlene mccarthy for taking on this work on behalf of parliament. i would also like to point out that the work you have done is precisely in the spirit of what i asked erkki liikanen to do, namely to do a thorough job, surrounded by very good experts, and to come up with recommendations on the basis of which we will complete all the calibration studies in the coming weeks. and thank you to the fictional reporters who worked with you. you have succeeded in securing a large majority in the committee on the lines of this report. so, obviously, it reflects a wide diversity of opinions, which is not surprising to me. this is a complex subject, as your rapporteur, arlene mccarthy, with whom i have spoken on this subject many times, well knows. moreover, whenever structural reforms are considered, there are bound to be different views. i would like to highlight a few of these differences. firstly, as regards the objectives of this reform, you clearly state the need to put an end to the so-called 'implied support' of the states for some of the risky activities of the banks. this question of 'implied support' is a point which we are particularly concerned with in the current impact study. the challenge is that banks now pay a fair price for the risks they take - including market risk - and thus are no longer structurally encouraged or incited to prefer speculative activities to financing the real economy. secondly, for what activities can public support still be envisaged? the report examines this question and mentions a number of them, but you are wise to leave this question open because it is also very complex and we will only be able to answer it after we have completed our internal evaluation. thirdly, another point is the complementarity of the structural reforms with all the other financial reforms already adopted or in the process of being adopted. and you saw last week an agreement in the council that will allow the trilogue to be started on the resolution. we are also well advanced now for the implementation of the basel rules in 2014. i am convinced, ladies and gentlemen, that this structural reform will be complementary to all the others. it complements and reinforces some of their objectives. it therefore has its own added value, provided it is properly calibrated. that's what we're doing. in this respect, your report is - i repeat - a good illustration. he referred repeatedly to the directive on bank recovery and resolution. the rules we are about to adopt will be groundbreaking. the draft provides for the possibility of imposing ex officio structural separation on a case-by-case basis if the competent authority deems it necessary to ensure the 'solvability' of the bank in question, in other words its ability to be the subject of an orderly resolution. but this project, which we are discussing, does not allow for horizontal reform in this area, even though this is one of the issues we must examine. i spoke about the resolution, and i also said a word about crd iv, which has the same objectives of robustness. overall, i believe we need to intervene where necessary, in the light of clearly defined prudential and corporate governance objectives. i think that is one of the keys to successful structural reform: not waiting for everything, carefully defining its objectives and adapting the implementation measures. fourthly, as regards the legal form of this initiative, the report mentions a directive, which is consistent with the wish that the forthcoming proposal should be limited to 'principles' which each member state will then have to put into practice. if, however, we have to go into some details on this question in order to make the necessary distinctions, we shall do so. finally, the national reforms under way are starting points - i mentioned them earlier in several countries - in a debate which will ultimately concern only a limited number of the largest european banking groups, a few dozen at most. the crisis, which is not over, has taught us that some groups are more difficult to supervise or deal with in times of great difficulty than others, simply because of their complexity and internal organization. these groups were in fact structurally inclined - as i said earlier - to prefer market activities with higher potential returns but also higher risks and where losses are absorbed by the deposit bank. however, the crisis has shown us that no model - diverse or not - has made it through the crisis without a hitch. in sum, i am convinced that we must respect, within the european framework, the diversity which makes our banking sector strong and resilient. but we must also ensure that the structure of the banks favours the financing of the economy, of the territories, of enterprises, of smes, rather than speculation. we must also ensure that the most risky activities can no longer endanger entire banking groups. finally, i will ensure that european banks remain competitive and are not penalized in comparison with their main global competitors. europe must be an example; it must not be as naive in this area as in others. we must therefore find a balance that preserves the competitiveness of our banks, without accepting that high-risk activities with very little social benefit endanger the activities that are necessary for financing the economy, the regions and small and mediumsized enterprises. these are the main lines of the thinking behind the legislative proposal on which my teams and i are working hard. i must say, ladies and gentlemen, in all sincerity, that my staff are not extendable at will. they are doing a great job. they were focused on supervision, on resolution; the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council and parliament on the subject of the european parliament's role in the european union. and that is why this text on the structure of banks, following on from the liikanen report and with the light of your report, mrs mccarthy, will probably be presented next october.
on behalf of the s&d group. mr president, the reforms already adopted in the banking sector will strengthen the capital requirements and liquidity conditions of financial institutions. we are close to establishing a european framework for the resolution of banking institutions that avoids moral hazard by giving priority to the protection of depositors and avoiding bailouts by taxpayers. but the reform of the banking system is incomplete. financial stability, price formation and the financing of the real economy require structural measures to ensure the effective separation of risks between deposit and investment banking. these measures should take into account the comparative importance of banking intermediation in the european economy and the benefits that universal banking provides to its customers. the liikanen report also noted that the crisis is not related to the banking business model. the commissioner has announced that the pending regulatory initiatives to be presented in october must be designed with both ambition and rigour. after a thorough impact assessment, the report adopted by the committee on economic affairs puts it this way, proposing principle-based legislation to reduce risk and complexity, ensure competition and limit interconnections that are a source of systemic risk. the socialist group supports the mccarthy report because it shares the need for a system of separation which always preserves the operation of the essential activities of the banking sector and allows for early and effective intervention by the supervisory authorities. i would like to congratulate the rapporteur and all her collaborators.

in writing. − in favour. on 4 march 2013 latvia requested a convergence report pursuant to article 140(1) of the treaty on the functioning of the european union (tfeu). the criteria for latvia to adopt the euro on 1 january 2014 are laid out in article 140(1) tfeu. latvia is currently a ‘member state with a derogation’, thus not a member of the euro area. article 140(2) tfeu states that the council, on the basis of the reports from the commission and the ecb and after consulting the european parliament shall, acting by a qualified majority on a proposal from the commission, decide which member states with a derogation fulfil the necessary conditions on the basis of the criteria set out in article 140(1) tfeu, and abrogate the derogations of the member states concerned. on 5 june 2013 the commission proposed in its convergence report that latvia adopts the euro from 1 january 2014. the european parliament has to examine the convergence report with the related legal proposal and issue an opinion. despite certain reservations on individual issues, the rapporteur recommends that the derogation be lifted with effect from 1 january 2014.

in writing. - i voted in favour of this resolution because it seeks to improve road safety conditions in the european union. the resolution sets out the fundamental objective of reducing without delay the number of serious injuries on european roads. the resolution draws attention to vulnerable road users, who together account for 50% of all fatalities in urban accidents in the eu. the resolution also proposes measures to help member states meet the above objective, such as improving emergency and relief services, promoting training in first aid for the civilian population, improving post-accident care and the long-term rehabilitation of accident victims. i have voted in favour of this report because of the role that all this can play in improving the safety of european roads.
in writing. − in favour. pedestrians and cyclists together account for 50 % of all urban road fatalities and a large share of serious injuries. thus, we support the monitoring and further development of technical standards and policies for the protection of the most vulnerable road users – the elderly, young children, disabled persons and cyclists, and call on the commission to provide an overview of urban areas with a 30 km/h speed limit and the effects of that limit on reducing fatalities and serious injuries.
in writing. - i voted in favour of this report because it draws the attention of the hungarian authorities to the violation of fundamental rights which the constitutional reform under way represents. the hungarian government, by this amendment to the constitution, has succeeded in shielding its political decisions and imposing them unilaterally without any consultation or appeal. the report complains about violations of fundamental rights, such as the lack of independence of the judiciary, the lack of guarantees for press freedom and pluralism, the need for electoral reform to guarantee balanced representation in the national electoral committee, etc. a significant number of these complaints to the hungarian government affect the fundamental rights of hungarian citizens, but it also calls on all member states to ensure that their parliaments monitor and respect fundamental rights. i have therefore voted in favour of this report.
in writing. − in favour. for the first time in its history, parliament today declared that legal and constitutional changes in a member state are incompatible with the values of the eu set out in article 2 of the treaty on european union. there is a long list of areas in which hungary is at odds with european values: the independence of the data protection authorities, independence of the judiciary, media pluralism, rights of minorities and rights of the political opposition. the recently adopted fourth amendment to the constitution, in particular, is a reason for serious concern as it gravely undermines the role of the consitutional court. ever since victor orban’s fidesz party obtained a two thirds majority in the hungarian parliament in 2010, there has been a systemic and general trend of changes to hungary’s constitutional and legal framework that are incompatible with common european values as referred to in article 2 of the treaty on european union – democracy, rule of law, liberty, equality and respect for human rights, including the rights of people belonging to minorities.
in writing. - i voted in favour of this resolution because it is a fundamental statement of solidarity with the victims of the numerous floods which have affected many european citizens throughout the year. during the last six months, many european countries have been affected by excessive rainfall and it is essential to provide condolences and institutional support to the relatives and friends of those who have died or disappeared. the resolution, however, not only aims at this but also includes proposals to ensure that such disasters do not happen again. the resolution stresses the role of civil protection mechanisms, stresses the importance of planning investments to avoid the severe impact of these serious events, calls for the organisation of joint emergency responses, etc., and calls for the use of the european union solidarity fund to help the victims. that is why i voted in favour of this resolution.

in writing. - i voted against this report because it dilutes the proposal of the high-level group of experts appointed by the commission to make a proposal for reform of the banking sector. although the proposal put forward by these experts is far from the reform that united left would propose for the european banking sector, it is an interesting proposal because it advocates the separation of banking activity between commercial banks and investment banks. this would ensure the safety of customers' funds and prevent them from being used for speculative activities. this proposal has been further watered down by the amendments of the epp and alde groups, leaving the proposal in a vacuum and eliminating the positive influence this report could have on the future of the eu banking sector. i have therefore voted against this report.
in writing. − in favour. currently in the eu, if you want to start a bank, you can basically engage in any kind of activity you want, as long as you meet the minimum capital requirements set out in the capital requirements directive/regulation. the problem is that, for many risks, banks are effectively asked to work out what they think is an adequate cushion to absorb 99.9 % of losses over a year. the crisis has shown that banks systematically (and often wilfully) underestimated such risks, were undercapitalised when sub-prime, lehmans and the credit crunch hit, and then had to be bailed out to prevent a systemic implosion and stop the economy at large grinding to a halt.
in writing. - i voted in favour of this report because it represents an improvement in the functioning of the audit procedure for european union funds and a step forward in the fight against fraud in european funds. the european commission and olaf reports on the european union's activity in the field of defence of its financial interests and the fight against fraud in 2011 are analysed. these reports express the most important criticisms of the weaknesses in the european union's budgetary control systems for both revenue and expenditure. the commission has already taken a number of measures to combat fraud in the community. i voted in favour of this report because it expresses fundamental criticisms of the eu's control systems.
in writing. − in favour. the eu and the member states share responsibility for the protection of the union’s financial interests and the fight against fraud, and close cooperation between the commission and the member states is essential. the member states have the primary responsibility for implementing some 80 % of the union budget, as well as for the collection of own resources, inter alia in the form of vat and customs duties. the commission has recently undertaken a number of important initiatives on anti-fraud policy measures. thus, parliament stresses that countering fraud and any other illegal activities affecting the financial interests of the union is the obligation of the commission and the member states, as enshrined in the treaty on the functioning of the european union.
in writing. - i voted in favour of this report because it expresses the weaknesses in the approach to this integrated internal control framework. the report includes information on the current margins of error offered by the audit activities carried out by the commission services. in order to integrate member states' audits as part of the single control system, minimum criteria must be met which are not currently met and therefore relying on member states' systems as the only control system would allow for an increase in fraud. the report warns of the dangers that must be avoided before an integrated system is set up and therefore supports the requirement to maintain a double check to enable the audit systems of the member states to be monitored. i voted in favour of this report to maintain the surveillance of the national control systems.
in writing. this report provides an update on the difficulties faced by the european commission and the court of auditors of the union in controlling expenditure. i want to support this report because it encourages the european commission to prevent the slippage of expenditure which is detrimental to the accounts of the european union and thus achieve the sound financial management that citizens expect from their representations, both national and european.
in writing. − in favour. in june 2005, the commission adopted a road map to an integrated internal control framework. the aim was to fulfil its commitment to achieve a positive statement of assurance (das) before the end of its mandate. the implementation of the action plan started in 2006. this working document firstly aims to assess the progress made and the results achieved by the commission in implementing this road map. in its second part, this document raises issues and questions on the future of the integrated internal control framework.

vice-president of the commission. − mr president, first of all i would like to welcome the very strong position that parliament has taken in relation to the prism programme and the alleged spying on the eu and eu member states’ diplomatic premises. this debate has certainly been heard well beyond the borders of the european union. it is important that the united states understands that the european parliament is serious about these issues and that our citizens’ right to privacy is not negotiable. concerning the external affairs and espionage questions, the high representative of the union for foreign affairs and security policy, cathy ashton, is in contact with the us authorities at the highest level. she is seeking explanations and i am sure that she will address this house when she receives answers. i deal with the data protection angle of this debate. here i would like to say how important it is that the message has gone out from all sides of this house that parliament will work towards the swift adoption of the data protection package. parliament knows that any delay in the adoption of data protection reform plays into the hands of those who do not share the objective of high-level data protection in europe. completing the negotiations on the package should be a key deliverable for the committee on civil liberties, justice and home affairs and for parliament as a whole. it is in your hands. concerning the eu-us negotiations on an umbrella agreement, many questions have been raised. we have held 15 rounds of negotiations so far, and i welcome the fact that this house calls on the us to make progress on a number of important points still being negotiated, most of all the question of reciprocity. this is the kind of support i need from parliament in these negotiations. some progress has been made thus far, and agreement on around half of the provisions has been found, but it is now time to address key issues such as equal treatment of eu and us citizens and effective judicial redress. i can tell this house that we would have had an agreement a long time ago if i had given up on these points, but i have not done so because i cannot understand why, for example, a us citizen has the right to redress in the eu while an eu citizen does not have the right to redress in the united states. the reason why we are continuing to negotiate is because i am keeping that point on the table. if i had given that up, we would have signed the agreement already. i will not sign an agreement so long as we do not have reciprocity and have not found solutions in accordance with european law on difficult issues such as data retention. parliament has also asked questions about how to determine the facts and figures regarding what has happened with the prism scandal. i agree. we cannot generalise: we have to know what has really happened. in order to ensure a correctly calibrated policy response, the eu and the us have agreed at ministerial level to set up a transatlantic group of data protection and security experts to clarify what has happened, and to start this clarification process in july. to that end i have received, as i told you yesterday, a letter from us attorney general eric holder, which i followed up with him in a telephone conversation: so the clarification process can now start. this is a fact-finding group, not a political body. it is not a forum for negotiations with the us but rather a place in which to establish, firstly, the functioning and the scale of the programme; secondly, the nature and the scope of oversight of the programme and the question of judicial redress for eu citizens; and, thirdly, how the information gathered via the programme was useful for national security purposes. the political decisions will be taken in this house and by the commission. that is why the commission will keep this house regularly informed on the group’s findings. a final word on another strand of today’s discussions: many members have made a link between the alleged spying on the eu and member states’ diplomatic missions and the transatlantic trade and investment partnership (ttip). as i mentioned in my opening remarks, this question was discussed yesterday by the college of commissioners. the college considers that the beginning of the eu-us trade negotiations should not be affected. however, the commission will make it very clear that, for such negotiations to succeed, there needs to be confidence, transparency and clarity among the negotiation partners. that is why, in parallel with the trade discussions, there will be discussions on security and on data protection. we need to restore confidence. without confidence, strong collaboration between the parties will not be possible.

president-in-office of the council, on behalf of the vice-president of the commission/high representative of the union for foreign affairs and security policy. − mr president, even as we speak, dramatic events in the egyptian capital are underway. this is a moment for all of us in this house to call on the parties to avoid violence and escalating tensions and to engage in the search for a solution to the crisis through dialogue. the moment is indeed critical and the european union special representatives (eusrs) must send an unequivocal message in support of the democratic transition. only a political process leading to an early return to democracy will solve the present crisis. the high representative/vice-president, baroness ashton, this morning urged both sides to show restraint and asked all parties to find a political solution, based on a substantial and inclusive dialogue. as the high representative has stressed since the beginning of the arab spring, deep democracy is not only about elections and majorities. it is much more than that – an independent judiciary, an active civil society and respect for human rights and fundamental freedoms, including freedom of expression. democracy is ultimately about listening to citizens and making compromises, ensuring that the voices of all the people and not simply the majority are heard. we see with deep concern that the demonstrations are turning more and more violent with loss of life and many injured. this is to be deplored. the large number of female protestors being sexually abused is deeply troubling. our thoughts are with the families of these victims. the high representative was in egypt last week and discussed the situation with the president, as well as with the opposition, with this clear message: we have argued since the beginning that the revolution belongs to the egyptian people. the political forces must ensure that the demands and aspirations of the egyptian citizens must be addressed through dialogue and compromise. we will continue to engage at all levels to say loud and clear that the voices of the egyptian people must be heard. the biggest challenge, and indeed the biggest risk for egypt, is the polarisation of its society and political system. as we have all witnessed, millions of protestors took to the streets in egypt demanding the resignation of president morsi and calling for early elections. tens of thousands of islamists maintained their sit-in with smaller protests in some provincial centres. only a year ago mohamed morsi from the muslim brotherhood was appointed egypt’s first democratically elected president, a milestone in egypt’s democratic transition that the eu and the international community welcomed. president morsi immediately announced himself the representative of all egyptians and he smoothly organised a civilian handover of power from the military. since then the eu has invested time and effort to support the democratic evolution of the country, engaging at all levels of government and opposition. eusr bernardino leon has spent months engaged in shuttle diplomacy to cairo to meet with the government, presidency and the whole political opposition in order to build confidence and to find common ground on political and economic issues. all interlocutors agreed that egypt was facing economic and political challenges and they all wanted to do something about it. they also agreed that they have to talk to each other but simply did not seem able to do so. unfortunately the long-awaited government reshuffle in early may did not yield the results wished for, but quite the contrary. at the same time the eu has also been very active in support of respect for human rights in egypt. the recent court ruling sentencing 43 employees of foreign ngos to prison is very worrying and cathy ashton and commissioner füle stressed the crucial role of civil society in egypt’s ongoing transition. eusr for human rights, stavros lambrinidis, travelled to cairo in february and again in mid-june, emphasising the importance of building a society based on the rule of law and on the respect for human rights. the eu has offered technical support to the draft ngo legislation and a law against violence towards women. tangible results of the eusr efforts can be seen in the agreement from the egyptian side to work closely with the venice commission on the draft ngo law. several of its recommendations have been acknowledged and egypt has confirmed its willingness to continue to work closely with the eu and the international community in order to address the remaining problematic provisions of the draft law. finally, concerning the court convictions of 43 ngos and individuals, egypt has confirmed that the egyptian authorities are waiting for a politically appropriate time in order to find a solution. apart from the political stalemate, mistrust and, in many areas, worrying human rights situations which possibly triggered such mass protests, it is a fact that more than two years on egyptians are feeling worse off than they were before 2011. unfortunately the finalisation of an imf arrangement to which fundamental reforms are linked has been continuously postponed. public services are deteriorating with daily power cuts and fuel shortages. the eu stands ready to assist the egyptian people in their efforts to complete their challenging democratic transition. this has been – and continues to be – the eu’s commitment to egypt, but egypt needs to help the eu to help egypt. there is an intrinsic link between political agreement and stability in the economic situation and the return of tourists and foreign direct investment of which egypt is in dire need. in order for our large-scale financial commitments to materialise, the eu and other international donors need political stability and true commitment to democratic and economic reforms. as i put it at the very beginning, the current situation in egypt is evolving very dramatically and now is the time for all of us to call on the parties to avoid violence and escalating tensions.

on behalf of the ppe group mr president, european citizens are increasingly affected by cybercrime. 8% of internet users in the union have suffered identity theft and 12% have been victims of some form of online fraud. furthermore, attacks against information systems have a considerable cross-border dimension, as the connecting elements are often located in different countries. and in view of the debate we have just had on espionage in the united states, i would like to welcome this directive which will allow for joint action by all the member states. i would like to congratulate mrs hohlmeier on her hard and effective work. this framework directive will bring the criminal law rules of the member states closer together on this type of crime, providing for effective, proportionate and dissuasive sanctions and improving cooperation between judicial and police authorities. i therefore encourage member states to implement the directive quickly and correctly to ensure that such behaviour is punished and thus prevent offenders from moving to member states with more lenient rules. in addition, data collection is necessary for the effective fight against cybercrime, but always taking into account that the directive complies with the recognised principles on the protection of personal data. this data will help specialised bodies such as europol and the european information network security agency to better assess the state of network and information security in europe. yes, mrs reding, it is true: on 11 january 2013 f3 was created, working for europol. i take this opportunity to stress its importance and to recommend its proper budget allocation.

trade in services in the world. the group of countries potentially participating in these negotiations represents more than half of our exports and of our imports of commercial services. opening markets to trade in services can therefore bring us important economic benefits. our objective is to negotiate an agreement that is not only ambitious and firmly anchored in the current world trade organization rules on trade in services, known as the gats (general agreement on trade in services), but that also, and most importantly, can be brought back to the gats at a later stage. we do not want to negotiate a ‘super free trade agreement’ between the potential members. we want to avoid creating a competitor to the gats and endangering the primacy of the wto system. the commission therefore appreciates the fact that the resolution is very supportive of the commission line: that, in order to allow for later ‘docking’ into the gats, it is necessary to incorporate gats core articles and concepts in the newly negotiated agreement. this is of the utmost importance, and including that element in the resolution sends a strong signal to our trading partners. the resolution is balanced in listing the services sectors in which the eu has offensive and defensive interests. we are encouraged to approach these negotiations in an ambitious manner, tailoring the objectives to the plurilateral context in which they are taking place. having said that, i would like to reassure you on some important issues that are addressed in the draft resolution. firstly, the commission is fully committed to defending european sensitivities on so-called services of general interest. let me once again make clear that liberalisation does not necessarily mean privatisation. these negotiations will not result in any requirement to privatise services such as water distribution. in this context it is surprising that concerns have been expressed about waste management falling within the scope of the negotiations. waste management is an environmental service, and typically an eu offensive interest, as is also pointed out in your resolution. if markets are made more open, our companies will be able more easily to export the state-of-the-art know-how that can help third countries improve their environmental conditions. secondly, i also note that the draft resolution recommends not entering into trade liberalisation commitments in relation to audiovisual services and cultural services. in the context of these negotiations, the commission will not negotiate eu market access commitments on audiovisual services. however, to exclude cultural services altogether would imply excluding, for example, services by news agencies, which are an eu offensive interest. thirdly, the commission is also aware that a cautious approach is necessary with regard to the temporary movement of natural persons for business purposes (the so-called mode 4). conditions for granting visas are not part of the wto services rulebook and will not therefore be part of these negotiations. discussions in this regard will be limited to issues of due process in administrative procedures and transparency. negotiations on a plurilateral trade in services agreement represent a great opportunity for the european union. i hope that parliament can support us further once the negotiations begin. commissioner de gucht and dg trade will keep you fully informed on the state of play.
on behalf of the ppe group madam president, as the commissioner has just said, trade in services is undoubtedly a key sector of our economies and of trade in the 21st century. this plurilateral agreement will enable us to move forward in trade in services between the european union and the 21 trading partners, following the stalemate of the doha round in december 2011. the resolution which will be voted on tomorrow by this parliament calls for the promotion of an ambitious agenda of offensive interests by the european union in many sectors. sectors such as financial, e-commerce, tourism and construction, among others. the agreement, as the commissioner has also said, must be broad and comprehensive and compatible with the general agreement on trade in services of the world trade organisation. the latter has a twofold purpose: to facilitate the participation of new members, who may be added at a later stage, and to allow for the possible multilateralisation of the agreement at a later stage. this open door to multilateralisation should be an incentive for the involvement, and in the future their accession to the agreement, of emerging economies such as brazil, china or india. the protectionist trend we are witnessing as a result of the world economic crisis calls for new bilateral or, as in this case, multilateral initiatives to help combat all measures restricting trade in services. finally, although the two-year deadline for its conclusion seems too ambitious, i believe that there is sufficient political will, especially in view of the serious economic situation and the benefits this agreement will bring to all parties.
mr president, first of all, i would like to say that i fully agree with what malcolm harbour has said here and i would like to stress that we are not just going to vote on one more resolution in this parliament today. during this term, we have worked hard in different areas to achieve the goal we set ourselves at the beginning of this term: completing the digital single market and making the most of the possibilities offered by the digital economy, the full potential of the so-called digital revolution. in this legislature, in this parliamentary seat, we have passed reports whose fundamental purpose was to achieve that goal, such as the september 2010 report completing the internal market for e-commerce, or more recently, in october 2012, the report completing the digital single market. a specific working group on the digital single market has also been set up. it has been in operation for more than two and a half years and has held a total of 16 meetings to date, with an average of 70 people attending each meeting, including members of this parliament, representatives of the european commission and also representatives of industry and the main consumer and business associations. in this context, the presence of vice-president neelie kroes and commissioner barnier at one of these meetings in june 2012 is noteworthy. this resolution is largely based on the work and conclusions reached at all the meetings and also on the reports mentioned above, but it is not limited to that. what we're voting on here is something much more important. we are now about to close the circle we started years ago with a strong parliamentary declaration that shows this commitment and in which we ask the other institutions - the commission and the council - to commit themselves equally to implementing the policies needed to make it effective. we have commissioner barnier here today, who has done a great job of bringing this about and has shown a great willingness and determination to make words into deeds. other commissioners have also made a major contribution to the fact that we are now definitely moving towards the achievement of a true digital single market. we have passed a number of legislative and non-legislative proposals during the course of the legislature and are in the parliamentary process to make a major step towards this goal. today i am talking, for example, about the consumer rights directive, the online dispute resolution regulation, the work on intellectual property rights, cloud computing, data protection, connectivity, to name just a few. let us do it and let us continue to work together towards the realization of the dream of a true digital single market in europe. i have always said, and i will continue to say, that the way out of the crisis is also digital. let's make it a reality.
mr president, commissioner, i will try to make efficient use of my 90 seconds, but i cannot help but start by congratulating the rapporteurs, my colleagues malcolm harbour and pablo arias. information and communication technologies are being a definitive accelerator of the development of this old project, which is now more than 50 years old and which is at the heart of the european project, which is the european internal market. information and communication technologies have been helping to make the european internal market fully operational over the last five years, developing that part of the market which we call the 'digital market', but which is only one aspect, one dimension, of the european internal market. i want to focus on an aspect which i think has not yet been sufficiently addressed by all of us who are putting our energies and efforts into this: the full digitalisation of the public sector. the public sector is of decisive importance in europe, it is an accelerator. if we really achieve full digitisation of the public sector, of european public administrations, we will be driving the development of the internal market and, with it, the european digital market forward at an extraordinary speed.
on behalf of the green group in the european parliament mr president, congratulations to the rapporteur for presenting a serious problem: saving public services such as health and social care. the troika's interference in national budgets, as well as the anti-social and austerity measures of some member states, have a direct social impact with consequences of poverty and social exclusion. these services are key, given the demographic and social consequences of the crisis, the severe impact of the crisis on access to healthcare for vulnerable groups is evidence of the severe austerity and social cuts that some member states have been pursuing. europe was an example of a social model and now europe is on the way to reducing social welfare, access to public services and equal opportunities. we are talking about the most vulnerable citizens, the most deprived, the most excluded, the poorest, those who have become poorer as a result of the crisis. we have almost 25% of people in europe who are not living in poverty. now, the face of the vulnerable person is not the same as it was a decade ago, now, anyone can be vulnerable: by losing a job, by losing a home, by having a low salary, by being young or by being old, any group can be chronically poor. we are seeing, without a doubt, the emergence of a new group of vulnerable women and men, the new needy. public services are therefore of great importance to our lives and their dismantling is evidence that the current european construction is contrary to essential human rights, preferring to dismantle basic services rather than support them. under the pretext of the crisis, many member states have consolidated the privatisation of health, promoting two types of health, one for the rich and the other for the poor, reduced services, limited public access to certain groups to health care and reimbursement of certain treatments, medicines, prosthetics, essential food, reimbursement of ambulance programmes, and social services such as addiction. some member states have also created barriers through social security rules. examples include cases where health insurance ceases after a period of unemployment or where systems deny access to urgent primary care for certain groups, such as undocumented immigrants, as is the case in spain. or the cases where systems that only consider full-time workers to the detriment of part-time or casual workers. women, especially ethnic minority women and migrant women, are also particularly disadvantaged. some member states are modifying or reforming their social security systems, and the number of people experiencing homelessness or in short-term accommodation is increasing in some member states, which in many cases jeopardises the continuity of social services. increasing co-financing costs and revenues are preventing these people from seeking care at an early stage, leading to the incidence of later, more expensive and urgent health care. the shame and stigma of seeking care for certain diseases, such as aids or even cancer, also leads to reduced services. the same applies to the wage cuts resulting from the abandonment of support, which have resulted, for example, in the closure of basic hospitals, as happened in galicia, my country, or in the case of health workers who emigrate, such as spanish nurses who go to the united kingdom or germany. examples of cuts in investment, as happened in my country, where 650 000 galicians are excluded, where 17 000 households do not receive a single euro and where 50% of young people are unemployed. please react to this very serious problem.

vice-president of the commission. − mr president, honourable members, tomorrow you will vote on the text of the directive on the right of access to a lawyer and to communicate upon arrest. that will be a big moment: i believe it will be a moment which shows that the european union stands for the rights of the individual. i would like to congratulate your rapporteur, ms antonescu, because not only was this difficult work, but she also had to exercise great diplomacy. together with the shadow rapporteurs, she succeeded in retaining the ambition of this very important directive, and that is an achievement of which this house can be proud. i would also like to echo the rapporteur by including the irish presidency in my tribute. building on the work of previous presidencies, it negotiated very hard to get the job done and to reach a good agreement. it is just over two years now since our proposal was tabled in june 2011 and, thanks to the commitment and spirit of compromise on all sides, an agreement has been reached. i know that the discussions were not always easy – it was hard to find compromises, for instance on the matter of remedies and on derogations – but we now have a text that retains the original level of ambition and is compatible with the standards of the european court of human rights. for me, access to a lawyer is at the core of procedural rights, and it is central to what citizens and practitioners across the union expect from us. there are 8 million criminal proceedings in the eu every year, and the right of defence for anyone suspected of a crime is recognised as a basic element of a fair trial. under this directive, citizens will have a right to have a lawyer present when they are questioned by the police. when a suspect is arrested, he or she will have the opportunity to communicate with family. if suspects are outside their country, they will have the right to be in contact with their country’s consulate. very importantly too, the confidentiality of meetings and any form of communication between a suspect and his lawyer will be respected in order to ensure the effective exercise of the rights of the defence. the derogations are very narrow and limited to exceptional circumstances, such as geographical remoteness. persons subject to a european arrest warrant will have the possibility of legal advice both in the country where the arrest is made and in the country where the warrant was issued. this dual representation is a major novelty being introduced by the directive. it will serve to increase the effectiveness of the european arrest warrant and will guarantee the applicability in practice of the rights concerned. it will also be our task to look at the implementation of this directive, crucially with regard to consistency with, and the practical applicability of, existing eu legislation such as, for example, the european arrest warrant. the directive thus makes a decisive contribution to strengthening the mutual trust that is needed to implement the european arrest warrant or other eu mutual recognition instruments. after its final adoption, we will have to work on the transposition of this piece of legislation. the commission will closely follow how the directive is transposed in the member states’ legal systems and will scrutinise how things work in practice. in due time, it will present a report evaluating the directive’s implementation on the ground. i am very proud of what we are doing here and what we have achieved in the area of procedural rights. remember that we have a directive on interpretation and translation, a directive on the right to information and, now, a directive on access to a lawyer – and in parallel we have been working on the victims directive, which was adopted last year and which ensures that victims are treated with respect, that they have procedural rights to be informed, supported and protected, and that they have access to justice and can actively participate in criminal proceedings. step by step we are strengthening the european area of justice and the rule of law that binds the european union. to round up our work on the procedural rights agenda, the commission intends to present measures on the presumption of innocence, on special safeguards for suspects and accused persons who are children, and on legal aid. it is still my intention to present these this autumn. let me conclude by stressing that i have the greatest respect for the european parliament’s role as co-legislator in the area of criminal law. we have made great progress and i think it will be important during the european election campaign to tell our citizens about parliament’s contribution as co-legislator to what has been achieved and about the success stories.
mr president, as the alternative rapporteur for this directive from the socialist group, i would like to stress, again today, that tomorrow we are going to vote on a very important part of the package of procedural guarantees which the swedish presidency has started by drawing up this road map. this package was urgent if we wanted to make a europe of law. so far, we have fought for a secure europe with the european arrest warrant, although we hope that the commission will address its evolution and reform as soon as possible. but now, with this directive, we are also making it possible for this europe to be fairer, also for people who have a european arrest warrant on them. in this directive we have fought for everyone to have a lawyer from the moment they know that they are suspected. i have to say to mrs antonescu, to the commission and to the irish presidency that we have finally managed to reach agreements on very important issues, because this is not a directive on combating terrorism but a directive on guarantees. so everything we have achieved on confidentiality, on limitation, on exceptions, etc. becomes one big text. unfortunately, this right of access will not be a reality for everyone. the commission has refused to include free legal aid in this right, where the suspect has no financial means. nor does it consider the case of the disabled and minors. as this legislature is far advanced, we fear we are setting the minimums only for those suspects who can afford this right of access. neither the vulnerable nor the minors are here. let us hope that this legislature will not put an end to this serious deficiency.
mr president, this directive strengthens the criminal procedure: it provides for more guarantees, more justice and better quality. suspects and accused persons shall have access to a lawyer from the earliest stage of the proceedings, whether or not they have been deprived of their liberty; such lawyer may request a notification of the proceedings and, in addition, there shall be no limitations on the duration and frequency of his meetings. suspects and accused persons will have the right of communication at the time of arrest with a person of their choice and, last but not least, communications between the suspect and his lawyer will be carried out in strict confidentiality, without exceptions - in my view. i would like to congratulate elena oana antonescu on an excellent job which involves tremendous tenacity and dedication in the face of such a complicated issue and, finally, i would like to encourage the commission to present the report on free legal aid.
mr president, as a lawyer for four decades, i welcome the important step that is being taken today, but at the same time i regret that this directive does not cover the right to free justice, which is too scattered in the purely national sphere. i believe that free, quality and timely justice - as just said - as we conceptually have in spain thanks to the shift - even if the current minister does not show enthusiasm for the institution and the fair remuneration of young lawyers - would guarantee the rights of the accused and ensure faster and more consistent justice. it does not have to involve a higher cost to the public purse and can be beneficial for everyone, especially for freedom and democracy.
mr president, i would like to thank mrs antonescu for her work. all the directives which are designed to affect the criminal systems of the member states are complex, but they contribute to improving the protection of fundamental rights. this directive will remind them all that the european court of human rights does not consider evidence obtained in police interrogations without lawyers present to be valid. it will also improve the procedures for complaints against exceptions to the general rule of facilitating access to legal aid. i hope we can make some progress next time. i understand the difficulties in the fight against organised crime, because we have suffered this scourge in my country, but i regret that these exceptions have led to some cases of torture. i believe that the video surveillance of incommunicado detentions, already implemented by the ertzaintza (basque police), prevents this risk. it might be a good idea to incorporate it into the minimum threshold of safeguards that all police forces in europe must observe. mrs. reding, remember this as good practice for all european police forces.

of conventional biofuels in the 10% target is the central element of our commission proposal. a cap on conventional biofuels at approximately their current market share provides a balance between the committee on economic and monetary affairs and industrial policy has adopted a number of amendments to the proposal. - mr president, no one in this house disputes that indirect land use change exists and that it is a phenomenon that must be addressed. we all agree that we must put a limit on the production of conventional biofuels and encourage the development of advanced biofuels. the sensitive point is the iluc factors. the available studies based on models and not on direct measurement give different figures, and these will always be subject to change as more information becomes available or models are revised. furthermore, as models are refined, the factors go down. turning figures, which are currently being discussed and are rapidly evolving, into binding legislation for the member states, with potentially harmful effects on this booming industrial sector, is an imprudence which i hope the house will not commit. it is preferable to set a cap on conventional biofuels that is not detrimental to investments already made, combined with a specific target for advanced biofuels. we therefore share the aim of this legislation, but we are obliged to find a way of achieving it.

member of the commission. mr president, i would like to thank the rapporteur for his report. i am grateful to parliament for the contribution our efforts are making to the completion of the internal market and for the fact that our communication on this subject has led to intensive and constructive consultation in parliament. the initiative we have today is fully supported. the question may be asked: why do we want to complete a single market for electricity and gas? we have the single market for other products and services. it is the foundation of the european union for 500 million workers, entrepreneurs, producers, consumers and service providers! electricity and gas were the late-born child here, they are only 17 and 15 years old respectively when they are subject to european law. we believe that electricity and gas are not quite the same as cars, textiles and food, but we are convinced that the internal market, when completed, will also bring benefits in the energy sector, first and foremost for the consumer, the european citizen, both in private life and in the workplace, in the household and in industry, if the citizen is empowered as a consumer. we therefore support the approach in your own-initiative report to put the consumer at the centre by calling for transparency, by giving him strong rights, by giving him opportunities for choice and exchange in competition, by also allowing him to be active and to become an exporter on the market, not only as a consumer but also as a producer and self-producer, through micro-production. that is why the two accounts today fit together. we believe that the single market has made great progress in the wholesale sector, but that the benefits of the single market have not yet been realised by the end consumer. in order to complete the end-user market, we must first of all promote the further development of networks at every level: transmission networks, cross-border networks, large super-line and pipelines. unfortunately, this often means that the distribution networks and their intelligent control are not adequately addressed in public debate, including the last meters and the intelligent recording of electricity consumption in households and industry on the spot. we are therefore faced with a vast new network whose standard-setting is our task. that's partly moderation and planning, where we can shorten approval times. but ultimately, the member states and their tsos, their utilities and their on-site approval procedures are just as important. we are often asked when the single market will be completed and we have the target of 2014. by 2014, we will have achieved a lot: common grid quality, common standards. but i would argue that completion will remain an ongoing task for many years to come, for example by strongly advising against any further regulation of consumer prices. we believe that regulated retail prices are not sensible. in some member states, retail prices are regulated and therefore do not represent the full cost of electricity production or gas purchase. then someone else will pay. the situation in spain in the electricity sector, where billions are lost, and another 5 billion are added every year, and this must eventually be paid for by the taxpayer, cannot be a solution. we believe that the right way is to have the price/price formation in the market, in competition, regulated by supply and demand and controlled by the regulator, and not to have the price regulated. we are currently having an emerging debate in the electricity sector on capacity mechanisms and backup strategies. the commission will be submitting proposals in the autumn. we believe that some backup potential is necessary to maintain security of supply in the face of an increasing number of still volatile renewables. but 28 capacity mechanisms parallel and separate fragmented we think are wrong. we believe that this is why the rapid expansion of interconnectors to compensate for the imbalances between member states is the right way, the more cost-effective way and the more market-oriented way. we are convinced that the clear definition of how the internal market is to be completed will also encourage private investment. the commission has already taken a number of measures to improve the energy efficiency of buildings and industry, including the introduction of a new energy efficiency standard for buildings and industry. mrs merkies raised the subject of micro-generation. we believe, as you do, that micro-production will become more important, especially in the private sector, for its own use, but also for subcontracting to public networks. we believe that small chp plants can be of complementary importance here. what do we advise? it is often said that we need only large or only small installations. i think we should solve this. we need some large units in the future and an increasing number of decentralized small units. not either or, but both is the answer to our energy consumption! while some people talk only about production, others only about increasing efficiency, my advice is generally that we need more efficiency and yet modern, sustainable, affordable production. some people talk about offshore wind and desertec, others talk about the windmill, decentralized generation and geothermal and photovoltaic in the village. the energy demand of europe and the world will be so great that, in general, the answer is not either or, but both and, that is, everything. this is why we support micro-generation with our european programmes - a proven programme is the intelligent energy europe programme - both politically and financially, but also in research, and we will continue to do so in the coming years in our various activities, including smart cities and communities. we also need the member states on the subject of micro-generation. appeals from strasbourg alone will not help. if we, mrs merkies, turn to some of the member states of central and eastern europe with your idea, which i support, for example, the response is still relatively muted, because it is still thought of in large units and new large units. we are faced with the common task of forming opinions, also in this house, and of explaining this to our colleagues and of providing the necessary support to the local actors. i am grateful for both reports and hope that the adoption of the resolution will support our work also vis-à-vis the member states. there is a clear commitment in the european council, in parliament, in the commission to an internal market for electricity and gas, and we should see it completed in the next few years. the consumer will be grateful.

the following is the report by mr antolín sánchez presedo, on behalf of the committee on economic and monetary affairs, on the proposal for a directive of the european parliament and of the council on credit agreements for residential immovable property (com ((2011) 0142 c7-0085/2011 2011/0062 ((cod)) (a7-0202/2012).
the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the financial sector is not subject to excessive regulation. today we are debating and voting on the first mortgage directive in the european union. it's legislation of enormous importance to families and economic recovery. 70% of europeans live in their own homes, most of which have been purchased with mortgage credit. the volume of mortgages exceeds 52% of community gdp and its growth potential is considerable. in eleven member states its share of gdp is still below 30%. it is legislation that improves the single market, advancing financial integration. eight years ago the green paper proposed community action to lower the cost of credit, to expand the range of ancillary products, to reduce credit risk and to strengthen consumer protection. promoting responsible lending is essential to build confidence in mortgage markets, damaged by a crisis triggered by financial misconduct, and around housing markets. this directive, which is necessary to meet the commitments made within the g20, incorporates the international principles adopted by the financial stability board, placing the european union at the forefront of global mortgage law. it establishes a robust framework for a more transparent and professional, secure and competitive market with a high level of consumer protection and financial inclusion. lenders, intermediaries and their representatives must meet minimum requirements of competence and knowledge and must comply with obligations regarding their business conduct. the admission and supervision of all of them, including non-credit institutions, is ensured. personalised and comparable pre-contractual information in accordance with a european standard must be provided, the consumer's creditworthiness must be assessed and products which are artificially linked and do not respect the consumer's choice must not be marketed. the property valuation document, which was carried out by a professional valuator acting independently, must also be kept. the directive for the first time requires member states to take measures for financial education of consumers, a seven-day period for reflection on pre-contractual offers or withdrawals from contracts and the possibility of receiving advice based on the best interests of consumers and differentiated from mere commercial advice. provisions are made for contracts with special risks, such as foreign currency and variable rate mortgages. the commission will therefore be required to provide for a variety of calculations and scenarios and precise rules to mitigate exchange rate risks and avoid interest rate manipulation. the first response, in case of problems, cannot be foreclosure. surcharges for non-payment should be limited to compensating for the costs incurred and should only be authorised where member states set ceilings for them. member states, which may always take additional measures compatible with fair solutions to the problems arising from the crisis, may not prevent payment for services when the parties so wish and must ensure that best efforts are made to obtain the price of the goods executed. when debt exists, a minimum of survival must be ensured and over-indebtedness in the long term avoided. although the directive must be transposed within two years, its new principles should guide the application of the member states' national law from the moment of its entry into force. beyond the directive, further work is needed to ensure responsible lending. the directive identifies issues that need to be addressed in depth in its first review, such as traceability, the post-contractual phase, the availability and comparability of price data or the transparency of penalties. it also mandates the commission to draw up a report on private over-indebtedness, the monitoring of credit registers and the move towards more flexible and reliable markets. it is said that the european fiscal union will require the issuing of eurobonds. the full maturity of the mortgage market will come when there is a euro banknote market. this directive is a step in that direction. i am grateful to the rapporteurs and all the collaborators who have made this result possible.
i am speaking on behalf of the gue/ngl group. mr president, i would like to thank mr sánchez presedo for his efforts to try to make all the member states of the european union see that the first home is not a commodity, it is a right: a right that must be protected. unfortunately, the european commission has so far acted more like a branch of the big banks than as a body of the european union guaranteeing that right. in southern europe and elsewhere, evictions have created absolutely unnecessary pain (in greece, portugal, spain - in the latter country alone, 400 000 evictions) for people who are left on the streets, who have no protection; and the european commission is only interested today in securing the big profits of big banks. when attempts have been made to regulate it - for example, by the regional government of andalusia, in spain - the european commission has immediately said no, that it cannot be regulated by a decree-law guaranteeing the social function of housing. that is why this step is very important, and i thank mr sánchez presedo for continuing to work to make this right - the right to housing - a reality and a reality that must be protected in order to put an end to the financial frauds that the european commission and the central bank have encouraged.
mr president, first of all i would like to congratulate the rapporteur and the alternative rapporteurs, as well as the commissioner for the internal market, on the great effort they have made to get this directive through. it has been an honour to work with them on this subject of particular sensitivity for europeans and also for spaniards. as i said, this is one of the main directives of this parliament, since the right to decent housing is a basic right for all european citizens. mortgage loans are a particularly sensitive element, and the romans already gave them special protection. this protection, which is a longstanding european tradition, is reflected in the text we are voting on today. the protection of the borrower is a constant in the text, so the emphasis is on transparency between the parties, who are required to have minimum knowledge and competence requirements. as regards enforcement - a point of particular interest in my country - the directive provides for mandatory minimum requirements and the possibility for contractors to include a clause on the payment of a fee, as already provided for in the spanish legal order. in addition, spanish legislation on spanish loans has also been reformed and follows the line of this directive to avoid cases of abusive clauses and to ensure limits on default and that lenders negotiate before executing. it is therefore a particularly sensitive directive, and as such has been worked on by parliament, which will benefit the european citizen by creating a stable framework of greater legal certainty and uniformity in the european union. finally, i would like to call on the parties to unblock the remaining issues and this directive can become a reality as soon as possible.

keeping that promise today.
president-in-office of the council. − mr president, honourable members, this was indeed a very important and very interesting debate; it was especially interesting that some of you recalled national practices. mr zalba recalled practices from his country. my conclusion is that really the consumer side is the most important side. i can understand why this is so; it is because in the mortgage deal it is the consumer who takes out the mortgage who is the weaker side of the contract. there is no politics involved; this is absolutely normal legal practice to defend the weaker part of the contract. we must do this by putting regulation in place, but by also by relying on market forces. of course, the market can resolve many, many difficult issues by itself, but this market should be regulated and this is one of the purposes of this directive. the real conclusion is that the consumer side is very important: mr de backer, mr strejček, mr lamberts, mr meyer, ms thein, and many other colleagues here in this hall have talked about this. but, this leads to another of my thoughts, which is that we really see it as urgent that this question be resolved. we have a piece of quite good quality legislation, but this quality is not perfect. mr pallone, i very much like your idea that if we look for perfection in legislation, as if we were looking for the most perfect car, we will end up with none. i agree with you, so i think that the urgency which was stressed in many of the contributions is really the urgency with which we should look for the result. i therefore call on you again to vote in favour of this directive so that we can finish with it at the first reading. i can promise that the council will be very happy to agree, as a co-legislator, to the final result voted today.

unfortunately necessary, as we have seen - to take sanctions to deter or to repress. the proposal to regulate the 'shadow' banking system and the monetary funds is now on your table. we are continuing our efforts because, as mrs regner has said, we still have work to do in the months ahead. mr klinz said something important about the evolution of the financial markets, which is extremely rapid. we must be able to adapt, to evolve, to revisit this subject to try to keep up with the speed at which the financial markets are changing. sometimes, some in these financial markets will try to circumvent or circumvent the rules to avoid certain sanctions. again, we will have a short memory and we will have to be uncompromising. that is why the revision clause in this text is important: it will enable us to adapt the rules, to evaluate the content of this text which we are adopting today. mrs swinburne, you feel that the 15% penalty on turnover is not enough. i understand your point of view and i can agree with you on this, but it is a compromise between the various member states and parliament. i would remind you that this is a minimum which is now mandatory for the first time. there is nothing to prevent member states - including your own - from going much further if they find that 15% penalty not enough. in any case, we will assess this point, as we will all the others, in the context of the review clause. i want to emphasize that the signal that we are sending and that you are sending today by your vote is extremely important with regard to a number of people who have thought that everything was allowed in the financial markets, and to whom we had allowed everything. now, thanks to the vote of parliament and the work of the council, that will no longer be the case.

i have just mentioned are also very important and provide answers to so many of the daily questions that need to be answered. we have indeed focused a great deal of our efforts on finding a balanced solution for the reciprocity and suspension mechanisms. we needed to find effective instruments of solidarity which, while not neglecting the union's external relations, would give a response of solidarity to situations of discriminatory treatment of our citizens. i understand and respect the concerns of some colleagues about the impact of these mechanisms on third countries, but we must protect european citizens and seek solutions to the problems that millions of citizens are currently facing. i think of poles, romanians, bulgarians, czechs or cypriots. this agreement contains this solution and also does not seek confrontation with third countries, all the while protecting the powers that the lisbon treaty gives parliament. we all know the horizontal problem of the use of delegated and implementing acts, but there is general agreement that this issue should be studied on a case-by-case basis. all the legal arguments are open to interpretation, but it is clear that the use of legislative mechanisms depends on the legal purpose behind the decision to be taken. the fact that the text was adopted unanimously by the council is proof of the suitability of these solutions, and that until july it had the almost unanimous support of all the political groups in this house. if we read the history of this file, we see that what we have today is a reflection of what we talked about in 2011, at the beginning of the debate. we all draw red lines that we have not crossed: automaticity, solidarity, interinstitutional equality and respect for the union's external relations. and that is why i can present this agreement to you today and defend it, knowing that it is the best answer we can give to the challenge we set ourselves more than two years ago.
member of the commission. − madam president, honourable members, despite the problems with the reciprocity mechanisms which i explained in my opening remarks, i prefer now to focus on the positive elements of this compromise and, above all, on the fact that we will now have a suspension mechanism which ensures the credibility of our visa policy and provides it with a tool to fight abuses. rest assured that this mechanism is a last resort and that the commission will ensure that it is only used if and when all the conditions are met. the parliament will be regularly informed of the different steps related to the implementation of the two mechanisms. i am aware of the importance of ensuring visa-free travel between the schengen area and our closest partners and neighbours. arriving at the visa-free regime was often a long and complex process and we will not reverse it carelessly without considering all the consequences. let me say a few words on the western balkans visa policy. first of all, the suspension mechanism is not an instrument especially designed to cover the western balkan countries. it is of a general application for all countries enjoying a visa-free regime with the schengen area and could be applied to any of them, including any countries that will benefit from a visa waiver in the future. however, the situation in the western balkans requires our special attention. this is due to its impact on the eu’s enlargement policy and the eu’s visa liberalisation and asylum policies and practice on the one hand, and on the other hand it is due to still high but decreasing numbers of asylum applications by nationals of the western balkan countries in certain eu member states. we are working with the western balkan countries and affected member states to monitor the situation closely and find solutions. once the suspension mechanism is available we cannot exclude that, if the current situation continues, one or more member states will trigger the mechanism. it must, however, be clear that triggering this mechanism will not automatically lead to suspending the visa waiver. the commission will have to assess whether the conditions of the mechanisms are met and we have to assess the gravity of the situation. the parliament will be informed of the situation throughout the procedure.
