in writing. − in favour. the current crisis puts significant constraints on public finances of the member states. moreover, in the context of the ongoing financial and economic crisis, sub-national (regional and local) authorities are increasingly faced with a challenging conundrum as regards their capacity to secure productive investment. on the one hand, they witness a sharp decrease in their revenues, as central governments cut transfers and ask regional and local governments to contribute towards austerity, while on the other they have to secure increasingly demanding social services, as result of the crisis, putting an extra pressure on their public purses. in this particular context, the ep considers it important to make concrete proposals in order to allow all possible flexibility for the national co-financing of eu development expenditure in a context of rigorous implementation of the stability and growth pact. this will be done by analysing to what extent the current crisis has impacted on the capacity of sub-national authorities to pursue the objectives of growth and jobs contained in the europe 2020 strategy and by suggesting ways to improve the financing capacity of these entities towards productive investments.
in writing. - the economic crisis has led to a decline in productive activity, a worrying rise in unemployment and an accentuation of the structural problems of each country or region, seriously increasing interterritorial social and economic disparities. national governments have been forced to apply more austere budgets and therefore local and regional authorities - whose role is essential in the path towards the europe 2020 targets on jobs, growth and social cohesion - have been faced with less funding at a time of growing need. given these conditions, i think it is appropriate to support the call for the measures of the stability and growth pact to be made more flexible and for the macroeconomic principles and conditions of cohesion policy to be revised, an effective instrument for employment and growth which would only penalize those regions already hit by the crisis.
mr president, this report responds to a historic request from the fisheries committee of this parliament to the european commission in relation to agreements with third countries, in which it has historically called for coherence within the european union between fisheries, trade and development policies, the need for a general strategy with the pacific and a fisheries strategy based on a regional approach. i believe that these policies can help to improve relations between the european union and the pacific, to improve the fight against illegal fishing, to improve legal security for european vessels - which i have to say represent only 2% of the vessels present there, because the rest are mostly asian - and to increase the development of the fishing community in third countries, both in infrastructure and in processing enterprises, because that has to be the european contribution: also the economic and social development of those countries. the european presence is a guarantee of fighting illegal fishing and, as i say, of doing so with greater transparency and greater involvement of the sector and of this parliament.
in writing. - i did not vote in favour of the report because, although it contains various points which i consider to be positive, both for fishermen and for the pacific countries, it places the negotiations in the fisheries sector within the framework of an association agreement. by including this fisheries agreement in the negotiations for an association agreement with the pacific, the european union is once again demonstrating that it does not look after the interests of the peoples with whom it has relations, but that it makes its negotiations conditional on accepting its economic imperialism and the interests of its multinational companies. an association agreement with the pacific countries can only produce relations of economic dependence, since these are two regions which are profoundly unequal. my group tried to remove the references to the association agreement, but without success, and that is why i did not vote in favour of this report.
in writing. − in favour. this report recommends that a long term-fisheries strategy be established for the western and central pacific area which takes into account the need for eu policies to be coordinated in order to enhance potential synergies, achieve a multiplier effect that maximises the benefits both for the pacific states and for the eu countries, and raise the eu’s profile in that region. the pacific is extremely rich in fish, and is the largest fishing ground for highly migratory species, and in particular tuna, with 80% of the world’s catch. this is especially the case for the western and central pacific, where 49% of such fish were taken in 2010 and 52% in 2011. there are seven regional groups of acp countries, five of which are in africa, one in the caribbean and the other in the pacific. the pacific region consists of 15 island states: the cook islands, east timor, fiji, kiribati, the marshall islands, the federated states of micronesia, nauru, niue, palau, papua new guinea, samoa, the solomon islands, tonga, tuvalu and vanuatu.
in writing. - i could not vote in favour of this report because, although it seeks to make progress in improving fisheries relations between member states and third countries with waters in the mediterranean and the black sea, it does so without respecting the sovereignty of other countries. the report covers absolutely necessary points such as the establishment of international maritime zones for the conservation of species in the said seas, harmonization of fishing rules, etc. however, the report presents this negotiation in terms which are absolutely arrogant and intrusive. the report proposes that the remaining mediterranean and black sea countries should adhere to the principles of the cfp and introduces terms on the control and safety of waters by the eu and the member states. i have not voted for this report because of its interventionist nature.
in writing. − in favour. by 2025, urban development in the mediterranean may reach a level of 60 %, with a third of the population concentrated in coastal areas, thus doubling the demand on water and on fishing resources. the mediterranean sea carries 30 % of the world’s maritime traffic. the mediterranean and the black sea have specific characteristics from an oceanographic, fisheries, environmental and socio-economic perspective. the management of maritime and coastal areas is complex and involves various private and public authorities. the mediterranean and black sea basins have a very low water renewal rate (80-90 years and 140 years respectively) and are therefore extremely sensitive to marine pollution. approximately 75 % of the fish stocks of the mediterranean sea are overexploited. legal regimes governing access by vessels to national fisheries vary according to the nationality of the vessel. given the above situation, we should be very concerned over greater competition for fewer stocks and marine resources, leading to the creation of regional tensions and possible disputes between coastal states about maritime areas. increased efforts at regional, national and eu level towards enhancing the regulation of access to resources are needed.
president-in-office of the council. − madam president, i am grateful for this opportunity to contribute and respond to the question from the industry, research and energy committee. i am sure that we all agree that the european research area (era), with its strong links to innovation and education policy, is of fundamental importance to the future development and prosperity of the european union. the notion of a european research area dates back to early 2000, and over the intervening years has been shaped to respond to the changing research environment. both the european council and council have played a key role in giving direction to the range of measures which have been required to put the era in place. back in 2000, the european council recognized the importance of ensuring that europe was able to compete globally, and that a key to this was to develop a knowledge-based society. it underlined the importance of research and development to the generation of economic growth, employment and social cohesion, and it launched the first steps on the path to establishing a european research area. since then, the council has regularly assessed progress and provided guidance on the additional measures needed for the successful completion of the era. in december last year the council adopted conclusions on a reinforced european research area partnership for excellence and growth in which a number of specific points for action were identified. as we all know, at times of austerity it is a challenge to maintain high levels of public investment in r&d. recently we have seen a decline in research as a percentage of overall government spending in some member states. that is why we opted for open national-level competition, which is essential if we are to derive maximum value from public investment in research. we also support member states and the regions in developing smart specialisation strategies to enable them to use structural funds for research and innovation. an era can only work effectively if we can achieve economies of scale through cooperation between member states. one of the best examples is the joint programming process and the cooperation on initiatives to address some of the main challenges we face in our society today. another example is the focus on developing world-class facilities and research infrastructures. these are essential if we are to attract talent and stimulate innovation through science and education. to achieve a fully open labour market for researchers, the council highlighted the need for transparent, open and merit-based recruitment, which would make research careers more attractive. it also stressed the importance of improving human resources policies within research organisations, and promoting innovative doctoral training and cooperation between the academic and business worlds. this has to include improved mobility and the mutual recognition of academic degrees. gender inequality means that the potential of female researchers frequently goes to waste. that is why the council called for the strengthening of both national and eu strategies in order to provide better opportunities for female researchers. the council also recognised the importance of more extensive and more rapid access to scientific publications and data in order to assist researchers and businesses to make better use of the findings of publicly funded research. monitoring all these initiatives is, of course, the key. the council has underlined the importance of tracking progress on achieving the era, and has invited the commission to develop a robust monitoring mechanism. a first progress report was presented by the commission on 20 september this year. close monitoring is essential. it enables us to track progress, and where necessary, identify areas where further work is needed or where new initiatives might be required. we remain fully committed to achieving an effective european research area. it is a vital tool to help us compete globally, to expand our knowledge and expertise, and to help deliver prosperity and progress for our citizens. i know that the parliament fully shares this objective, for which i am very grateful.
member of the commission. − madam president, i would like to thank you for giving the commission the opportunity to answer questions on the european research area. the european research area matters because it represents a structural reform and strengthening of a crucial sector of the economy – r&d – that underpins the entire knowledge economy in europe. we have set the goal of 3% r&d investment in the eu by 2020, but we cannot have increased investment without reform to ensure that our science systems spend the money usefully and efficiently. era has been around as a concept – as mrs sartori and the president said – since 2000, but when the european council set the deadline of 2014 for the completion of era, this concentrated our minds and acted as an impulse and impetus for the commission’s communication on era published in july 2012. we redoubled our efforts, identified the reforms and shortcomings that must be tackled and established the broader reinforced partnerships so that we could give era our best shot. the first era progress report, as you heard, was adopted on 20 september in time for the european council meeting this month where innovation is on the agenda. that report comes to some very interesting findings. for example, national research programmes still operate according to different rules, for example on reporting, which makes transnational research cooperation difficult. there are a host of barriers to research and mobility, including very limited accessibility to grants by non-nationals or portability of grants across borders. open, transparent and merit-based recruitment practices are still not broadly implemented for all research positions. for example, only 10% of vacancies are advertised at european level via the euraxess jobs portal. on gender, very disappointingly, only 34% of research performing organisations responding to our survey offer flexible careers and only 18% have recruitment and promotion practices specifically designed to combat the waste of female talent. this report is the first comprehensive analysis of era but it is very much a work in progress. we are pushing the member states to provide the data and information that we lack to carry out a more robust exercise next year. on the basis of this, we will take a long, hard look at what progress has been made and, on that basis, i will make recommendations to my successor on what needs to be done. the bottom line is that era is at a crossroads. we will need to take some very tough decisions next year. as i have said before, all options are on the table and nothing is ruled out. i am obviously very happy that the debate is taking place and will be delighted to answer questions that are raised by the members.
the commission's proposal for a directive on the protection of the environment against the adverse effects of certain substances and mixtures is a very good one. however, although european funds play an important role in our science and innovation system, i would like to remind you that 94% of research funding is still in national hands. the commission's proposal is to be submitted to the council for adoption by the end of the year. as the progress report on the era shows, progress has certainly been made in structuring the european research area, but not as much as we would like, largely because of the voluntary nature of the measures developed. at the same time, we have good examples - such as the eric regulation - showing how community legislation can overcome the obstacles to the free movement of both knowledge and researchers in europe. commissioner, i believe that if we want to have a strong and dynamic european science and innovation system, the time has come to deepen the construction of the era, also by going through the legislative process, and thus to really overcome the national, legislative and administrative barriers which still hinder the creation of a genuine internal market in knowledge.
member of the commission. − mr president, first of all let me thank all those speakers – because we have had a lot of speakers, it has been a very lively debate – and i think we owe a debt of gratitude to mrs sartori and mr berlinguer for organising the debate. i think generally there has been a great convergence on the objectives of era, and there is a feeling (which i also have myself) of impatience at the lack of progress and a great sense of urgency about what needs to be done. next year, obviously, we are going to have this major reflection that i talked about, so in other words it is crunch time for era next year and – as i said at the beginning and i repeat again – nothing is off the table, everything is on the table. remember that whatever we decide to do, the european parliament is going to be a very important partner with us in going forward. i was asked a number of specific questions. about the eit: this of course is the knowledge triangle so fundamentally important to all we are trying to do. the jrc, giving scientific advice to all of our policy, must be based on the best, most excellent scientific advice that is available and that advice is given right across the commission in all the different directorates-general. i was also asked about synergies with the structural funds. johannes hahn and i have worked really closely to ensure that we have this synergy – and you know, mr van nistelrooij, that for the first time ever in horizon 2020 you can match structural funds with horizon 2020 funds in the same project, for different aspects of it, but in the same project. i think that is a really great step forward. another question was: is it the intention of the commission to standardise european research systems? nothing could be further from the truth. of course we are not in the business of doing this, but we would like them to align their rules so that we can have this great interaction that we want to see happening in a genuine european research area. the difference in salaries and the brain drains occupied the minds of the council of ministers when we met last november in luxembourg. one of the aspects that we worked out at the time was that we would have a specific package of proposals that would help to counteract this innovation divide, this difficulty that particularly newer member states and indeed regions within europe have. so we have this whole package of era chairs, of the teaming, of the twinning actions, of the bonus in salaries of up to eur 8 000 all designed to help combat the brain drain. obviously, we will look at that when we have the interim evaluation to see how well that is working. i believe that it is going to work really well. to the council i would say: obviously we in the commission, but also – as you have heard, mr president – all of the members here, are looking to the council at the end of this month to give us the kind of strong conclusions that will drive us forward. i would say that president grybauskaitė, who has long experience in the commission, will understand the kind of impetus that a strong conclusion from the european council can give both the commission and indeed the european parliament. i am delighted that mrs sartori and mr berlinguer will bring forward an era manifesto which will be, as they describe, a concrete roadmap for era policy and i look forward very much to joining them on 16 october 2013 for the launch of the manifesto.
president-in-office of the council. − mr president, it is a very pleasing to participate in a debate in which i can clearly support nearly everything that was said. i wish to thank all the members for their questions and remarks. i very much welcome the commitment of this parliament to help support the creation of a fully-fledged european research area. lithuania has had research and innovation high on its presidency agenda. together with the commission, we will launch the horizon 2020 programme during the ict 2030 conference in vilnius on 6 to 8 november. i would like to take this opportunity to welcome to this landmark event all those interested. moreover, as the commissioner mentioned, we have been actively preparing for the october european council, which will focus on innovation and ict issues. this will, i am sure, give very clear guidance to our further work in this regard. by way of conclusion to this afternoon’s debate, i should like to refer to the most recent exchange of views between ministers on era, which took place on 27 september. the debate that our ministers held answered many of the questions that were raised during this afternoon’s discussion. the ministerial discussions confirmed our shared commitment to the successful completion of era. many ministers underlined the importance of promoting research and innovation as a driver of the economy and as potential provider of new jobs. specific points raised included: the need for better and increased use of public administration tools to foster innovation, particularly through public procurement procedures; on behalf of the s&d group. mr president, it is truly unusual for us to be having this debate in the european parliament today on a convention dating from 2011 which has not yet been ratified by the majority of the member states of the european union. i have listened carefully to the council, i have listened carefully to the commission and i think that the time for complacent speeches is over, because while we are listening to these speeches, every day thousands of women are having their lives cut short by men who kill them for the simple fact that they are women. we are talking about a violation of human rights, about the need to ratify this convention so that the member states can assume legal responsibilities, which they must apply to combat the greatest social laceration that exists at the moment in the world and in the european union. i also take this opportunity to urge the spanish government to ratify, to expedite all the procedures for ratifying this convention. it is not surprising that a country that was a pioneer in the european union with the implementation of the law against gender violence to date has not yet ratified it. finally, the socialist and democratic group has been calling for some time now and demanding that the commission take all the necessary initiatives to ensure that there is a legislative legal framework in the european union to combat violence against women.
on behalf of the green group, i am facing this debate today shocked after hearing about the death of a 14-year-old girl in tárrega at the hands of an 18-year-old boy. unfortunately, this is not unusual in the european union: in spain, since 2003, more than 600 women have been killed by men because of the fact that, as my colleague iratxe garcía said, they were women. and this is not just something to condemn: it is something to tackle; it is something to end; it is something to eliminate, once and for all, from our realities, in europe and the rest of the world. it is not a problem that can be reduced to a question of age, a question of geography, or even social status. it is a universal problem, it is a universal issue, it is a universal challenge and a universal obligation that must be met. the istanbul convention is therefore one instrument among many others which needs to be led, but it is also necessary to take account of its insufficiency. it is incomprehensible, in any case, that so many countries, including spain, have still not ratified the istanbul convention, and that only two of the european union have taken this step. it is urgently and fundamentally necessary to resolve this question, but it is also very necessary - and i ask commissioner de gucht to convey to commissioner reding our request - that we at european level provide ourselves with the legal framework necessary to be able to combat this scourge with all the instruments at our disposal. if we do not have the basic instruments to be able to combat this issue, it will be very difficult for us to move from rhetoric to action. and that is why it is so important that we ratify the istanbul convention as soon as possible, but also, and above all, that the european union should have the necessary instruments to do what it has to do, which is to put an end to this question once and for all.
member of the commission. − mr president, i would like to thank colleagues for this very instructive debate in which a number of practical and political questions have also been put. for example, what is the commission doing to encourage the signing of the convention? in april 2013, for example, the commission organised an exchange on national good practice in spain on combating violence against women, where a council of europe representative promoted the convention. but of course all of you come from a member state, and up to now only two member states have ratified it. maybe it would also make sense that, at a national level, you insist that your national parliaments follow the proper procedures and complete the ratification, because in quite a few cases it is not a question of their being against a convention of the council of europe but simply that it is not a priority on the agenda of national parliaments. i think you should act on this at a national level as well. let me also comment on mrs ronzulli’s remark that there are so few people in this room. this is true, and it is a scandal, but maybe mrs ronzulli should also ask herself where she is when other topics are being discussed. the most important political question that was put was of course whether the commission is going to bring forward a legal instrument aimed at combating violence against women. i have to say that the commission does not intend to adopt any specific criminal legislation on violence against women, as violence against women is not among the so-called ‘euro-crimes’ that are listed in article 83 of the lisbon treaty, and in principle is not a transnational form of crime. i will read out article 83 to you: ‘the european parliament and the council may, by means of directives adopted in accordance with the ordinary legislative procedure, establish minimum rules concerning the definition of criminal offences and sanctions in the areas of particularly serious crime with a cross-border dimension resulting from the nature or impact of such offences or from a special need to combat them on a common basis. ‘these areas of crime are the following: terrorism, trafficking in human beings and sexual exploitation of women and children, illicit drug trafficking, illicit arms trafficking, money laundering, corruption, counterfeiting of means of payment, computer crime and organised crime. ‘on the basis of developments in crime the council may adopt a decision identifying other areas of crime that meet the criteria specified in this paragraph. it shall act unanimously after obtaining the consent of the european parliament’. that is the reason why we do not take an initiative in this respect, but the commission will assist member states in the implementation of recent eu legal measures adopted in the areas of civil and criminal justice, for example the victims directive and the european protection order. it will also closely monitor their effective implementation. the commission will also continue to develop targeted and consistent initiatives to support member states in achieving tangible results in eradicating all forms of violence against women, making full use of the eu competences.

mr president, china is the world's largest exporter, the third largest economy and an energy powerhouse. china is therefore a priority and an opportunity for the european union. but there are problems: there are problems like counterfeiting - 54% of counterfeits that enter the european union come through china. in 1979, china recognizes intellectual property rights; in 2010 it enters the wto. he makes legislation, but he doesn't enforce it. that's the problem. and imports of technology can profoundly harm industry, such as photovoltaic panels. it's also the number one emitter of co2. there is social dumping. there are problems of fighting organised crime. in our ports - in the port of valencia, in my community - we detect the massive entry of containers with a lot of forged documents, in other words, money laundering. this agreement can be an opportunity to impose the legislative constraints and also to mark reciprocity. it is essential that this be recognised in this agreement.
mr president, i think it is important to welcome this agreement. the commissioner has said that this agreement will help to increase investment on both sides, investment which we certainly need in europe. it will also help to protect european investment in china, which is undoubtedly capital. it is also an agreement which comes at a very important time for europe, because we are all aware that the internationalisation of our economy will be one of the pillars of economic recovery. i therefore stress the importance of this agreement. our partner, china, is one of the major players in the global economy. the constant economic development of the region is also of great importance. the new shanghai free trade zone has recently come into force, an experiment that will undoubtedly have consequences for the chinese economy. in addition, china has recently decided to join the negotiations of the services agreement known as tisa. so, it's about time. it's time to try and tackle these negotiations. i would also encourage the commissioner, as he has said, to address market access. but, finally, i would like to stress that it is important to solve the wine problem, which is a very important sector for countries like spain.
madam president, given that taiwan is the 18th largest economy in the world, the economic relationship between the union and taiwan is very remarkable and very necessary. their trade relations have increased more than twelvefold in the last few decades, and now, with the possibility of a trade agreement, we could consolidate and, of course, intensify these relations. the economic factors, ladies and gentlemen, together with the high democratic standards, make taiwan a very important strategic partner. i would therefore encourage the commission, mr de gucht, to start negotiations on trade and investment agreements with taiwan. i shall quote a few facts to illustrate my request. taiwan became a full member of the world trade organization in 2002; in 2010, visa liberalisation was approved in this house - i was the rapporteur. in june 2010, taiwan signed the ecfa agreement and the agreement on intellectual property rights with the people's republic of china. it has also concluded 31 bilateral investment agreements with a number of countries, including japan, and has resumed its talks on the framework agreement with the united states. taiwan and singapore, as noted above, concluded their negotiations for an economic cooperation agreement and, without having diplomatic relations with new zealand, taiwan signed its first economic agreement with new zealand. finally, madam president, ladies and gentlemen, taiwan has free trade agreements with panama, el salvador, honduras, guatemala and nicaragua. it is therefore very important that the commission should start negotiations on the trade and investment agreement as soon as possible.
mr president, the resolution on the conflict in syria which is to be voted on in the european parliament is a call for the european union to exercise its responsibility to protect the syrian people and therefore to express not only compassion but solidarity, and to do so by appealing to the responsibility of the member states and of the union as a whole. it is not enough to simply provide economic support to the border countries which are receiving these millions of displaced persons: the european union must make full use of the instruments at its disposal - because we are facing a full review of the common european asylum system - in order to apply article 25 of the visa regulation, which allows the issuing of visas on humanitarian grounds; to implement article 5 of the schengen borders code regulation, which allows temporary admission precisely on humanitarian grounds; to make full use of the resources available in the resettlement programme of the european asylum and migration fund; to use the available resource of permanent residence and not only temporary residence; to ensure that the burden is not only borne at this time by the countries which have experienced the greatest flows - germany and sweden - but by the union as a whole, and that the inadmissible practice is put to an end and the principle of international law, non-refoulement, is countered.

madam president, commissioner, it is clear that this directive is an important step which will help european professionals to carry out their work in any state of the union. in my view, the directive has a very important weak point. although it is stated that the recognition of a professional qualification requires knowledge of the language of the member state in which the profession is to be practised, in practice only the official language of the state will be taken into account. it is not ensured that in nations and regions where there is also another language other than the official language of the state, such as basque in the basque country, knowledge of it must be demonstrated. a doctor could practice in the basque country, catalonia, galicia, corsica or brittany without knowing the language of those nations, with the communication problem with his patients that this entails. this is not a fair situation and does not comply with the union's basic principles of respecting and preserving the linguistic diversity of europe. as it is written, it may prevent the requirement of language proficiency in basque to practice in the basque country. i therefore ask you to vote against the second part of amendment no 160. ladies and gentlemen, the world is going through a profound crisis which is shaking up previously prosperous economies. despite these difficult circumstances, europe remains the leading partner of an africa which is the repository of one third of the world's natural resources, has a vibrant youth and is now positioned as one of the most promising markets for the future. on both sides, we have a historic opportunity to strengthen our relations and to boost trade and investment for more growth, jobs and shared prosperity. in a context of openness and globalisation, we must also bear in mind the competition that opens africa to the rest of the world, and the rest of the world to africa. it is by improving our procedures and methods, by reducing the time taken to design and implement our projects and programmes that our partnership will be able to live up to our ambitions and the requirements of competitiveness. at the same time, let us work together to bring the negotiations on the economic partnership agreements to a successful conclusion. this is not an easy job, my friends. from africa, i can tell you that it raises concerns and questions because it gives the impression of challenging an agreed asymmetrical solidarity. the fear is that these agreements will have a negative impact on our customs revenue and damage our still embryonic industrial fabric. but i believe in the virtue of dialogue between partners in good faith to identify the impact of epas and to define predictable and effective accompanying measures to serve our common interests. the economic community of west african states (ecowas) is preparing for this with an extraordinary summit in dakar in a few days' time. this is an opportunity for me to welcome the remarkable work being done by the acp-eu joint assembly in this regard. i believe in renewed african-european cooperation, with access to energy, modernisation of agriculture, infrastructure development, education, training and youth employment as its main priorities. the promotion of training and employment for young people is not only a matter of social justice, but also and above all of protecting young people from the feeling of abandonment and despair which is the source of extremist tendencies and fuels the networks of illegal immigration, of which the recent tragedy in lampedusa is a tragic illustration. i would also like to talk to you about the high priority we give to energy and infrastructure as factors for growth and integration in africa. and that's the focus of the africa infrastructure development program, pida, which contains 51 priority projects at a total cost of $68 billion over the 2012-2020 period. as chairman of the nepad steering committee, i invite our european partners, who know africa better than anyone, to join us in making this new initiative a reality, because the spirit of nepad is less about aid than about investing in profitable projects for a win-win partnership. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, when my fellow citizens put their trust in me last year, they expressed a strong desire for change in the public governance of the country. with my team, i set about the task by implementing a comprehensive programme of good governance and institutional reforms to consolidate our democratic tradition, promote development and lay the foundations for better social justice. it is in this capacity that i have taken the exceptional decision to initiate a constitutional reform to bring back the seven-year term for which i was elected to a five-year term renewable once. (applause) i would like to thank my ambition for senegal is to work towards strengthening our democracy, towards a society that fights impunity, injustice and misgovernance, a society that feeds on our values of solidarity and sharing. and in this march of progress for senegal and africa, there is room for europe and each of its nations represented here, in the name of our common destiny, in the name of our shared values, and by virtue of the bonds of fidelity, of faithful friendship, which unite us. thank you for your kind attention. mr president, there is an error in the amendment which is, moreover, a very clear error: where it says after it should say before. i mean, the other way around. i have spoken to other political groups and they agree. the result would be:projects for which the request for development consent was introduced before. this is against retroactivity, we are voting against retroactivity, that is to say, we are advocating that projects which are already in the bureaucratic system and have been started do not have to apply the new legislation.
is what you are proposing a technical correction, which the whole house should agree to, or is it an oral amendment?

in writing. - i voted against this report because i consider that this interinstitutional agreement represents another setback for the imposition of austerity policy in europe. the agreement provides for the introduction of european parliament control of the accounts and activities of the european central bank. the report introduces the rules on the control to which the ecb will be subject, but this is an integrated control within the single supervisory mechanism. the mechanism is a tool designed to remove the sovereignty of the member states in favour of the markets, by requiring that not only monetary operations but also the fiscal policy of the member states must conform to the criteria imposed by the ecb, which are the opinions of international capital. that is why i voted against this report.
in writing. − i voted in favour. the interinstitutional agreement under consideration is the result of complex negotiations that ended in early september 2013, enabling parliament to approve the regulation on the single supervisory mechanism (ssm). the european council of 28-29 june 2012 had called for the establishment of a banking union for countries in the euro area, based on three pillars: a single banking supervision system, a european resolution fund (mechanism) to deal with bank failures and a european deposit guarantee scheme. the commission’s proposals on the ssm, which confer on the european central bank the task of supervising the banks of both the eurozone and any member states wishing to participate in the ssm, were adopted on 12 september 2012. the day after these proposals were adopted by the commission, parliament adopted a resolution on proposals for a european banking union (ebu), stressing that ‘any major change in supervision, including shifts to other institutions, must be accompanied by an equivalent increase in transparency and accountability of such institutions vis-à-vis parliament, which must have full questioning rights and full powers in relation to appointment and budgetary procedures’.
in writing. − the european central bank will assume, in accordance with the treaties, banking supervision tasks in the euro area and in the other member states participating in the new single supervisory mechanism. this is the first pillar of banking union, which is essential to break the vicious circle between private and sovereign debt and to strengthen economic and monetary union. the interinstitutional agreement adopted this morning ensures that the transfer of supervisory powers from the member states to the community level is carried out without democratic deficit and under the control of the european parliament. as rapporteur of the s&d group on the new legislative package, i participated in the negotiation of this agreement which ensures transparency, accountability and accountability for the ecb in the exercise of its supervisory tasks. the european parliament will have a decisive role in the appointment of the chair of the supervisory board, will receive information and will be able to conduct investigations on the functioning of the new supervisory authority, among other aspects. it shall ensure the effectiveness of community legislation and the proper performance of its supervisory tasks within the framework of a code of conduct applicable to its staff.
in writing. - i voted in favour of this decision because i think it is a good proposal for the proper functioning of this type of multilateral delegation of the european parliament. the report sets out the number of components for each of the delegations of this type that exist in the ep to redeploy its members in the light of the latest changes. it also provides for the disappearance of the eu-croatia joint delegation on the occasion of its definitive accession to the union. it is a technical decision which allows parliament to function properly and does not contain any controversial points. that is why i voted in favour of this decision.
in writing. − in favour. no problems with accepting the new proposal of seats.
in writing. - i voted in favour of this report because it delays the adoption of the management plan proposed by the european council and the council of the european union. my opposition to this discharge, as well as that of my group in this parliament, is based on two points: firstly, these institutions make an inefficient use of resources and have been accused of a lack of transparency in their expenditure items and secondly, this procedure for the approval of extraordinary management violates the principles of democratic control of the budget of the european institutions. in addition, the council does not answer the questions of the committee responsible by rejecting the legitimacy and scope of democratic control of european accounts. it is to curb the council's intention to operate independently of the control of the other institutions of the union that i have voted in favour of this report.
in writing. − in favour. in the annual report concerning the financial year 2011, the court of auditors included observations on the european council and the council concerning procurement procedures relating to cleaning services and the purchase of service clothing and shoes, in which certain weaknesses in the application of selection and award criteria were identified.
in writing. - i voted in favour of the zanoni report on the assessment of the impact of certain public and private projects on the environment. there are no economic excuses for not carrying out an adequate environmental risk assessment of certain practices that have been shown to be potentially dangerous. we are talking about sustainable development, human security and the safeguarding of the environment. we cannot avoid this by justifying the increase in the cost of production. this report directly concerns my region, cantabria, where there is a growing interest in extracting shale gas by fracking. the evidence that it is a dangerous technique in the form of earthquakes and polluted water, and the absence of a safe technology support my stance against this technique. today we are asking in this report that before any extraction is carried out, it should be ensured that any drilling in the area does not also pose any risks to the environment or to the inhabitants. the moratorium decided by the regional government is not enough: it has to be the central government that considers the decisions we are taking from the eu.
in writing. - i think that the renewal and strengthening of the environmental impact directive is very important. it is important, among other things, because of the pressure that energy lobbies are exerting to push for the exploitation of shale gas by hydraulic fracturing, which will now have to overcome stricter environmental requirements. i voted in favour for that reason, among others.
in writing. - i'm with you. today's vote is very important because it will allow us to better predict and assess the impact of activities and projects that affect our environment before they are implemented. avoiding, reducing or offsetting negative impacts on climate, environment, biodiversity and health is no longer an option but an obligation. the commission has also proposed that the european parliament should be consulted on the draft directive on the protection of the environment. we hope that the spanish state will transpose this directive as a matter of urgency and apply it retroactively, exceptionally, to projects which have proved to be environmental failures, such as the castor project. despite pressure from the oil industry lobbies and some member states, exploration and exploitation of shale gas will be subject to this regulation. the european parliament is committed to transparency and public participation with this vote. this is a major breakthrough that confirms that fracking should be banned in europe. the icv and the greens continue to stand with the anti-fracking social movements in europe.
in writing. - i voted in favour of this report because it proposes a revision of directive 94/25/ec setting stricter limits for nox and hydrocarbon emissions from the construction of new recreational craft. this restriction follows an environmental impact report by the european commission on motor vessels which highlights the need to reduce emissions and noise levels from such vessels. the report, however, defends a measure which should be criticised because it accepts an extension of almost six years for the industry to adapt, and does not include limits on the noise level of the vessels in question. it is a proposal which does not address the environmental impacts which the commission had pointed out, but i have voted in favour of it by imposing stricter limits on pollution from such vessels.
in writing. − in favour. this is an update of the recreational craft directive 94/25/ec (and subsequent amending directive 2003/44/ec) to set pollutant (nox, hydrocarbons, particulate matter and noise) limits for new recreational crafts (boats) placed on the eu market, in line with technological development, international standards and the new legislative framework. com also proposed to enlarge the scope to include personal watercraft (powered surfboards etc). nlf means inclusion of provisions describing inclusion of economic operators, competencies of conformity assessment bodies and market surveillance authorities, new conformity assessment modules and ce marking.
mr president, i abstained on this initiative, which is good for professional mobility at the expense of bilingual linguistic communities such as the basque country. the host state of a professional shall check whether he or she knows the language provided that it is an official language in europe. official national languages such as basque and others are automatically excluded. if, as the commissioner has said, all people and all territories are necessary for growth and competitiveness, what should we think if we do not see ourselves recognized and respected in it? what will commissioner vassiliou think? the problem is that negotiations are always with the member states alone, which, as in the case of spain, are an obstacle to the real recognition of linguistic rights. it is also inconsistent with the decision of this parliament, which recently approved the alfonsi report on the protection of minority languages. in writing. - it is clear that this directive is an important step which will help european professionals to carry out their work in any state of the union. in my view, the directive has a very important weak point. although it is stated that the recognition of a professional qualification requires knowledge of the language of the member state in which the profession is to be practised, in practice only the official language of the state will be taken into account. in countries and regions where there is another language other than the official language of the state, such as basque in the basque country, there is no requirement to prove knowledge of it. a doctor could practice in the basque country, catalonia, galicia, corsica or brittany without knowing the language of those nations, with the communication problem with his patients that this entails. that is not fair, and it is not in keeping with the union's basic principles of respecting and preserving the linguistic and cultural diversity of europe. as it is written, it may prevent the request for language proficiency in basque to practice in the basque country. as the second part of amendment no 160 has been passed, i decided that i could not vote in favour and i abstained.
in writing. - i could not vote in favour of this report because, although it improves the recognition of professional qualifications between member states, it does so with the intention of improving flexibility and adapting them to the interests of the common market. the report goes into detail on the technical aspects of administrative cooperation between member states through the electronic information system for the internal market (imi), the introduction of a professional card for the recognition of professional qualifications at european level. the report makes a controversial point about the recognition of nurses across the continent. i could not therefore vote in favour of this report.
in writing. − abstention. despite a rather good text, the fact (again) of enforcing that each member state will have only one official language considered is something we cannot accept. in many states there are several languages that need to be taken into account. for that reason, i abstained.
in writing. − labour mobility is one of the great benefits of the eu and in order to promote the free movement of professionals, the creation of a european professional card has been deemed necessary. the main purpose of this card is to facilitate the recognition of professional qualifications in cases where a professional establishes himself in another member state for the purpose of carrying out his activity. the directive also provides for a partial restriction of access to another member state, by means of 'fitness tests', but only in order to ensure that professionals who move are qualified in their country of origin in order to be able to practise in another member state. i believe it is important to provide those professionals who wish to pursue their activity in another member state with all the means necessary to access that activity on equal terms; this directive will effectively regulate this process by recognising the professional competence of every eu citizen on an equal footing.
in writing. − i voted against the second part of amendment 160 because the current text excludes catalan as one of the languages that workers may know in order to satisfy the recognition requirements. the fact that the only languages included are those that are official at eu level undermines the position of the catalan language in the labour market.
in writing. - i voted in favour of this report because it implies the recognition of the human right to freedom of movement. visa policy is often used as a tool to restrict the exercise of this right by states. our position on the rights of migrants is that of full respect for their right to cross any border and any administrative limitation is in itself an attack on them. the development of such an agreement on visa facilitation with armenia is aimed at improving the rights of migrants and that is why i voted in favour of this report.
in writing. − in favour. the proposals seek to conclude two agreements with the republic of armenia. the first agreement concerns facilitation of travel. not yet visa-free, the agreement sets out simplified conditions for the issue of multiple-entry visas. the new rules will make the procedures quicker (the decision will have to be taken within 10 days, in urgent cases two days or less), cheaper (the visa fee for processing applications of armenian citizens shall amount to eur 35) and less bureaucratic (the documents to be presented regarding the purpose of the journey have been simplified for some categories of persons, in particular for close relatives, members of official delegations, students, teachers, business people, scientists, etc. and there are also simplified criteria for issuing multiple-entry visas). the armenian government already abolished the visa obligation for eu citizens, with effect from 10 january 2013. we approve the visa facilitation agreement. our amendment to postpone the entry into force of that agreement until a similar agreement with azerbaijan enters into force has been declared inadmissible.
in writing. - i voted against this report because the legal status of 'illegal resident' represents a denial by states of their responsibility as guarantors of the human rights of all human beings, regardless of the state from which they come. my rejection of the figure of 'illegal resident' is also because it is a tool for the administration to point out a group of people such as migrants. the administration points out that far-right groups are carrying out violent acts against them, inciting racial hatred as a way to solve the crisis. the administrations share responsibility for such acts, and that is why i voted against this report.
in writing. − against. the second agreement concerns readmission. the readmission obligation covers both own nationals and third-country nationals and stateless persons (if they have a visa, residence permit or have stayed on the territory of another party). the readmission obligation with regard to own nationals also covers family members (i.e. spouses and minor unmarried children). we approved the visa facilitation agreement. our amendment to postpone the entry into force of that agreement until a similar agreement with azerbaijan enters into force has been declared inadmissible. as regards the readmission agreement, we have serious concerns. on one hand, in accordance with article 72(1) of the partnership and cooperation agreement with armenia, there is a general obligation of readmission of nationals. on the other, the present agreement also covers third-country nationals and stateless persons. armenia has a number of ethnic armenian refugees from azerbaijan, whose situation is not properly resolved. besides, we are against linking visa facilitation with readmission as such. thus, we reject the readmission agreement.
in writing. - i voted against this report because it represents a step backwards in the improvement of consumer information systems in the field of food properties. food information systems are essential to ensure that consumers are able to make well-informed choices. this report seeks to reject the proposal for a council regulation establishing a list of permitted claims on the properties of food other than those relating to the reduction of disease risk and to the development of children. this regulation aims to improve the information available to consumers on the beneficial effects of food. i have therefore decided to vote against this report.
in writing. − against. this text opposes adoption of the draft commission regulation amending regulation (ec) 432/2012 establishing a list of permitted health claims made on foods, other than those referring to the reduction of disease risk and to children’s development and health and considers that the draft commission regulation is not compatible with the aim and content of the basic act.
in writing. - i voted in favour of this report because it rejects the commission proposal for a regulation on products of animal origin. the commission proposal in this area does not take into account the difficulty that slaughterhouses with a high volume of activity cannot monitor precisely each animal slaughtered. there are many risks for consumers in products of animal origin, and in slaughterhouses with more than 500 animals slaughtered per day it is difficult not only to detect health risks for consumers, but also to verify animal welfare, or any animal health problems that may reduce their market value. this proposal must be rejected in order to develop stricter legislation. i have therefore voted in favour of this report.
in writing. − in favour. it opposes the adoption of the draft commission regulation amending annexes to regulations (ec) no 853/2004, (ec) no 854/2004 of the european parliament and of the council and regulation (ec) no 2074/2005, considers that the draft commission regulation is not compatible with the aim and content of the basic act, and considers that measures proposed in the draft commission regulation should, in the first place, be considered in the context of the above-mentioned commission proposal on official controls, of 6 may 2013, before any specific measures on reducing control tasks of official veterinarians are taken.
in writing. - i could not vote in favour of this report because, although it presents positive aspects of the necessary economic cooperation with china, it only deals with compliance with international trade and investment agreements. the report makes no reference to political cooperation between the two powers, a debate which should be present in the negotiations without being intrusive. the report also introduces the obligation to comply with the general agreement on trade in services, the protection of intellectual rights, accepts the decisions of the international centre for settlement of investment disputes (icsid) to resolve investment problems. the report accepts the tools of neoliberalism for negotiations with china. that is why i could not vote in favour of this report.
in writing. − against. we have tabled a green alternative resolution: this is the first negotiation on an eu-china contractual relationship in trade and investment matters, which will receive quite a lot of attention. moreover, on such controversial issues as isds, where the outcome in inta is likely to be replicated in plenary, several meps from other groups (s&d, gue and alde) should have had redlines and thus support our broader line. we have also retabled our most important inta am to the main resolution with rcv attached to them in order to put pressure on such key issues as isds, hr impact assessment, consistency with the eu’s external action objectives or the preservation of policy space and capability of the parties to legislate.
in writing. − china is one of the world's leading investment markets and in the eu 26 of the 28 member states currently have bilateral investment agreements in force with china. the eu stresses the importance of greater economic, social and environmental engagement between the two in order to boost both economies by creating synergies that would promote competitiveness and ensure greater transparency. the common objective of both is sustainable growth and job creation and to this end the eu sees the need to strengthen cooperation and dialogue, which are indispensable to improve investment relations. the eu has expressed the urgency of a change in china's attitude to minimally guarantee these rights. this report sets out the guidelines to be followed in order to promote and protect investors and i believe that if china succeeds in making its economic and social policies more flexible and bringing them closer to the european regulatory framework, it will be possible to encourage smes to have greater access to external markets in the future, thus boosting their internationalisation.
in writing. − even though i understand that some sectors are more vulnerable than others, when it comes to starting a negotiation between two parties it is important that we keep everything on the table. this is why i have voted in favour of amendment 26 to the text. the overall package is clearly in the interest of the majority of stakeholders and we cannot lose this window of opportunity for setting up the negotiations.
in writing. - i voted against this report because it represents a firm commitment to neoliberal institutions and at the same time it may lead to diplomatic problems with the people's republic of china. the report is a political assessment of the relationship between the two countries, and this assessment is strongly interventionist in nature, since it considers the european model of representative democracy, which is currently in crisis, to be the only one acceptable in the rest of the world. the report also stresses the need to ensure that the eu is able to take full advantage of the opportunities offered by the new technologies. i have therefore voted against this report.
in writing. − against. the majority in inta was in favour of ‘urging the commission to start talks for eu-taiwan investment agreements’. moreover, such over-simplistic considerations as the fact that ‘any decision to start negotiations should be based on economic reasons and should not be interlinked with the evaluation of bilateral relations between the eu and the people’s republic of china’ also went through. our position was that we did not share the sense of urgency in asking the commission to launch negotiations, not only for the reasons outlined in the background, but also because the eu and taiwan are already well integrated economically, tariffs are already generally at low levels on both sides and the eu is already taiwan’s main investment partner. moreover, the parties already have a well institutionalised dialogue on trade and investment issues aimed at tackling bilateral irritants. given the overstretched staff resources of dg trade (and inta and the ep have already acknowledged this issue many times), such a push on the commission would be in contradiction with the request to focus on real priorities. moreover, we, as greens, are generally critical of a systematic recourse to bilateral negotiations.
in writing. − i support this motion for eu-taiwan trade relations because this is a win-win situation for both economies and access to this market has true potential for our companies. i also hope that this is a step forward to sharing european values such as democracy, the respect for human rights and the rule of law.
in writing. - i voted against this report because it involves a worsening of the working conditions of pilots which may lead to an increase in the risk for passengers. this report clearly implies the introduction of the will of the airline lobbies into the policy proposed by the european commission. there is no scientific argument to ensure that the working hours imposed by this report are safe, and on the contrary, there is a very large number of arguments that claim an increase in risks. pilots take a major responsibility for the lives of passengers and airlines have managed to reduce their labour costs at the expense of safety. this increase in risks for passengers is intolerable and that is why i voted against this report.

member of the commission. − mr president, i would like to thank eva joly for asking this question. it enables me, on behalf of the high commissioner, to discuss the very important matter of caste-based discrimination in several world societies. we are strongly committed to fighting all forms of discrimination. combating discrimination is high on the list of human rights priorities in the current eu strategic framework and action plan on human rights and democracy. caste-based discrimination is an essential part of it. the eeas, the commission and member states make use of a number of tools and instruments such as bilateral dialogue and eu financial support to civil society organisations. caste-based discrimination is systematically included in our regular human rights dialogue and in our regular contacts with human rights defenders. this concerns our partner countries in which this human rights issue is particularly relevant, such as india, nepal, bangladesh and pakistan, but also mauritania. the eu provides support to address caste-based discrimination and the consequences thereof by means of eu instruments, in particular the european instrument for democracy and human rights (eidhr). the eidhr strategy documents for 2011 to 2013 contain an explicit reference to caste-based discrimination. allow me to give you a practical example. in india, caste-based discrimination is considered a cross-cutting human rights and development issue and is included in many calls for proposals. the commission has funded projects worth eur 4 million on discrimination and violence against women and girls. we are also taking a multi-layered approach based on the promotion of human rights and the socio-economic and psychological emancipation of victims. development aid has supported initiatives that promote access to education, labour rights, and the rights of women and minorities. the eu funds several projects in bangladesh that focus on poverty reduction and the rights of the most vulnerable and impoverished groups. we are also funding projects that aim to improve access to justice for victims of caste-based discrimination. in this regard, the commission is devoting eur 30 million to projects in bangladesh and pakistan that aim to improve access to and the functioning of local justice and police systems. allow me to stress that humanitarian aid is always non-discriminatory, based on needs, and pays particular attention to the most vulnerable. consequently, humanitarian work funded by the european commission in south asia explicitly addresses caste-based discrimination and refers to the lowest castes as among the most vulnerable when taking funding decisions. at the multilateral level, we have been very active in the un context and have contributed to the work of the former un sub-commission for promotion and protection of human rights. we also contributed to the debate on caste-based discrimination in the un universal periodic review for india, pakistan, sri lanka, nepal and bangladesh. in conclusion, caste-based discrimination is a high priority for the eu. we want to combat it and we do so in the most comprehensive and member of the commission. − mr president, i know that this is a concern which this house has raised several times over the last month and we share the concerns about the human rights situation in russia. let me start by assuring you that the concerns expressed here have been met with determination and consistency in our response. from the outset the european union has made clear that we believe that russia should respect its international commitments and strive for a system fully based on the rule of law, respect for human rights and an ever more democratic society. we have repeatedly flagged the inconsistencies between these commitments and the new laws recently adopted on libel, treason, demonstrations, ngo foreign funding, blasphemy, so-called homosexual propaganda, as well as on internet control. the questions that you have raised essentially draw on two of these recent pieces of legislation: the law on foreign agents and the law on promotion of non-traditional sexual relations among children and minors, as it is called. i would like to highlight the ways in which we in the european union have reacted since last june. first, we have continued to pursue intensive diplomatic efforts to express our concerns with regard to the adoption and implementation of these laws. the high representative has reacted publicly every time new problematic laws were passed, which has made our position very clear and very well known. we have also systematically raised these issues in all our discussion with our russian counterparts. we are convinced that the law prohibiting so-called homosexual propaganda stigmatises particular groups and individuals and leads to violence. therefore, we have called on russia to amend this legislation in our human rights consultations, but also in other political dialogues. i, myself, have regular contact with the russian authorities especially from the ministry of justice and interior, and i have raised this question numerous times in moscow and in meetings here in brussels and elsewhere. we have also engaged in moscow in dedicated exchanges with representatives of the presidential council for civil society and human rights, who have been at the forefront of the proposals to amend these laws. these questions were raised at the yekaterinburg summit last june. in particular, vice-president/high representative ashton emphasised the eu concerns with the shrinking space for civil society, which is leading russia in the wrong direction. we further stressed the importance of having a better format for our human rights consultation, which in our view should take place in moscow and with the participation of russian ministers. the next round of talks is foreseen for the end of the year. thirdly, we have also been active on the multilateral front. most recently, the european union called upon the united nations human rights council on 17 september, during its 24th session, to pay urgent attention to the situation in russia with regard to these two pieces of legislation, and called upon the russian federation to uphold its commitment to protect the enjoyment of basic rights of expression, of assembly and of opinion by all. we invited russia to actively strive towards a more conducive attitude regarding the inclusion and tolerance of minorities in russian society. we have issued similar statements in the council of europe and in the osce. we very much hope that russia will look again at these texts and the implementation of the legislation and fully heed the recommendation by the venice commission, due early next year. the very existence of a number of human rights ngos in the russian federation is at stake. some of them, like golos, an election-monitoring organisation, have been closed or fined. around 70 organisations have been warned not to receive foreign funding, or have received a notice of violation according to which they should register as a ‘foreign agent’. this label is a clear attempt to discredit these organisations or to silence them through self-censorship, harassment, or by cutting down their sources of financing. therefore, our efforts have also aimed at continuing to support these ngos so as to help them continue their legitimate work. we believe that our support in areas as different as the rights of conscripts, the protection of journalists and minority rights contribute to the establishment of the rule of law in russia. we will continue supporting civil society organisations, notably through the eidhr in russia. we will continue to keep in constant contact, in moscow, in the regions and in brussels, with these organisations. the eu special representative for human rights, mr stavros lambrinidis, is engaged with human rights officials and with civil society and he will travel to russia at the end of this month. over the last month we took every opportunity to restate our firm support for their work, whilst stressing that they are not, in any way, anyone’s agent. this message was stressed during the visit of the eeas senior officials to russia at the end of september. it was repeated by eeas senior officials during the last general assembly of the eu-russia civil society forum just this monday and we also, together with the member states, engage actively in trial observation to assess the fairness of the justice system. the crackdown on civil society, the discrimination against sexual minorities and the persisting deficiencies in the rule of law will not be without effect on bilateral relations with russia. russia should know that these developments will not strengthen our relationship. we believe it is in russia’s best interest to foster the rule of law and to adopt legislation in conformity with its commitment and the values shared by the members of the council of europe. we stand ready to support russia, our neighbour and strategic partner, in doing so, in a frank and, we hope, constructive dialogue.
i would like to add my condolences to the family of mr martens, whose death we have just learned. but i want to pay tribute to him in the sense that everyone knows he was not from my 'political family' and yet both his and mine share a set of values which are linked to the issue we are discussing this morning: respect for human rights, respect for the human condition. the human condition can be violated in different ways, by different causes of inequality, by different failures to respect fundamental rights, and one of them, of course, has to do with the free choice of sexual orientation of each person. i therefore believe that when we are asking russia to respect the rule of law, we are not defending the rights of just a certain number of people, whether they are older or younger, but the rights of everyone, because it is the human condition that is put at risk when those rights are violated. i therefore encourage, support and encourage the work being done by the commission and mr lambrinidis. and we must send a clear message to russia - an important neighbour, as you have just said - that our whole relationship is a global relationship, and in that global relationship there are not only economic or energy interests: there are fundamentally the values we defend in the union.

member of the commission. − mr president, i would like first to thank the committee on international trade and, in particular, the rapporteur, mr proust, for the intensive work and constructive approach during the negotiation process. doing our utmost to prevent the manufacture of illicit drugs is, simply, our moral duty. in that regard, efforts made by the eu authorities and industry in controlling the external trade in certain legal substances used for the manufacturing of illicit drugs are already quite significant. but these efforts must now be extended to new substances that drug manufacturers are using in order to replace precursors which the existing legislation already controls. this is why i consider the amendment to the regulation on the international trade in drug precursors as a major step forward in our fight against the illicit manufacture of drugs. firstly, the regulation will respond to the united nations’ call for better monitoring of international trade in medicines containing ephedrine or pseudoephedrine. this will help to prevent their use in producing the illicit drug methamphetamine while maintaining fair access to medicines. secondly, the new regulation will provide the union with fast-reaction mechanisms to address trafficking trends in new chemicals used as drug precursors. it enables the relevant eu authorities to seize shipments of those chemicals if they have sufficient evidence that they are intended for the production of illicit drugs. furthermore, it foresees the possibility of incorporating newly-identified substances firstly into voluntary monitoring by the industry and, where necessary, into the list of substances formally controlled by the customs authorities. this is a major contribution to international efforts against the diversion of drug precursors and therefore a great achievement in the fight against the manufacturing of illicit drugs.
i am not saying that we should not be concerned about the drug problem, but that we should be concerned about the problem of drug trafficking. to date, medicinal products containing ephedrine and pseudoephedrine were excluded from controls. these commonly used medicines - as mentioned here - for colds and allergies, used by everyone, could be manipulated and from them could be extracted the so-called drug precursors, narcotics. this regulation controls the movement of these substances through customs. it has to be easy and accessible, simplified, free of cost. the rapporteur has had a very good idea, which is to simplify the report by adding a new category, and this opens up the way for the future in the face of new substances that may appear. the truth is that this little report is in favour of the fight against drugs. we hope that the meetings taking place in the framework of the codecision procedure will not hinder its development and will make it possible to implement this new regulation, which is an important contribution to the fight against drugs, as soon as possible.
